course.title: NumPy Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete Numerical Computing Program
course.tagline: Learn NumPy. Master Arrays. Build Data Science Skills.
course.description: NumPy from the first array to linear algebra, broadcasting, memory layout, random simulation and real Data Science workflows. Hinglish explanations, runnable code and ten practice sections per module.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic and an idea of what a matrix is
outcomes: Create and inspect ndarrays and reason about shape, size, ndim and dtype
Index, slice, reshape and broadcast arrays without Python loops
Use universal functions, aggregation and Boolean masks correctly
Tell a view from a copy and control memory usage
Generate reproducible random data and run Monte Carlo simulations
Solve linear systems and choose stable linear-algebra routines
Read and write numeric data with NPY/NPZ and text files
Handle NaN, infinity and masked arrays in real datasets
Vectorise code and benchmark it honestly
Move arrays between NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn

modules.title: NumPy Introduction and Fundamentals
modules.goal: Understand what NumPy is, why ndarrays beat Python lists for numeric work, and run your first array program.

topics.title: Create your first array
topics.body: np.array turns a Python list into an ndarray: one typed block of memory that supports vectorised maths, so mean() and shape are properties of the data rather than a loop you write.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a, a.mean(), a.shape)

topics.title: Vectorised arithmetic
topics.body: An operation between an array and a scalar is applied to every element by compiled code, which is why `a * 2` needs no loop and returns a new array instead of mutating `a`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a * 2)

topics.title: Typed memory, not a Python list
topics.body: Every ndarray has one dtype and a fixed itemsize, so nbytes tells you the real memory it occupies; a Python list stores pointers to separate objects and cannot answer that question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes)

topics.title: Two arrays combine elementwise
topics.body: Arithmetic between two same-shape arrays pairs position by position, so `a + b` is not concatenation and the result keeps the input shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)

topics.title: Indexing starts at zero
topics.body: The first element is index 0 and the last is -1, exactly like a Python list, so the same counting rules carry over before reshape changes anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Methods return plain results
topics.body: sum, min and max are methods on the array, so the answer arrives as a Python scalar you can print or compare without converting anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.sum(), a.max(), a.min())

topics.title: Convert back to a Python list
topics.body: tolist() turns an ndarray into nested Python lists, which is the right move when the receiver expects plain lists rather than array printing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Integers and floats carry different dtypes
topics.body: The dtype is inferred from the values you pass, so `np.array([1, 2])` is integer while `np.array([1.0, 2.0])` is float — one of them can hold 2.5 and the other cannot.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0, 2.0]).dtype)

topics.title: Add a scalar to every element
topics.body: A scalar is broadcast across the whole array, so one `+` replaces a loop. No Python-level iteration happens.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Compare an array with a scalar
topics.body: Comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape. That array is what every filter is built on.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 5, 9]) > 4)

topics.title: A Python loop still works over an array
topics.body: Iterating walks the first axis. It is fine for a handful of values and wrong for a million, where a vectorised expression wins.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

total = 0
for value in np.array([2, 4, 6]):
    total += int(value)
print(total)

topics.title: Every array reports its own type
topics.body: `np.array` always returns an `ndarray`. A Python `list` and an `ndarray` are not interchangeable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(type(np.array([1, 2])).__name__)

topics.title: Why NumPy exists
topics.body: A Python loop adds one number at a time and pays interpreter overhead per element; NumPy performs the same addition in compiled code over a contiguous buffer. That is the reason numerical work starts with an array, not a list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = [40, 55, 70, 85]
a = np.array(marks)
print(a.sum(), a.mean())
print(a.dtype, a.shape)

topics.title: An array versus a list
topics.body: A list can mix a string, a float and a nested list; an ndarray holds one dtype and reports one shape. Mixing types in an array silently promotes them all to a common dtype.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
mixed = np.array([1, 2.5, True])
print(mixed, mixed.dtype)

debug.title: The alias was never imported
debug.broken:
import numpy
print(np.arange(3))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3))
debug.error: NameError: name 'np' is not defined

debug.title: Assignment inside print
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a += 1)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
a += 1
print(a)
debug.error: SyntaxError: invalid syntax

debug.title: The array replaced the module name
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
np = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.arange(2))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.arange(2))
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'arange'

debug.title: The array was never built
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(arr.mean())
debug.error: NameError: name 'arr' is not defined
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(arr.mean())

debug.title: Text meets numbers
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]) + '3')
debug.error: numpy._core._exceptions._UFuncNoLoopError: ufunc 'add' did not contain a loop with signature matching types (dtype('int64'), dtype('<U1')) -> None
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]) + 3)

debug.title: A method name with a typo
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).meen())
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'meen'. Did you mean: 'mean'?
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).mean())

debug.title: Three values will not fit a 2x2
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2, 3]).reshape(2, 2))
debug.error: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 3 into shape (2,2)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]).reshape(2, 2))

debug.title: A total that was never defined
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2])
print(arr.sum() + total)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2])
total = 0
print(arr.sum() + total)
debug.error: NameError: name 'total' is not defined

debug.title: The maximum of nothing
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([]).max())
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([])
print(arr.max() if arr.size else "empty")
debug.error: ValueError: zero-size array to reduction operation maximum which has no identity

debug.title: An array has no append
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).append(3))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.append(np.array([1, 2]), 3))
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'append'

interviewBank.q: Why is a NumPy array faster than a Python list holding the same numbers?
interviewBank.answer: An ndarray owns one contiguous, typed block of memory, so arithmetic runs as one C loop over that block. A list stores pointers to Python objects, so every element costs a pointer chase, a type check and an allocation.

interviewBank.q: For `np.zeros((2, 3))`, how are `ndim` and `size` different?
interviewBank.answer: `ndim` is 2, the number of axes; `size` is 6, the number of elements. `shape` is the tuple `(2, 3)` that ties them together.

interviewBank.q: When would you still choose a Python list over an ndarray?
interviewBank.answer: When the data is heterogeneous, changes size constantly, or is really a record stream rather than a numeric block. An ndarray needs one dtype and pays a copy when it grows.

interviewBank.q: Why does the dtype belong to the array rather than to each element?
interviewBank.answer: One dtype per array lets NumPy store raw values in a typed buffer and pick a compiled loop for arithmetic. Per-element types would mean per-element checks, which is exactly the list overhead NumPy removes.

interviewBank.q: How does slicing a large array avoid copying memory?
interviewBank.answer: A slice only stores an offset, a shape and strides over the same buffer. No values move, so slicing a gigabyte costs a few numbers.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.array([1, 2.0])` contain floats?
interviewBank.answer: A single array needs one dtype, and NumPy promotes the integers to the common type float64 rather than keeping mixed values.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `np.array` and `np.asarray`?
interviewBank.answer: `asarray` returns the input unchanged when it is already an array of the requested dtype, while `array` copies by default.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `arr.sum()` over Python's `sum(arr)`?
interviewBank.answer: The method runs one compiled reduction over the buffer, while the builtin loops in Python with per-element overhead.

interviewBank.q: How do you get a plain Python number out of a one-element array?
interviewBank.answer: Call `.item()`, which returns a scalar rather than a 0-d array, or convert the single element with `int(...)`/`float(...)`.

interviewBank.q: A shop's daily sales are a Python list of 500 numbers and the total is needed once per page load. Why convert it to an array, and what is the cost of doing it on every request?
interviewBank.answer: An array makes the total one compiled reduction (`np.array(sales).sum()`) instead of a Python loop, but the conversion itself copies 500 values. Convert once when the data is loaded or cached, not on every request.

interviewBank.q: Marketing sends 30 marks as strings from a CSV. What breaks if you call np.array on them and then .mean()?
interviewBank.answer: np.array keeps them as a string dtype (or object), so .mean() raises because there is no numeric meaning. Convert with `.astype(float)` (or parse at load time) before any arithmetic.

defenseBank.q: Defend using NumPy rather than a list for 10,000 sensor readings.
defenseBank.answer: Ten thousand float64 values cost 80 KB contiguous instead of pointer-plus-object pairs, and one vectorised call replaces a Python loop. Filtering, averaging and slicing then operate without per-element overhead.

defenseBank.q: Why does `np.array([1, 2]) + 1` work while `[1, 2] + 1` raises?
defenseBank.answer: An ndarray implements elementwise arithmetic and broadcasts the scalar; a list only concatenates with another list, so adding an int is a type error.

defenseBank.q: A reviewer says NumPy is a thin wrapper over lists. Refute it.
defenseBank.answer: It owns its buffer, dtype, shape and strides, and its ufuncs run compiled loops over that buffer. A list has none of those properties, which is why NumPy can do arithmetic without allocating per element.

defenseBank.q: Defend using NumPy for a signal that must be filtered many times.
defenseBank.answer: The filter runs as vectorised arithmetic over one buffer, and repeated passes avoid per-element Python overhead. The same array can be reused without re-wrapping values.

defenseBank.q: Two arrays print the same numbers but behave differently. Explain why dtype is the reason.
defenseBank.answer: One may be integer and the other float, so division, overflow and equality all differ. Printing hides the dtype that decides those results.

defenseBank.q: Defend choosing an ndarray over a DataFrame for a single numeric column.
defenseBank.answer: There is nothing to label or align, so the frame only adds index bookkeeping. An array is smaller and its operations are the primitive ones the frame calls anyway.

defenseBank.q: Defend using `np.asarray` in a function that only reads its input.
defenseBank.answer: It avoids a copy when the caller already passes a matching array and still accepts plain lists, so the fast path stays fast.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `arr.tolist()` is expensive on a large array.
defenseBank.answer: Every element becomes a Python object, which discards the buffer advantage that made the array fast in the first place.

defenseBank.q: Defend keeping an array 2-D instead of squeezing it to 1-D.
defenseBank.answer: Squeezing changes the axis contract and the direction later broadcasts align to, so a shape that looked tidy can silently change results.

tasks.title: Mean of four readings
tasks.statement: Store the mean of `np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])` as a float in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = float(np.array([2, 4, 6, 8]).mean())
print(result)
tasks.hint: The array method `.mean()` returns a float already — no loop, no manual division.

tasks.title: How many above one
tasks.statement: Count how many elements of `np.array([0, 1, 2, 3])` are greater than 1 and store the count as an int in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int((np.array([0, 1, 2, 3]) > 1).sum())
print(result)
tasks.hint: Compare the array with 1 to get a boolean mask, then `.sum()` counts the True values.

tasks.title: Gap between largest and smallest
tasks.statement: Store the difference between the largest and smallest value of `np.array([3, 10, 7])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 10, 7])
result = int(a.max() - a.min())
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.max()` and `.min()` each return one value; subtract them and keep it an int.

tasks.title: ints become floats on request
tasks.statement: Build a float array from `[1, 2]` and store it in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.array([1, 2], dtype=float)
print(result)
tasks.check: assert result.dtype == np.float64 and np.allclose(result, [1.0, 2.0]), f'got {result!r} as {result.dtype}'
tasks.hint: Either pass `dtype=float` when building, or call `.astype(float)` afterwards.

tasks.title: Text keeps its values
tasks.statement: Store `np.array(['a', 'b'])` as a plain list in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.array(['a', 'b']).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.tolist()` returns plain Python strings, not NumPy scalars.

tasks.title: Shape of a nested list
tasks.statement: Store the shape of the array built from `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).shape
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.shape` is a tuple of axis lengths — store it unchanged.

tasks.title: Read the last value
tasks.statement: Store the last value of `np.array([5, 6, 7])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array([5, 6, 7])[-1])
print(result)
tasks.hint: A negative index counts from the end: `-1` is the last element.

tasks.title: Squares of a range
tasks.statement: Store the squares of 0, 1, 2 and 3 as a list in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (np.arange(4) ** 2).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: Square the whole array with `** 2`, then convert with `.tolist()`.

tasks.title: Product of three values
tasks.statement: Store the product of `np.array([2, 3, 4])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array([2, 3, 4]).prod())
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.prod()` multiplies every element; wrap the result in `int()`.

tasks.title: Sum of squares
tasks.statement: Store the sum of the squares of 1, 2 and 3, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int((np.arange(1, 4) ** 2).sum())
print(result)
tasks.hint: Square the array first, then reduce with `.sum()`.

tasks.title: Subtract two vectors
tasks.statement: Subtract `np.array([1, 2])` from `np.array([10, 20])` and store the list form in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (np.array([10, 20]) - np.array([1, 2])).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: Array minus array pairs positions; convert the result with `.tolist()`.

tasks.title: Halve a range
tasks.statement: Divide `np.arange(4)` by 2 and store the list form in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (np.arange(4) / 2).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: Divide the array by 2 — the result is float, so `.tolist()` gives 0.0, 0.5, …

tasks.title: Count every element
tasks.statement: Store the number of elements in `np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]).size)
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.size` counts all cells; `.shape` would count per axis instead.

tasks.title: Repeat a value four times
tasks.statement: Store four copies of 3 in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.repeat(3, 4)
print(result)
tasks.hint: `np.full(4, 3)` writes one value into four cells.

tasks.title: Element-wise product of two vectors
tasks.statement: Multiply `np.array([2, 3, 4])` by `np.array([3, 2, 1])` element by element and store the list form in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.multiply(np.array([2, 3, 4]), np.array([3, 2, 1])).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: `*` multiplies position by position; `@` would be matrix multiplication.

tasks.title: Booleans add up
tasks.statement: Store the number of True values in `np.array([True, False, True])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array([True, False, True]).sum())
print(result)
tasks.hint: A boolean array stores True as 1, so `.sum()` counts them.

tasks.title: Smallest of a small grid
tasks.statement: Store the smallest value of `np.array([[4, 2], [9, 1]])`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array([[4, 2], [9, 1]]).min())
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.min()` reduces every axis by default, whatever the shape.

tasks.title: Reciprocals of one and two
tasks.statement: Store the reciprocal of every value of `np.arange(1, 3)` as a list in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (1 / np.arange(1, 3)).tolist()
print(result)
tasks.hint: Divide 1 by the array; the result is float, then `.tolist()`.

tasks.title: Distance between two numbers
tasks.statement: Store the absolute difference between 3 and 8, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.abs(3 - 8))
print(result)
tasks.hint: `np.abs(3 - 8)` keeps the sign out of the answer; store an int.

tasks.title: Two arrays are equal
tasks.statement: Store whether `np.array([1, 2])` and `np.array([1, 2])` hold the same values, as a bool, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = bool(np.array_equal(np.array([1, 2]), np.array([1, 2])))
print(result)
tasks.hint: `np.array_equal(a, b)` returns a single bool, unlike `==` which returns a mask.

tasks.title: Axes of a two-row grid
tasks.statement: Store how many axes `np.zeros((2, 2))` has, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.zeros((2, 2)).ndim)
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.ndim` reports how many axes an array has.

tasks.title: Sum of six readings
tasks.statement: Store the sum of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` as an int in `result`.

tasks.title: Largest of six readings
tasks.statement: Store the largest value of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` as an int in `result`.

tasks.title: Smallest of six readings
tasks.statement: Store the smallest value of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` as an int in `result`.
tasks.solution:

print(result)

tasks.title: Mean rounded to two places
tasks.statement: Store the mean of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])`, rounded to two decimals, in `result`.

tasks.title: Count values above five
tasks.statement: Count how many values of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` are greater than 5 and store the count in `result`.
tasks.solution:

tasks.title: Shift every reading by ten
tasks.statement: Add 10 to every value of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` and store the list form in `result`.

tasks.title: First three readings

tasks.title: Last two readings

tasks.title: Reverse the readings

tasks.title: Square every reading

tasks.title: Spread of six readings
tasks.statement: Store the difference between the largest and smallest value of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` as an int in `result`.
tasks.solution:

tasks.title: Integer array kind
tasks.statement: Store the dtype kind of `np.array([3, 7, 2])` in `result` — it should be the single character numpy uses for integers.
tasks.solution:

print(result)

tasks.title: Array becomes a Python list
tasks.statement: Convert `np.array([3.5, 7.5])` to a plain Python list and store it in `result`.
tasks.solution:

print(result)
tasks.check: assert result == [3.5, 7.5] and isinstance(result, list), f'unexpected {result!r}'

tasks.title: Count the even readings
tasks.statement: Count how many values of `np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1])` are even and store the count in `result`.
tasks.solution:

print(result)

tasks.title: Total without a loop
tasks.statement: Build the array `np.array([4, 8, 15, 16])` and store its total, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([4, 8, 15, 16])
result = int(values.sum())
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.sum()` is the vectorised total.

tasks.title: Double, then take the first two
tasks.statement: Starting from `np.arange(1, 6)`, multiply every element by 2 and store the first two elements in `result`.
tasks.solution:

print(result)
tasks.hint: Multiply the array, then slice `[:2]`; `.tolist()` at the end.

tasks.title: Count the values above ten
tasks.statement: Count how many elements of `np.array([4, 11, 10, 15, 3])` are greater than 10 and store the count as an int in `result`.
tasks.solution:

a = np.array([4, 11, 10, 15, 3])
result = int((a > 10).sum())
print(result)
tasks.hint: Build the mask with `> 10`, then count with `.sum()`.

tasks.title: Back to a Python list

tasks.solution:

print(result)

learn.title: Create your first array
learn.body: np.array turns a Python list into an ndarray: one typed block of memory that supports vectorised maths, so mean() and shape are properties of the data rather than a loop you write.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a, a.mean(), a.shape)
learn.simple: Socho tumhare paas paanch chocolate hain aur tum unka total nikalna chahte ho. Python list me har chocolate alag pocket me hai; np.array unhe ek hi dabbe me line se rakh deta hai. Ab total, average ya shape poochhne par NumPy poore dabbe par ek saath kaam karta hai, ek-ek chocolate uthane ki zaroorat nahi.
learn.pro: np.array converts a Python sequence into an ndarray: one contiguous, typed buffer whose shape and values travel together. Because the data is homogeneous and contiguous, reductions and elementwise operations run in compiled loops rather than Python-level iteration, which is why a.mean() and a.shape are O(n) and O(1) respectively instead of a hand-written accumulator.
steps: Import NumPy as np — that alias is the convention every reader expects.
Pass a Python list to np.array; the values decide the dtype.
Read shape and dtype before printing values, so the data's structure is explicit.
learn.visual:
list:  [10, 20, 30, 40]
         ↓ np.array
array:  [10 20 30 40]   shape (4,)  dtype int64
learn.realWorld: A shop's daily sales arrive as a Python list; converting it once to an array makes the total, average and best day single calls instead of loops.
mistakes: Calling np.array() with no argument — it needs a sequence.
Comparing a list and an array with == and expecting a single True/False; NumPy returns an elementwise mask.
revision: np.array(sequence) → one typed, contiguous ndarray.
shape is the structure, dtype is the element type, and both are printed for free.

learn.title: Vectorised arithmetic
learn.body: An operation between an array and a scalar is applied to every element by compiled code, which is why `a * 2` needs no loop and returns a new array instead of mutating `a`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a * 2)
learn.simple: Vectorised ka matlab: ek hi instruction me poori list par kaam. `a * 2` likho to NumPy har number ko double kar deta hai, tumhe `for` loop likhne ki zaroorat nahi. Jaise teacher poori class ko ek saath 'page 10 kholo' bolti hai, har bachche ko alag se nahi.
learn.pro: A ufunc applies a scalar or array operand to every element through a compiled loop, so `a * 2` allocates one output array and performs no Python bytecode per element. The win is both asymptotic constant factor and cache-friendly traversal; it does not change the big-O of the operation itself, which is still linear in the number of elements.
steps: Write the arithmetic expression for one element, not a loop over elements.
Pass the array where the single value stood.
Print the result's shape to confirm it preserved the input shape.
learn.visual:
a        = [1 2 3]
a * 2    = [2 4 6]     one compiled pass, no Python loop
learn.realWorld: Converting a column of prices from dollars to rupees is one multiplication by the exchange rate, applied to every row at once.
mistakes: Writing a Python for loop anyway, which pays interpreter overhead per element.
Expecting an in-place change — the expression returns a new array.
revision: Vectorised code describes the whole array, not one element.
The result is a new array with the same shape.

learn.title: Typed memory, not a Python list
learn.body: Every ndarray has one dtype and a fixed itemsize, so nbytes tells you the real memory it occupies; a Python list stores pointers to separate objects and cannot answer that question.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes)
learn.simple: Python list me har cheez apni jagah baithi hoti hai — number, text, kuch bhi — isliye list ko har item ka address yaad rakhna padta hai. NumPy array me sab items ek hi type ke hote hain, isliye wo ek compact box jaisa hota hai aur `nbytes` se pata chal jata hai kitni jagah le raha hai.
learn.pro: An ndarray stores homogeneous elements in one buffer with a fixed itemsize; a Python list stores pointers to separately allocated objects plus per-object overhead. That is why nbytes is exact for an array while sys.getsizeof(list) only counts the pointer array, and why dtype changes trade range and precision against memory.
steps: Create the array and read dtype.
Multiply itemsize by size to confirm nbytes.
Create the same data as float64 and compare nbytes.
learn.visual:
int64  : 8 bytes × 5 = 40 bytes
float64: 8 bytes × 5 = 40 bytes
int8   : 1 byte  × 5 =  5 bytes
learn.realWorld: A million-row sensor log fits in 8 MB as float64 and 1 MB as int8 when the readings are small whole numbers.
mistakes: Assuming a Python list's memory is its element count — the list also stores pointers.
Downcasting without checking range, which silently wraps values.
revision: nbytes = itemsize × size.
dtype is a memory decision as well as a precision decision.

learn.title: Two arrays combine elementwise
learn.body: Arithmetic between two same-shape arrays pairs position by position, so `a + b` is not concatenation and the result keeps the input shape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)
learn.simple: Do arrays ko `+` karne par NumPy unhe jodta nahi, balki ghar-ghar jaakar jodta hai: pehla number pehle se, doosra doosre se. Isliye `[1, 2] + [10, 20]` ka answer `[11, 22]` aata hai, `[1, 2, 10, 20]` nahi — wo list wala kaam hai.
learn.pro: Binary ufuncs pair operands by position when their shapes broadcast, producing an array of the broadcast result shape. Addition is therefore not concatenation; concatenation is a separate reshaping operation (np.concatenate) with its own axis argument.
learn.syntax: a + b   |   a - b   |   a * b   |   a / b
steps: Confirm both arrays have the same shape.
Apply the operator; positions pair up.
Check the result shape matches the operands.
learn.realWorld: Adding yesterday's per-product sales to today's gives a per-product total, without touching product names or order.
mistakes: Expecting [1 2 3 10 20 30]; that is concatenation.
Mixing shapes that cannot broadcast and reading the error as a data problem.
revision: Arithmetic pairs positions, it does not append.
Shape errors are checked before the data is.

learn.title: Indexing starts at zero
learn.body: The first element is index 0 and the last is -1, exactly like a Python list, so the same counting rules carry over before reshape changes anything.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[0], a[-1])
learn.simple: Ginti 0 se shuru hoti hai, 1 se nahi. Pehla item `a[0]` hai, doosra `a[1]`, aur last item `a[-1]` se bhi mil jata hai. Ye rule Python list jaisa hi hai, isliye list wali aadat yahan bhi kaam karti hai.
learn.pro: Indexing is zero-based and negative indices count from the end, exactly as in Python sequences; on an ndarray the same rule generalises per axis for multidimensional arrays. Basic indexing returns a view, not a copy, so writes through the index mutate the original buffer.
steps: Count from zero to reach the first element.
Use a negative index to count from the end.
Slice with start:stop to take a range, remembering stop is excluded.
learn.realWorld: The first and last reading of a day are a[0] and a[-1]; the morning block is a[0:6].
mistakes: a[4] on a 4-element array — out of bounds, not the last element.
Expecting a[1:3] to include index 3.
revision: Zero-based, negative counts from the end.
Slices exclude the stop index.

learn.title: Methods return plain results
learn.body: sum, min and max are methods on the array, so the answer arrives as a Python scalar you can print or compare without converting anything.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.sum(), a.max(), a.min())
learn.simple: `a.sum()` ya `a.max()` likhne par jawab ek simple number hota hai, poora array nahi. Us number ko tum seedha print kar sakte ho, compare kar sakte ho, ya kisi doosre kaam me daal sakte ho.
learn.pro: Reduction methods return NumPy scalars (or arrays when axis is given), not Python ints/floats; they behave like numbers in arithmetic and printing but carry a dtype. Use axis to reduce along one dimension and keepdims to preserve rank for broadcasting against the original array.
steps: Call the reduction method directly on the array.
Print the value and its type to see it is a NumPy scalar.
Pass axis when the reduction should collapse only one dimension.
learn.realWorld: A dashboard needs one best score and one total; both come from methods, not loops.
mistakes: Calling the Python builtin sum(a) and losing dtype and speed.
Using axis on a 1-D array and expecting a different number.
revision: Reductions return scalars unless axis is given.
The method form is the vectorised one.

learn.title: Convert back to a Python list
learn.body: tolist() turns an ndarray into nested Python lists, which is the right move when the receiver expects plain lists rather than array printing.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.tolist())
learn.simple: Kabhi kisi function ko NumPy array nahi, simple list chahiye hoti hai. Tab `a.tolist()` use karo — array wahi rehta hai, bas uski list wali copy mil jati hai jise koi bhi Python code samajh leta hai.
learn.pro: tolist() recursively converts an ndarray to nested Python lists, turning NumPy scalars into native ints/floats. It is a copy, so later changes to the array do not appear in the list; it is the right boundary when an API requires plain Python containers or JSON serialisation.
steps: Call tolist() on the array.
Check the result contains native ints/floats rather than NumPy scalars.
Pass that list to the API or JSON encoder that needed it.
learn.realWorld: A JSON endpoint cannot serialise an ndarray; tolist() is the one-line boundary fix.
mistakes: Believing tolist() changes the original array — it returns a copy.
Serialising the array directly and getting a TypeError.
revision: tolist() is a copy to plain Python containers.
Use it at the boundary, not inside numerical code.

learn.title: Integers and floats carry different dtypes
learn.body: The dtype is inferred from the values you pass, so `np.array([1, 2])` is integer while `np.array([1.0, 2.0])` is float — one of them can hold 2.5 and the other cannot.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0, 2.0]).dtype)
learn.simple: Agar tum `np.array([1, 2])` likhte ho to NumPy sochta hai 'ye pure number hain' aur integer array banata hai — isme 2.5 nahi rakha ja sakta. `[1.0, 2.0]` likho to float array banta hai, jo decimal sambhal leta hai.
learn.pro: dtype is inferred from the input values: an all-integer sequence yields a platform int (int64 on 64-bit), a sequence containing a float yields float64. Integer arrays cannot hold fractional values without an explicit cast, and casting a float to an integer truncates toward zero.
steps: Inspect dtype for an integer list and a float list.
Try storing 2.5 in an integer array through astype and observe truncation.
Choose float64 when fractions must survive.
learn.visual:
[1 2]      dtype int64    → cannot hold 2.5
[1.0 2.0]  dtype float64  → holds 2.5
learn.realWorld: Marks out of 100 are integers; a percentage average is a float, and mixing them silently truncates unless the dtype is chosen deliberately.
mistakes: Assuming astype rounds — it truncates toward zero.
Building an integer array from sensor decimals and losing the decimals.
revision: dtype is inferred from the values.
Cast deliberately, and round before casting if precision matters.

learn.title: Add a scalar to every element
learn.body: A scalar is broadcast across the whole array, so one `+` replaces a loop. No Python-level iteration happens.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)
learn.simple: Ek number ko poore array me jodna ho to bas `a + 5` likho. NumPy us 5 ko har cell me pahucha deta hai — yehi broadcasting ka sabse chhota example hai.
learn.pro: Broadcasting stretches the scalar across every position without materialising a repeated array, so `a + 5` is a single ufunc call over the buffer. Because no temporary of the array's shape is created for the scalar, the extra memory cost is the output array only.
steps: Write the expression with the scalar.
Confirm the shape did not change.
Change the scalar and re-run to see it applied everywhere.
learn.realWorld: Adding a fixed delivery fee to every order in a day's array is one addition.
mistakes: Looping to add the same number.
Expecting an in-place update; a new array is returned.
revision: Scalars broadcast across the whole array.
This is the smallest example of broadcasting.

learn.title: Compare an array with a scalar
learn.body: Comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape. That array is what every filter is built on.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 5, 9]) > 4)
learn.simple: `a > 10` likhne par tumhe True/False ka array milta hai — har number ke liye ek jawab. Yahi boolean mask aage filtering ka poora base banta hai: mask ke andar jahan True hai, wahi values chunti hain.
learn.pro: Comparison ufuncs return a bool array of the broadcast shape rather than a single truth value, which is why `if a > 10:` must be replaced by `.any()` or `.all()`. The mask is then used for boolean indexing, where True positions select elements and the result is a copy.
steps: Compare the array with the threshold to get a boolean array.
Pass that mask back into the array to select the matching values.
Count with mask.sum() when only the number matters.
learn.realWorld: Filtering students who scored above 80 is one comparison plus one index.
mistakes: Writing if a > 10: — a multi-element array has no single truth value.
Forgetting the mask must match the array's shape.
revision: Comparisons return a mask, not a bool.
The mask selects; it does not modify.

learn.title: A Python loop still works over an array
learn.body: Iterating walks the first axis. It is fine for a handful of values and wrong for a million, where a vectorised expression wins.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

total = 0
for value in np.array([2, 4, 6]):
    total += int(value)
print(total)
learn.simple: Array par normal `for` loop bhi chal jata hai — wo ek-ek karke values deta hai. Chhote data par theek hai, lekin lakhon numbers par ye dheema pad jata hai, kyunki tab kaam Python karta hai, NumPy nahi.
learn.pro: Iteration over an ndarray yields subarrays along the first axis and executes Python-level bytecode per step, which dominates cost at scale. Prefer vectorised expressions or reductions; where a loop is unavoidable, keep the body minimal and consider np.frompyfunc or compiled helpers rather than per-element Python calls.
learn.syntax: for value in a:   |   for row in matrix:
steps: Iterate to see what one step yields (element for 1-D, row for 2-D).
Compare the loop result with the vectorised expression.
Keep the loop only where per-element control flow is genuinely needed.
learn.visual:
1-D: each step → element
2-D: each step → whole row  [1 2 3]
learn.realWorld: Printing a formatted line per row is a fair use of a loop; summing a million values is not.
mistakes: Using a loop for arithmetic that has a vectorised form.
Assuming iteration over a 2-D array gives single numbers.
revision: Iteration walks the first axis.
Loops are for control flow, not for bulk arithmetic.

learn.title: Every array reports its own type
learn.body: `np.array` always returns an `ndarray`. A Python `list` and an `ndarray` are not interchangeable.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(type(np.array([1, 2])).__name__)
learn.simple: `np.array(...)` hamesha ek `ndarray` deta hai. Python list aur ndarray ek jaise dikhte hain, par same cheez nahi hain — list me `.mean()` nahi hota, aur ndarray me list wale kuch methods nahi hote.
learn.pro: np.array returns an instance of numpy.ndarray (a subclass such as np.matrix is deprecated for new code), and type checks should use isinstance(value, np.ndarray). Lists and arrays are not interchangeable: arrays expose dtype, shape and strides, while lists expose list methods; conversion is explicit via np.asarray or .tolist().
steps: Check the type after np.array.
Try calling a list method on the array and read the error.
Convert explicitly with np.asarray or tolist at the boundary.
learn.realWorld: A helper that accepts either a list or an array should call np.asarray once at the top instead of branching everywhere.
mistakes: Checking type(a) == list for an array.
Assuming np.matrix is the modern return type — it is legacy.
revision: np.array always returns ndarray.
Normalise inputs at functions' edges.

learn.title: Why NumPy exists
learn.body: A Python loop adds one number at a time and pays interpreter overhead per element; NumPy performs the same addition in compiled code over a contiguous buffer. That is the reason numerical work starts with an array, not a list.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
marks = [40, 55, 70, 85]
a = np.array(marks)
print(a.sum(), a.mean())
print(a.dtype, a.shape)
steps: Sum a list with Python's builtin to see the loop-based path.
Convert to an array and use the method.
Compare the code shape: one expression versus a loop plus accumulator.
learn.visual:
Python:  loop → add → append   (interpreter per element)
NumPy :  one call over the buffer (compiled)
learn.realWorld: A CSV with a million prices is summed in milliseconds as an array and in noticeable seconds as a Python loop.
mistakes: Assuming NumPy is faster for a handful of values — the constant cost can dominate.
Assuming every operation is faster; dtype conversions still cost.
revision: NumPy's win is compiled, contiguous, homogeneous work.
Measure before claiming a speedup.

learn.title: An array versus a list
learn.body: A list can mix a string, a float and a nested list; an ndarray holds one dtype and reports one shape. Mixing types in an array silently promotes them all to a common dtype.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
mixed = np.array([1, 2.5, True])
print(mixed, mixed.dtype)
steps: Build an array from mixed values.
Read the dtype to see the promotion.
Build a list with the same values and note it keeps each type.
learn.visual:
list : [1, 2.5, True]   types kept
array: [1.  2.5 1. ]   dtype float64
learn.realWorld: A column read from a spreadsheet is one type; NumPy enforces that, which is why cleaning happens before the array is built.
mistakes: Mixing text and numbers and losing the text to a string dtype.
Assuming True stays a separate boolean beside floats.
revision: Arrays are homogeneous; lists are not.
Promotion is silent — check dtype after building.

interview.q: Why is a NumPy array faster than a Python list holding the same numbers?
interview.answer: An ndarray owns one contiguous, typed block of memory, so arithmetic runs as one C loop over that block. A list stores pointers to Python objects, so every element costs a pointer chase, a type check and an allocation.

interview.q: For `np.zeros((2, 3))`, how are `ndim` and `size` different?
interview.answer: `ndim` is 2, the number of axes; `size` is 6, the number of elements. `shape` is the tuple `(2, 3)` that ties them together.

interview.q: When would you still choose a Python list over an ndarray?
interview.answer: When the data is heterogeneous, changes size constantly, or is really a record stream rather than a numeric block. An ndarray needs one dtype and pays a copy when it grows.

interview.q: Why does the dtype belong to the array rather than to each element?
interview.answer: One dtype per array lets NumPy store raw values in a typed buffer and pick a compiled loop for arithmetic. Per-element types would mean per-element checks, which is exactly the list overhead NumPy removes.

interview.q: How does slicing a large array avoid copying memory?
interview.answer: A slice only stores an offset, a shape and strides over the same buffer. No values move, so slicing a gigabyte costs a few numbers.

interview.q: Why does `np.array([1, 2.0])` contain floats?
interview.answer: A single array needs one dtype, and NumPy promotes the integers to the common type float64 rather than keeping mixed values.

interview.q: What is the difference between `np.array` and `np.asarray`?
interview.answer: `asarray` returns the input unchanged when it is already an array of the requested dtype, while `array` copies by default.

interview.q: Why prefer `arr.sum()` over Python's `sum(arr)`?
interview.answer: The method runs one compiled reduction over the buffer, while the builtin loops in Python with per-element overhead.

interview.q: How do you get a plain Python number out of a one-element array?
interview.answer: Call `.item()`, which returns a scalar rather than a 0-d array, or convert the single element with `int(...)`/`float(...)`.

interview.q: A shop's daily sales are a Python list of 500 numbers and the total is needed once per page load. Why convert it to an array, and what is the cost of doing it on every request?
interview.answer: An array makes the total one compiled reduction (`np.array(sales).sum()`) instead of a Python loop, but the conversion itself copies 500 values. Convert once when the data is loaded or cached, not on every request.

interview.q: Marketing sends 30 marks as strings from a CSV. What breaks if you call np.array on them and then .mean()?
interview.answer: np.array keeps them as a string dtype (or object), so .mean() raises because there is no numeric meaning. Convert with `.astype(float)` (or parse at load time) before any arithmetic.

defense.q: Defend using NumPy rather than a list for 10,000 sensor readings.
defense.answer: Ten thousand float64 values cost 80 KB contiguous instead of pointer-plus-object pairs, and one vectorised call replaces a Python loop. Filtering, averaging and slicing then operate without per-element overhead.

defense.q: Why does `np.array([1, 2]) + 1` work while `[1, 2] + 1` raises?
defense.answer: An ndarray implements elementwise arithmetic and broadcasts the scalar; a list only concatenates with another list, so adding an int is a type error.

defense.q: A reviewer says NumPy is a thin wrapper over lists. Refute it.
defense.answer: It owns its buffer, dtype, shape and strides, and its ufuncs run compiled loops over that buffer. A list has none of those properties, which is why NumPy can do arithmetic without allocating per element.

defense.q: Defend using NumPy for a signal that must be filtered many times.
defense.answer: The filter runs as vectorised arithmetic over one buffer, and repeated passes avoid per-element Python overhead. The same array can be reused without re-wrapping values.

defense.q: Two arrays print the same numbers but behave differently. Explain why dtype is the reason.
defense.answer: One may be integer and the other float, so division, overflow and equality all differ. Printing hides the dtype that decides those results.

defense.q: Defend choosing an ndarray over a DataFrame for a single numeric column.
defense.answer: There is nothing to label or align, so the frame only adds index bookkeeping. An array is smaller and its operations are the primitive ones the frame calls anyway.

defense.q: Defend using `np.asarray` in a function that only reads its input.
defense.answer: It avoids a copy when the caller already passes a matching array and still accepts plain lists, so the fast path stays fast.

defense.q: Explain why `arr.tolist()` is expensive on a large array.
defense.answer: Every element becomes a Python object, which discards the buffer advantage that made the array fast in the first place.

defense.q: Defend keeping an array 2-D instead of squeezing it to 1-D.
defense.answer: Squeezing changes the axis contract and the direction later broadcasts align to, so a shape that looked tidy can silently change results.

modules.title: ndarray Fundamentals
modules.goal: Read an array's shape, size, ndim, dtype and axes correctly before writing any operation on it.

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)

topics.title: dtype and itemsize
topics.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)

topics.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
topics.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))

topics.title: len counts the first axis only
topics.body: len() reports the length of axis 0, not the number of elements, so for a (3, 4) array len is 3 while size is 12.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(len(a), a.size)

topics.title: Transpose swaps the shape
topics.body: Transposing reverses the axis order, so a (3, 4) array becomes (4, 3) and every operation that follows reads the new shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(a.T.shape)

topics.title: Mixed literals promote to float
topics.body: One float in the input is enough to make the whole array float64, because a single dtype has to hold every value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)

topics.title: A zero-dimensional array has no axes
topics.body: `np.array(7)` is a 0-d array: it has one value, ndim 0 and an empty shape tuple, which is how a scalar crosses into array code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
s = np.array(7)
print(s.ndim, s.shape)

topics.title: Bytes are shape times itemsize
topics.body: nbytes is size multiplied by itemsize, so a float32 array of six elements costs 24 bytes and a float64 one would cost 48.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.float32)
print(a.nbytes)

topics.title: ndim counts the axes
topics.body: `ndim` is how many indices you need to reach a single value; `size` is how many values exist in total.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.ndim, a.size)

topics.title: Ten zeros are one dimension
topics.body: A one-dimensional array has a trailing comma in its shape. That is a 1-tuple, not a scalar.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(10).shape)

topics.title: Shape is a tuple you can index
topics.body: `shape` is data, not a method. Read `shape[0]` for rows and `shape[1]` for columns instead of calling it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.shape[0], a.shape[1])

topics.title: A matrix of one row still has two axes
topics.body: Wrapping a list in a list adds an axis even when there is only one element in it. Shape `(1, 2)` is a matrix, `(2,)` is a vector.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[7, 8]]).shape)

topics.title: Every attribute of an ndarray
topics.body: shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize and nbytes answer different questions about the same buffer, and strides tells you how many elements each axis step moves.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes, a.strides)

topics.title: np.empty is not filled with zeros
topics.body: empty allocates the buffer without writing values, so whatever was in memory is what you read. Use zeros when you need a known starting value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
print(z, z.dtype)
print(np.zeros((2, 2)).shape)

lab.title: Shape detective
lab.brief: Given a target shape, construct an array with that shape and prove it with .shape.

interviewBank.q: How do you find the number of rows of an array without hard-coding the rank?
interviewBank.answer: Use `arr.shape[0]`. Axis 0 is rows by convention, whatever the rank.

interviewBank.q: Why can a scalar array have `shape == ()` and `ndim == 0`?
interviewBank.answer: It is a single value with no axes: the shape tuple is empty and the rank is zero, which is still a valid ndarray rather than a Python float.

interviewBank.q: What does a dtype tell you that a shape does not?
interviewBank.answer: The shape says how values are arranged; the dtype says what each value is and how many bytes it takes, which decides overflow, precision and the result of arithmetic.

interviewBank.q: How do you read a shape of `(2, 3, 4)` in words?
interviewBank.answer: Two blocks, each holding three rows of four values. Reading right to left gives the fastest-varying axis first.

interviewBank.q: What is `size` in terms of `shape`?
interviewBank.answer: The product of the shape entries. An empty axis makes the product zero.

interviewBank.q: Why is `len(arr)` not the number of elements?
interviewBank.answer: `len` reports the length of the first axis only, so a `(2, 3)` array has `len` 2 and size 6.

interviewBank.q: What does `arr.reshape(2, -1)` do with the second dimension?
interviewBank.answer: It infers that dimension from the element count and raises if the total is not divisible by 2.

interviewBank.q: How do you check that two arrays have the same shape?
interviewBank.answer: Compare `a.shape == b.shape`; shapes are tuples, so the comparison is exact and cheap.

interviewBank.q: What is a 0-d array?
interviewBank.answer: A single value with no axes: its shape is `()` and it still supports NumPy operations.

interviewBank.q: A bug report says an image has shape (0, 256, 3). What does that tell you about the array, and what will happen when you plot it?
interviewBank.answer: The first axis (height) is zero, so the array holds no pixels at all. Plotting or reshaping will fail or render nothing; the bug is upstream where the image was read, not in the plotting call.

interviewBank.q: Someone allocates np.empty((1000, 1000)) to save time and sees random huge numbers. Is NumPy broken?
interviewBank.answer: No — empty only allocates the buffer without writing values, so it exposes whatever was in memory. Use np.zeros or np.full when a known starting value is required.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `shape` before arithmetic in a data pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: Most silent numeric bugs are shape bugs, and a shape check turns a wrong answer into a loud failure at the boundary. It also documents the contract the next stage expects.

defenseBank.q: Two arrays have 6 elements each but will not broadcast. Explain why size is not enough.
defenseBank.answer: Broadcasting compares axes from the right, so `(2, 3)` and `(3, 2)` disagree on both axes even though both hold 6 values. Compatibility is per-axis, not per-total.

defenseBank.q: You can store a vector as `(3,)` or `(3, 1)`. Defend the one you keep in a matrix pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: `(3, 1)` is explicit that it is a column, so it broadcasts across columns the way matrix code expects. `(3,)` aliases to the last axis and silently repeats in the wrong direction.

defenseBank.q: Defend asserting `ndim` at a function boundary.
defenseBank.answer: A function written for 2-D input silently misbehaves on 3-D data by reducing the wrong axis. The assertion turns that into an immediate error.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a 3-D array is not "three lists".
defenseBank.answer: It is one buffer addressed by three strides, so it can be sliced, transposed and broadcast as a single object. Three lists would be three objects with no shared shape.

defenseBank.q: Defend naming axes in comments instead of using bare axis numbers.
defenseBank.answer: `axis=1` is meaningless without the shape in mind, and a wrong axis is a silent wrong answer. A comment such as `# axis 1 = features` is the cheapest guard.

defenseBank.q: Defend asserting `shape` rather than `size` at a function boundary.
defenseBank.answer: A size can match while the layout is wrong, and layout is what every later reduction and broadcast depends on.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `len(arr)` misleads on a 2-D array.
defenseBank.answer: It returns the length of axis 0 only, not the number of elements, so `(2, 3)` reports 2.

defenseBank.q: Defend reading `arr.ndim` instead of trusting a comment about rank.
defenseBank.answer: The attribute cannot drift from the data, while a comment survives refactors that change the shape.

tasks.title: Axes of a vector
tasks.statement: Store how many axes `np.zeros(7)` has, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.zeros(7).ndim)
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.ndim` counts axes; a flat vector has one, never two.

tasks.title: Rows and columns of a grid
tasks.statement: Store the shape of `np.ones((6, 2))` in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.ones((6, 2)).shape
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.shape` is a tuple — store it exactly as returned, do not convert it to a list.

tasks.title: Kind of a float dtype
tasks.statement: Store the dtype kind character of `np.ones(2)` in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.ones(2).dtype.kind
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.dtype.kind` gives one character: `f` for floating, `i` for integer, `b` for boolean.

tasks.title: Elements in three axes
tasks.statement: Store the total element count of `np.ones((2, 3, 4))`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.ones((2, 3, 4)).size)
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.size` multiplies every axis length together — no loop needed.

tasks.title: Shape after flattening
tasks.statement: Store the shape of `np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)` after `ravel()` in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3).ravel().shape
print(result)
tasks.hint: `.ravel()` flattens to one axis; ask the result for `.shape` instead of guessing.

tasks.title: A scalar has no axes
tasks.statement: Store how many axes `np.array(5)` has, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = int(np.array(5).ndim)
print(result)
tasks.hint: A zero-dimensional array still reports `.ndim` — the answer is 0, not 1.

tasks.title: Shape of a column
tasks.statement: Store the shape of `np.array([[1], [2]])` in `result`.

print(result)
tasks.hint: A list of one-value rows keeps a second axis of length 1.

tasks.title: Compare shapes with ==

tasks.hint: Compare the `.shape` tuple directly with `(2, 3)`; tuples compare element by element.

tasks.title: An empty axis holds nothing
tasks.statement: Store the element count of `np.zeros((0, 5))`, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:

print(result)

learn.title: shape, size and ndim
learn.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)
learn.simple: Shape batata hai array ka dhancha — jaise 2 rows aur 3 columns. Size batata hai total kitne number hain, aur ndim batata hai kitne 'dabbe' (axes) hain: ek line ka ndim 1, table ka 2.
learn.pro: Shape is a tuple of axis lengths, size is their product, and ndim is the count of axes. Printing all three together is the fastest way to catch a transposed or flattened array before it reaches a model.
learn.syntax: a.shape → tuple   |   a.size → int   |   a.ndim → int
steps: Build the 2×3 array and print all three attributes in one call.
Read shape as (rows, columns) and check size is their product.
Count the entries of shape to confirm ndim.
learn.visual:
a.shape = (2, 3)   rows × columns
a.size  = 6        cells
a.ndim  = 2        number of axes
learn.realWorld: A model expects a feature matrix and fails on shape; printing shape, size and ndim first tells you whether the data is transposed or flattened.
mistakes: Reading shape as (columns, rows) and transposing the wrong way.
Using len(a) when the total cell count is what is needed.
revision: shape is the structure, size is the cell count, ndim is the axis count.
size == product(shape).

learn.title: dtype and itemsize
learn.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)
learn.simple: Dtype batata hai array me kaise number hain — pure integer ya decimal (float). Itemsize batata hai ek number kitni memory leta hai, jaise int64 ka 8 byte.
learn.pro: dtype fixes the element type and itemsize its width in bytes; nbytes is their product with size. Downcasting to a narrower dtype is a deliberate memory trade that must be checked against the value range.
steps: Build an integer array and print dtype.
Print itemsize and note it is bytes per element, not per array.
Multiply itemsize by size to reach nbytes.
learn.visual:
dtype int64 → itemsize 8 bytes
3 elements  → nbytes 24
learn.realWorld: A million-row column of small integers costs 8 MB as int64 and 1 MB as int8 — the dtype decision is the memory decision.
mistakes: Assuming itemsize changes with array length.
Casting to a smaller dtype without checking the value range.
revision: dtype names the element type; itemsize is its width in bytes.
nbytes = itemsize × size.

learn.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
learn.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))
learn.simple: Jis axis ka naam doge, wahi axis gayab ho jaata hai. axis=0 ka matlab rows ko mila do (columns bachenge), axis=1 ka matlab columns ko mila do.
learn.pro: The axis argument names the axis that is reduced away, not the one preserved. A (2, 3) reduction with axis=0 returns three values, one per column, and drops the row dimension.
steps: Sum a 2×2 array with axis=0 and read the result shape.
Sum with axis=1 and compare which values disappeared.
Say out loud which axis vanished in each case.
learn.realWorld: Monthly sales per product: axis=0 totals each product across months, axis=1 totals each month across products.
mistakes: Thinking axis names the direction that stays.
Expecting the same shape back from a reduction.
revision: The named axis is the one removed.
Reductions drop one dimension.

learn.title: len counts the first axis only
learn.body: len() reports the length of axis 0, not the number of elements, so for a (3, 4) array len is 3 while size is 12.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(len(a), a.size)
learn.simple: len(array) sirf pehla axis ginta hai — table me rows. Saare numbers ginne hain to size use karo.
learn.pro: len calls the first axis length, so on a (3, 4) array it returns 3 while size returns 12. Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter, and never use len as a sample count.
steps: Build a 3×4 array and print len(a).
Compare it with a.size.
Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter.
learn.realWorld: Counting rows of a table is len(a); counting measured values is a.size — mixing them inflates sample counts.
mistakes: Assuming len gives the cell count.
Using len on a 0-d array and expecting 1.
revision: len is the first axis only.
size is every cell.

learn.title: Transpose swaps the shape
learn.body: Transposing reverses the axis order, so a (3, 4) array becomes (4, 3) and every operation that follows reads the new shape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(a.T.shape)
learn.simple: Transpose rows ko columns bana deta hai. Shape (3, 4) ka transpose (4, 3) ho jaata hai, par numbers ka order wahi rehta hai.
learn.pro: Transpose swaps the axis order, so the shape reverses and the strides swap with it. It returns a view of the same buffer, which is why the operation is free until a consumer demands C-contiguous data.
steps: Build a 3×4 array and print both shapes.
Transpose and print the shape again.
Note that values were not reordered, only the axes were swapped.
learn.realWorld: A CSV read as (features, samples) usually needs .T before a model that expects (samples, features).
mistakes: Believing .T copies the data — it is a view with swapped strides.
Transposing twice and forgetting the data is back to the original.
revision: Transpose swaps axes and shape.
It is a view until something forces a copy.

learn.title: Mixed literals promote to float
learn.body: One float in the input is enough to make the whole array float64, because a single dtype has to hold every value.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)
learn.simple: Agar list me ek bhi decimal hai, poora array float ban jaata hai — integer bhi 1.0 ban jaata hai. Ek dtype hi hota hai poore array ka.
learn.pro: NumPy promotes all elements to a single common dtype, so one float literal converts the integers to float64. That promotion changes memory width and makes exact equality unreliable, so pass dtype deliberately when it matters.
steps: Build an array from an int and a float.
Print the dtype and observe both values became floats.
Pass dtype explicitly when the promotion is unwanted.
learn.realWorld: One decimal in a price column silently turns the whole column into floats, which changes equality and memory behaviour.
mistakes: Expecting the integer to stay an integer in a mixed array.
Relying on exact equality after promotion.
revision: One dtype per array.
Mixed input promotes to the common type.

learn.title: A zero-dimensional array has no axes
learn.body: `np.array(7)` is a 0-d array: it has one value, ndim 0 and an empty shape tuple, which is how a scalar crosses into array code.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
s = np.array(7)
print(s.ndim, s.shape)
learn.simple: Ek single number ka array bhi array hota hai, par uska koi axis nahi hota (ndim 0, shape khaali). `.item()` se asli Python number milta hai.
learn.pro: A 0-d array holds one value with ndim 0 and shape (); reductions over every axis return one. Use .item() when a plain Python scalar is required, because the object is still an ndarray.
steps: Create an array from a single number.
Print ndim and shape to see () and 0.
Use .item() to get the plain Python scalar back.
learn.realWorld: A reduction over every axis returns a 0-d array; printing it looks like a number but it is still an ndarray.
mistakes: Indexing a 0-d array as if it had axes.
Comparing it to a Python int in a type check.
revision: 0-d means no axes, shape ().
.item() unwraps it.

learn.title: Bytes are shape times itemsize
learn.body: nbytes is size multiplied by itemsize, so a float32 array of six elements costs 24 bytes and a float64 one would cost 48.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.float32)
print(a.nbytes)
learn.simple: Total memory = number of elements × ek element ka size. float32 se float64 karoge to memory dugni ho jaayegi.
learn.pro: nbytes equals size multiplied by itemsize, so dtype is the lever on memory: float32 halves a float64 matrix. Account for copies separately, since a copy doubles the live footprint.
steps: Create a float32 array of shape (2, 3).
Print nbytes and square it against size × itemsize.
Repeat with float64 to see the memory double.
learn.realWorld: Choosing float32 for a large feature matrix halves memory and often changes nothing measurable in accuracy.
mistakes: Confusing nbytes with the Python object's overhead.
Forgetting that a copy doubles the count.
revision: nbytes = size × itemsize.
dtype width is the multiplier you control.

learn.title: ndim counts the axes
learn.body: `ndim` is how many indices you need to reach a single value; `size` is how many values exist in total.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.ndim, a.size)
learn.simple: Jitne brackets ke andar brackets, utne axes. 3D array me ndim 3 hota hai aur index bhi teen lagte hain.
learn.pro: ndim equals len(shape), and every axis needs its own index. In practice ndim identifies the convention you are holding — (batch, height, width) versus (batch, height, width, channels).
steps: Create a three-axis array.
Print ndim and size, and confirm size is the product of shape.
Index with three positions to see each axis used.
learn.realWorld: An image batch is (batch, height, width) or (batch, height, width, channels) — ndim tells you which convention you are holding.
mistakes: Counting shape entries by eye and getting it wrong.
Assuming a 2-D model accepts a 3-D batch.
revision: ndim = len(shape).
Each axis needs its own index.

learn.title: Ten zeros are one dimension
learn.body: A one-dimensional array has a trailing comma in its shape. That is a 1-tuple, not a scalar.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(10).shape)
learn.simple: `np.zeros(10)` me sirf 10 numbers hain, ek line. `(10, 1)` do axis hain — 10 rows aur 1 column, jo model ke liye column banta hai.
learn.pro: Shape (10,) is one axis while (10, 1) is two; broadcasting treats them differently. A feature matrix needs the explicit column axis, otherwise the vector broadcasts across rows and silently produces the wrong result.
steps: Create ten zeros and print the shape.
Notice the trailing comma: one axis, ten cells.
Compare with np.zeros((10, 1)) which has two axes.
learn.realWorld: A single feature column must be (n, 1) to broadcast as a column; (n,) silently broadcasts as a row.
mistakes: Treating (10,) and (10, 1) as the same shape.
Reshaping to (10,) and losing the column semantics.
revision: A 1-D shape is written with a trailing comma.
Column vectors need two axes.

learn.title: Shape is a tuple you can index
learn.body: `shape` is data, not a method. Read `shape[0]` for rows and `shape[1]` for columns instead of calling it.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.shape[0], a.shape[1])
learn.simple: Shape ek tuple hai, isliye shape[0] se rows aur shape[1] se columns nikal sakte ho — badi value hard-code karne ki zarurat nahi.
learn.pro: shape is an immutable tuple, so indexing it gives axis lengths you can reuse in allocations and reshapes. That keeps code correct when the row count changes between runs.
steps: Create a 2×2 array.
Read rows and columns from the tuple by position.
Use those values in a reshape or a loop bound.
learn.realWorld: Building a result array with np.zeros(a.shape[0]) is how code stays correct when the row count changes.
mistakes: Indexing shape[1] on a 1-D array.
Assuming shape is a list and calling .append.
revision: shape is an immutable tuple.
Position 0 is rows, 1 is columns.

learn.title: A matrix of one row still has two axes
learn.body: Wrapping a list in a list adds an axis even when there is only one element in it. Shape `(1, 2)` is a matrix, `(2,)` is a vector.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[7, 8]]).shape)
learn.simple: `[[7, 8]]` me bahar ka bracket ek extra axis banata hai, isliye shape (1, 2) hota hai. Model ko aksar aisa hi batch chahiye.
learn.pro: Nesting a list adds an axis, so [[7, 8]] is (1, 2) while [7, 8] is (2,). A single-sample batch must keep that leading axis or the model receives a vector instead of a batch.
steps: Build a nested list with one inner list.
Print the shape and note the leading 1.
Compare with np.array([7, 8]) which is 1-D.
learn.realWorld: Batching a single sample for a model needs (1, features); passing (features,) is the classic shape error.
mistakes: Dropping the outer list and losing the batch axis.
Squeezing a batch of one to save memory and breaking the model call.
revision: Nesting adds an axis.
Batch of one is still a batch.

learn.title: Every attribute of an ndarray
learn.body: shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize and nbytes answer different questions about the same buffer, and strides tells you how many elements each axis step moves.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes, a.strides)
learn.simple: Shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize, nbytes aur strides — ye saat cheezein array ke baare me sab kuch bata deti hain. Strides batate hain har axis me aage badhne par kitne byte chalo.
learn.pro: strides are byte steps per axis, so shape plus strides fully describe how a view maps onto its buffer. A transposed view keeps the same buffer with swapped strides, which is why the copy only happens later.
learn.syntax: shape · ndim · size · dtype · itemsize · nbytes · strides
steps: Reshape a range into a 3×4 array.
Print all attributes in one line.
Read strides as bytes to step per axis.
learn.visual:
shape (3, 4) · size 12 · dtype int64
strides (32, 8) = 4 elements, then 1
learn.realWorld: Disagreement between shape and strides is how a transposed view keeps the same buffer without copying.
mistakes: Reading strides in elements instead of bytes.
Assuming a reshape always changes strides.
revision: strides are byte steps per axis.
A view shares the buffer; strides differ.

learn.title: np.empty is not filled with zeros
learn.body: empty allocates the buffer without writing values, so whatever was in memory is what you read. Use zeros when you need a known starting value.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
print(z, z.dtype)
print(np.zeros((2, 2)).shape)
learn.simple: `np.empty` sirf jagah banata hai, usme zero nahi daalta — jo memory me pehle se tha wahi dikhta hai. Isliye use karne se pehle har cell bharni padti hai.
learn.pro: empty allocates without initialisation, so the values are whatever the buffer held. It is a legitimate preallocation only when every element is written before it is read.
steps: Create zeros to see a known starting state.
Create empty of the same shape and print its dtype and shape only.
Never print or rely on empty's values.
learn.realWorld: Preallocating an output buffer with empty is a legitimate speed trick — as long as every cell is written before it is read.
mistakes: Assuming empty contains zeros.
Reading an unwritten cell and treating garbage as data.
revision: empty skips initialisation for speed.
Write every cell before reading it.

interview.q: How do you find the number of rows of an array without hard-coding the rank?
interview.answer: Use `arr.shape[0]`. Axis 0 is rows by convention, whatever the rank.

interview.q: Why can a scalar array have `shape == ()` and `ndim == 0`?
interview.answer: It is a single value with no axes: the shape tuple is empty and the rank is zero, which is still a valid ndarray rather than a Python float.

interview.q: What does a dtype tell you that a shape does not?
interview.answer: The shape says how values are arranged; the dtype says what each value is and how many bytes it takes, which decides overflow, precision and the result of arithmetic.

interview.q: How do you read a shape of `(2, 3, 4)` in words?
interview.answer: Two blocks, each holding three rows of four values. Reading right to left gives the fastest-varying axis first.

interview.q: What is `size` in terms of `shape`?
interview.answer: The product of the shape entries. An empty axis makes the product zero.

interview.q: Why is `len(arr)` not the number of elements?
interview.answer: `len` reports the length of the first axis only, so a `(2, 3)` array has `len` 2 and size 6.

interview.q: What does `arr.reshape(2, -1)` do with the second dimension?
interview.answer: It infers that dimension from the element count and raises if the total is not divisible by 2.

interview.q: How do you check that two arrays have the same shape?
interview.answer: Compare `a.shape == b.shape`; shapes are tuples, so the comparison is exact and cheap.

interview.q: What is a 0-d array?
interview.answer: A single value with no axes: its shape is `()` and it still supports NumPy operations.

interview.q: A bug report says an image has shape (0, 256, 3). What does that tell you about the array, and what will happen when you plot it?
interview.answer: The first axis (height) is zero, so the array holds no pixels at all. Plotting or reshaping will fail or render nothing; the bug is upstream where the image was read, not in the plotting call.

interview.q: Someone allocates np.empty((1000, 1000)) to save time and sees random huge numbers. Is NumPy broken?
interview.answer: No — empty only allocates the buffer without writing values, so it exposes whatever was in memory. Use np.zeros or np.full when a known starting value is required.

defense.q: Defend checking `shape` before arithmetic in a data pipeline.
defense.answer: Most silent numeric bugs are shape bugs, and a shape check turns a wrong answer into a loud failure at the boundary. It also documents the contract the next stage expects.

defense.q: Two arrays have 6 elements each but will not broadcast. Explain why size is not enough.
defense.answer: Broadcasting compares axes from the right, so `(2, 3)` and `(3, 2)` disagree on both axes even though both hold 6 values. Compatibility is per-axis, not per-total.

defense.q: You can store a vector as `(3,)` or `(3, 1)`. Defend the one you keep in a matrix pipeline.
defense.answer: `(3, 1)` is explicit that it is a column, so it broadcasts across columns the way matrix code expects. `(3,)` aliases to the last axis and silently repeats in the wrong direction.

defense.q: Defend asserting `ndim` at a function boundary.
defense.answer: A function written for 2-D input silently misbehaves on 3-D data by reducing the wrong axis. The assertion turns that into an immediate error.

defense.q: Explain why a 3-D array is not "three lists".
defense.answer: It is one buffer addressed by three strides, so it can be sliced, transposed and broadcast as a single object. Three lists would be three objects with no shared shape.

defense.q: Defend naming axes in comments instead of using bare axis numbers.
defense.answer: `axis=1` is meaningless without the shape in mind, and a wrong axis is a silent wrong answer. A comment such as `# axis 1 = features` is the cheapest guard.

defense.q: Defend asserting `shape` rather than `size` at a function boundary.
defense.answer: A size can match while the layout is wrong, and layout is what every later reduction and broadcast depends on.

defense.q: Explain why `len(arr)` misleads on a 2-D array.
defense.answer: It returns the length of axis 0 only, not the number of elements, so `(2, 3)` reports 2.

defense.q: Defend reading `arr.ndim` instead of trusting a comment about rank.
defense.answer: The attribute cannot drift from the data, while a comment survives refactors that change the shape.
