modules.title: Array Creation and Initialization
modules.goal: Create arrays with zeros, ones, full, arange, linspace, eye and diag, and pick the right constructor for a dataset.

topics.title: zeros, ones and full
topics.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

topics.title: arange and linspace
topics.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

topics.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
topics.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

topics.title: zeros_like copies a shape
topics.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))

topics.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
topics.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))

topics.title: arange accepts a fractional step
topics.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))

topics.title: ones can take an integer dtype
topics.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))

topics.title: full repeats any value
topics.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))

topics.title: empty allocates without setting values
topics.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)

topics.title: identity builds an identity matrix
topics.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))

topics.title: arange counts down with a negative step
topics.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))

topics.title: linspace controls the step you get
topics.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: arange versus linspace
topics.body: arange takes a step and can miss the stop value; linspace takes a count and always includes both ends. For floats, linspace is usually the safer choice.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: Identity and eye
topics.body: eye builds an identity of any rectangular shape, while identity requires a square one. Both put ones on the main diagonal.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int))
print(np.identity(2, dtype=int))

interviewBank.q: When is `linspace` a better choice than `arange`?
interviewBank.answer: When the number of points matters and the endpoints must be exact. `linspace` computes each point from the count, avoiding the floating step error that can add or drop the last element of `arange`.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `zeros` and `empty`?
interviewBank.answer: `zeros` writes every element as 0; `empty` only allocates, so the values are whatever was in memory. Use `empty` only when you will overwrite all of it.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.eye(3, 4)` exist when `np.identity(3)` does?
interviewBank.answer: `eye` allows a rectangular shape and an offset diagonal via `k`; `identity` is only the square case.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.full` take a shape but `np.full_like` does not?
interviewBank.answer: `full_like` copies the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is why it takes that array instead of a shape.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.arange(5).reshape(1, -1)` produce?
interviewBank.answer: A single row with five columns: the `1` fixes the row count and `-1` infers the columns.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.zeros` slower than `np.empty`?
interviewBank.answer: `zeros` writes every element; `empty` only allocates, leaving whatever bytes were there.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.full_like(a, 7)` reuse from `a`?
interviewBank.answer: Its shape and dtype, so only the fill value is new.

interviewBank.q: How do you build a diagonal matrix from a vector?
interviewBank.answer: `np.diag(v)` places the values on the main diagonal of a square matrix.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.arange(5.0)` produce floats?
interviewBank.answer: The start value is a float, so the inferred dtype is float64 rather than an integer type.

interviewBank.q: A test fixture needs 50 points from 0 to 10 inclusive. Why is np.linspace(0, 10, 50) safer than np.arange(0, 10, 0.2)?
interviewBank.answer: linspace takes a count and always includes both ends; arange takes a step, can include the stop unexpectedly with float steps, and can produce 50 or 51 points depending on rounding. Choose by count when the count is the requirement.

interviewBank.q: An identity matrix is needed for a 3×4 system, but np.identity(3, 4) raises. What is the right call?
interviewBank.answer: identity only builds square matrices. Use np.eye(3, 4) (rows, columns), which puts ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape.

defenseBank.q: Defend using `arange` for indices and `linspace` for plotted ranges.
defenseBank.answer: Integer positions want an exact step and an exclusive stop, which is what `arange` gives. A plotted range wants a fixed count with both ends included, which `linspace` guarantees.

defenseBank.q: Why can `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` return eleven values instead of ten?
defenseBank.answer: The step is not exactly representable in binary, so repeated addition lands just below or above 1.0. A `linspace(0, 1, 10)` avoids the ambiguity.

defenseBank.q: Defend choosing the dtype at creation instead of fixing it later.
defenseBank.answer: The dtype decides memory and the arithmetic that follows; converting later copies the whole array and can change results. Declaring it once keeps the intent visible.

defenseBank.q: Defend `linspace` for a fixed number of dashboard points.
defenseBank.answer: The chart needs exactly N points across a closed range, and `linspace` guarantees the count and both endpoints without floating-step drift.

defenseBank.q: Why does `np.eye(3)` print floats?
defenseBank.answer: The default dtype is float64, because an identity is usually used in floating-point algebra. Pass `dtype=int` for an integer one.

defenseBank.q: Defend building an index array once and reusing it.
defenseBank.answer: Positions rarely change while data does, so recomputing them wastes work and risks drift. One array documents the layout the rest of the code assumes.

defenseBank.q: Defend `zeros_like` over an explicit shape when copying a layout.
defenseBank.answer: It keeps shape and dtype in one expression, so they cannot drift apart when the source changes.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.empty` is not a shortcut for zeros.
defenseBank.answer: It leaves whatever bytes were in memory, so values are arbitrary until written.

defenseBank.q: Defend computing an index grid once and reusing it.
defenseBank.answer: The positions do not depend on the data, and recomputing them only adds work and a chance to drift.

learn.title: zeros, ones and full
learn.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))
learn.simple: Zeros se sab 0 wala array, ones se sab 1 wala, aur full se kisi bhi number se bhara array banta hai. Shape dena zaruri hai.
learn.pro: Each takes the shape first: zeros and ones fill with 0 and 1 (float64 by default), full fills with any value. They are the three constructors for a known-shape buffer before real data arrives.
steps: Create a length-3 zeros array and print its dtype.
Create a 2×2 ones array and confirm the shape.
Fill a length-3 array with 7 using full.
learn.realWorld: A results buffer starts as zeros, a mask starts as ones, and a default price list starts as full — all three are one call with a known shape.
mistakes: Forgetting the shape argument needs a tuple for 2-D.
Expecting full to infer the dtype from the value.
revision: shape first, value second.
float64 is the default dtype.

learn.title: arange and linspace
learn.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))
learn.simple: arange me step dete hain ('har 2 kadam'), linspace me count dete hain ('mujhe 5 number chahiye'). Dono ke apne use hain.
learn.pro: arange fixes the step and derives the count; linspace fixes the count, includes both endpoints and derives the step. Choose by which quantity your problem actually specifies.
learn.syntax: np.arange(start, stop, step) · np.linspace(start, stop, count)
steps: Create a range with a step of 2 and read the values.
Create three evenly spaced values from 0 to 1.
Count both results to see which argument controls the length.
learn.realWorld: Axis ticks are linspace (a count), while index arithmetic is arange (a step).
mistakes: Using arange with a float step and getting an extra element.
Expecting arange to include the stop value.
revision: arange takes a step; linspace takes a count.
linspace includes both ends by default.

learn.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
learn.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))
learn.simple: Identity matrix me diagonal par 1 aur baaki 0 hote hain. diag se list ko diagonal matrix bana sakte hain, aur matrix se diagonal nikal bhi sakte hain.
learn.pro: eye and identity build matrices with ones on the main diagonal; diag is overloaded — given a vector it builds a diagonal matrix, given a matrix it extracts the diagonal. Read the argument type before trusting the result.
steps: Create a 2×2 identity and read the diagonal.
Build a diagonal matrix from a list.
Compare np.diag on a matrix (extracts) with a vector (builds).
learn.realWorld: Identity matrices appear in ridge regression and in one-hot encodings; diag builds covariance from variances.
mistakes: Assuming diag always builds a matrix.
Forgetting eye is float by default.
revision: eye is square identity; diag is context-dependent.
Pass dtype=int when the values are counts.

learn.title: zeros_like copies a shape
learn.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `zeros_like(a)` wahi shape aur dtype deta hai jo `a` ka hai, isliye shape hard-code karne ki zarurat nahi padti.
learn.pro: The _like constructors copy shape and dtype from an existing array, so an output buffer cannot drift when the input shape changes. Override dtype explicitly when the buffer must hold a different type.
steps: Create a source array and print its shape.
Call zeros_like and confirm the shape matches.
Override dtype with ones_like to get integer ones.
learn.realWorld: An output buffer that must match an input uses zeros_like, so the shape never drifts when the input changes.
mistakes: Assuming zeros_like copies the values.
Forgetting it copies the dtype too.
revision: _like copies shape and dtype.
Override dtype deliberately when needed.

learn.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
learn.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))
learn.simple: `endpoint=False` se aakhri value nahi aati — aur isse step bhi badal jaata hai, sirf last number nahi hatta.
learn.pro: With endpoint=False the range covers [start, stop) and the step becomes the full span divided by the count, not by count − 1. Both the values and the spacing change, which matters for bin edges.
steps: Create four points including the endpoint.
Repeat with endpoint=False and compare.
Note the step becomes the full range divided by the count.
learn.realWorld: Histogram bin edges exclude the last endpoint when the range is cyclic, such as angles or phase.
mistakes: Assuming endpoint=False keeps the same step.
Using it and then expecting the maximum value to appear.
revision: endpoint defaults to True.
Excluding it changes the spacing, not just the last value.

learn.title: arange accepts a fractional step
learn.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
learn.simple: arange me 0.25 jaisa decimal step bhi de sakte hain, par float galti se ek extra ya kam number aa sakta hai.
learn.pro: Fractional steps work but accumulate binary floating-point error, so the length can differ from the arithmetic expectation and the stop is never included. For a required count, linspace is the safer constructor.
steps: Create the range with a 0.25 step.
Count the values and compare with the expected four.
Check the last value against the stop.
learn.realWorld: Sampling a signal at a fractional interval is arange, but accumulated float error is why linspace is preferred for fixed counts.
mistakes: Expecting 1.0 to be included.
Trusting float steps to land exactly on the stop.
revision: Fractional steps work but accumulate error.
The stop is exclusive.

learn.title: ones can take an integer dtype
learn.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `np.ones(3)` float deta hai; agar pure integer chahiye to `dtype=int` likhna padta hai.
learn.pro: ones defaults to float64 regardless of the literal 1, so counters and masks need dtype=int. Leaving them float drags floating arithmetic and rounding into code that should stay integral.
steps: Create ones without a dtype and read the float dtype.
Repeat with dtype=int and read the values.
Use the integer version where counts must stay integral.
learn.realWorld: A counter array or a one-hot mask should be integer so later arithmetic does not drag floats through the pipeline.
mistakes: Assuming the dtype is inferred from the value 1.
Mixing float ones with integer counts in comparisons.
revision: ones defaults to float64.
dtype is an argument, not a guess.

learn.title: full repeats any value
learn.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `np.full((2, 2), 3)` do-ka-do array banata hai jisme har jagah 3 hota hai. Shape pehle, value baad me.
learn.pro: full(shape, value) is the general constant constructor, and dtype can be forced. It replaces the pattern of building zeros and then adding a scalar to every cell.
steps: Create a 2×2 array filled with 3.
Print the dtype to see it follows the value or the argument.
Use full for a constant baseline array.
learn.realWorld: A default discount table or a sentinel-filled buffer is one full call with a shape.
mistakes: Passing the value before the shape.
Forgetting the shape must be a tuple for 2-D.
revision: full is shape + value.
dtype can be forced.

learn.title: empty allocates without setting values
learn.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)
learn.simple: `np.empty(3)` sirf 3 jagah banata hai, number nahi daalta. Isme purani memory ka kachra dikh sakta hai.
learn.pro: empty performs allocation only, so the contents are undefined until written. It saves the zeroing pass in tight loops, at the cost of a real bug if any cell is read before assignment.
steps: Create empty of length 3 and print shape and dtype only.
Compare with zeros of the same shape.
Write every cell before reading it in real code.
learn.realWorld: A tight loop that fills a preallocated buffer uses empty to skip a pointless zeroing pass.
mistakes: Treating the values as zeros.
Shipping code that reads uninitialised cells.
revision: empty is allocation only.
Initialise before use.

learn.title: identity builds an identity matrix
learn.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))
learn.simple: `np.identity(2)` 2×2 ki identity deta hai — diagonal par 1. Ye sirf square (barabar rows-columns) ke liye hota hai.
learn.pro: identity(n) is the square special case of eye, so it accepts exactly one dimension. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication and a standard way to test a matmul implementation.
steps: Build a 2×2 identity and print it.
Compare with eye(2) and note they agree for square shapes.
Use eye when the matrix is rectangular.
learn.realWorld: Identity is the neutral element in matrix multiplication, used to initialise and to test a multiplication routine.
mistakes: Expecting identity to accept two dimensions.
Comparing identity to an integer matrix with == and getting False.
revision: identity is always square.
eye is the rectangular generalisation.

learn.title: arange counts down with a negative step
learn.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))
learn.simple: Negative step dene se range ulti chalti hai — `arange(5, 0, -1)` 5 se 1 tak deta hai, 0 nahi aata.
learn.pro: A negative step walks downward and still excludes the stop, so arange(5, 0, -1) yields 5 through 1. A sign mismatch between start, stop and step produces an empty array rather than an error.
steps: Create the descending range and read the values.
Confirm the stop is excluded.
Use it to build reversed index positions.
learn.realWorld: Rendering a stack from top to bottom, or walking a time series backwards, is a negative-step range.
mistakes: Using a negative step with start < stop and getting an empty array.
Expecting 0 in the output.
revision: Negative step counts down.
Stop stays exclusive.

learn.title: linspace controls the step you get
learn.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
learn.simple: Linspace me aap count dete ho, step khud nikalta hai: (stop − start) / (count − 1). Zyada points maange to step chhota ho jaayega.
learn.pro: linspace derives the step as the span divided by count − 1 so both endpoints are included. That is why increasing the count refines the grid without moving its ends.
steps: Create five points from 0 to 1.
Compute the step as range divided by (count − 1).
Change the count and observe the step change.
learn.realWorld: Plotting a smooth curve needs a density decision: more points, smaller step, same endpoints.
mistakes: Dividing by count instead of count − 1.
Assuming the step is an argument.
revision: linspace is endpoints + count.
Step = (stop − start) / (count − 1).

learn.title: arange versus linspace
learn.body: arange takes a step and can miss the stop value; linspace takes a count and always includes both ends. For floats, linspace is usually the safer choice.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
learn.simple: Step pata hai to arange, count pata hai to linspace. Plot ya grid ke liye aksar linspace behtar hota hai.
learn.pro: Pick arange when the step is the requirement and linspace when the sample count is; linspace also guarantees the endpoint. For plots and numerical grids the count is usually what you actually know.
learn.syntax: arange(start, stop, step) vs linspace(start, stop, count)
steps: Build the same range both ways and compare lengths.
Change the step and see arange's length change.
Change the count and see linspace's step change.
learn.visual:
arange(0,1,0.25) → 4 values, step fixed
linspace(0,1,5)  → 5 values, step derived
learn.realWorld: Grids for plotting and for numerical integration are linspace; index arithmetic is arange.
mistakes: Choosing arange for a required number of samples.
Choosing linspace when an exact step is the requirement.
revision: Pick by which quantity is fixed: step or count.
linspace includes the stop.

learn.title: Identity and eye
learn.body: eye builds an identity of any rectangular shape, while identity requires a square one. Both put ones on the main diagonal.

Pass dtype=int where integers matter.

interview.q: When is `linspace` a better choice than `arange`?
interview.answer: When the number of points matters and the endpoints must be exact. `linspace` computes each point from the count, avoiding the floating step error that can add or drop the last element of `arange`.

interview.q: What is the difference between `zeros` and `empty`?
interview.answer: `zeros` writes every element as 0; `empty` only allocates, so the values are whatever was in memory. Use `empty` only when you will overwrite all of it.

interview.q: Why does `np.eye(3, 4)` exist when `np.identity(3)` does?
interview.answer: `eye` allows a rectangular shape and an offset diagonal via `k`; `identity` is only the square case.

interview.q: Why does `np.full` take a shape but `np.full_like` does not?
interview.answer: `full_like` copies the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is why it takes that array instead of a shape.

interview.q: What does `np.arange(5).reshape(1, -1)` produce?
interview.answer: A single row with five columns: the `1` fixes the row count and `-1` infers the columns.

interview.q: Why is `np.zeros` slower than `np.empty`?
interview.answer: `zeros` writes every element; `empty` only allocates, leaving whatever bytes were there.

interview.q: What does `np.full_like(a, 7)` reuse from `a`?
interview.answer: Its shape and dtype, so only the fill value is new.

interview.q: How do you build a diagonal matrix from a vector?
interview.answer: `np.diag(v)` places the values on the main diagonal of a square matrix.

interview.q: Why does `np.arange(5.0)` produce floats?
interview.answer: The start value is a float, so the inferred dtype is float64 rather than an integer type.

interview.q: A test fixture needs 50 points from 0 to 10 inclusive. Why is np.linspace(0, 10, 50) safer than np.arange(0, 10, 0.2)?
interview.answer: linspace takes a count and always includes both ends; arange takes a step, can include the stop unexpectedly with float steps, and can produce 50 or 51 points depending on rounding. Choose by count when the count is the requirement.

interview.q: An identity matrix is needed for a 3×4 system, but np.identity(3, 4) raises. What is the right call?
interview.answer: identity only builds square matrices. Use np.eye(3, 4) (rows, columns), which puts ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape.

defense.q: Defend using `arange` for indices and `linspace` for plotted ranges.
defense.answer: Integer positions want an exact step and an exclusive stop, which is what `arange` gives. A plotted range wants a fixed count with both ends included, which `linspace` guarantees.

defense.q: Why can `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` return eleven values instead of ten?
defense.answer: The step is not exactly representable in binary, so repeated addition lands just below or above 1.0. A `linspace(0, 1, 10)` avoids the ambiguity.

defense.q: Defend choosing the dtype at creation instead of fixing it later.
defense.answer: The dtype decides memory and the arithmetic that follows; converting later copies the whole array and can change results. Declaring it once keeps the intent visible.

defense.q: Defend `linspace` for a fixed number of dashboard points.
defense.answer: The chart needs exactly N points across a closed range, and `linspace` guarantees the count and both endpoints without floating-step drift.

defense.q: Why does `np.eye(3)` print floats?
defense.answer: The default dtype is float64, because an identity is usually used in floating-point algebra. Pass `dtype=int` for an integer one.

defense.q: Defend building an index array once and reusing it.
defense.answer: Positions rarely change while data does, so recomputing them wastes work and risks drift. One array documents the layout the rest of the code assumes.

defense.q: Defend `zeros_like` over an explicit shape when copying a layout.
defense.answer: It keeps shape and dtype in one expression, so they cannot drift apart when the source changes.

defense.q: Explain why `np.empty` is not a shortcut for zeros.
defense.answer: It leaves whatever bytes were in memory, so values are arbitrary until written.

defense.q: Defend computing an index grid once and reusing it.
defense.answer: The positions do not depend on the data, and recomputing them only adds work and a chance to drift.

modules.title: Data Types and Type Conversion
modules.goal: Choose an explicit dtype, convert safely with astype and understand overflow, precision and memory cost.

topics.title: Converting with astype
topics.body: astype returns a NEW array with the requested dtype and truncates floats toward zero, so 1.7 becomes 1; the original array is untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.7, 2.9])
print(a.astype(int))

topics.title: Overflow is silent
topics.body: Integer dtypes wrap around on overflow instead of raising, so uint8 arithmetic can turn a large result into a small one — use a wider dtype when the range is not guaranteed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Smaller dtype, smaller memory
topics.body: float32 uses four bytes per element against eight for float64; choosing it deliberately cuts memory and bandwidth in half, at the cost of precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
print(a.dtype, a.nbytes)

topics.title: astype truncates toward zero
topics.body: Casting float to int does not round: it drops the fractional part, so 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int))

topics.title: Text becomes a number with astype
topics.body: Numeric strings cast cleanly to int or float, which is exactly why one bad token in a loaded column raises instead of silently becoming zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(float))

topics.title: Division always yields floats
topics.body: True division produces float64 even when both operands are integers, so `int / int` never silently loses the remainder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2]) / 2).dtype)

topics.title: Numbers become booleans by truthiness
topics.body: Casting to bool keeps only whether a value is non-zero, so 0 becomes False and every other number becomes True.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([0, 1, 2]).astype(bool))

topics.title: Count with a boolean array
topics.body: Booleans add as 1 and 0, so sum() on a mask counts the matches without any branching code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.sum())

topics.title: dtype reports the element type
topics.body: The dtype belongs to the whole array, not to each element. Mixing an int and a float array promotes to float.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0]).dtype)

topics.title: A float array prints a decimal point
topics.body: The printed form already tells you the dtype: `[1. 2.]` is float, `[1 2]` is int. Reading the output is faster than checking.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2], dtype=float))

topics.title: Each dtype has a size in bytes
topics.body: `itemsize` is bytes per element. Ten million `int64` values need 80 MB before any copy, which is why dtype choice is a memory decision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dtype('int64').itemsize, np.dtype('int32').itemsize)

topics.title: A comparison produces booleans
topics.body: Masks are a dtype, not a special object. `bool` arrays are one byte per element and are the currency of filtering.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([1, 2, 3]) > 1).dtype)

topics.title: Casting a float to an integer truncates
topics.body: astype does not round; it drops the fractional part toward zero. Convert after rounding when the value should not lose precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.9, -1.9, 2.5])
print(a.astype(np.int64))
print(np.round(a).astype(np.int64))

topics.title: Type promotion with result_type
topics.body: When two dtypes meet in an operation NumPy promotes to one that can hold both. result_type tells you which dtype that will be before you compute anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.result_type(np.int32, np.float32))
print((np.array([1], dtype=np.int8) + 0.5).dtype)

interviewBank.q: Why does adding `0.0` to an integer array change more than the values?
interviewBank.answer: It promotes the dtype to float64, doubling memory and changing later arithmetic. Integer division and overflow are no longer possible after that promotion.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between `float32` and `float64`?
interviewBank.answer: `float64` for accumulation and anything needing precision; `float32` when memory and bandwidth dominate and about seven significant digits are enough, as in many model inputs.

interviewBank.q: What is the risk of `astype(int)` on float data?
interviewBank.answer: It truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so 1.9 becomes 1, and it silently discards fractional data. For rounding, use `np.round` first and say so.

interviewBank.q: What do you gain and lose with `dtype="int8"`?
interviewBank.answer: Four times less memory than int64, at the cost of a range of only -128 to 127, so overflow becomes possible.

interviewBank.q: What happens to a float array cast to `int32`?
interviewBank.answer: Each value is truncated toward zero, losing the fractional part without warning.

interviewBank.q: Why is `0.1 + 0.2` not exactly `0.3` in float64?
interviewBank.answer: Neither decimal is representable exactly in binary, so the stored approximations add to a value one bit away from the nearest 0.3.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.result_type` decide?
interviewBank.answer: The dtype that a set of operands would promote to in an operation.

interviewBank.q: How do you inspect the range of an integer dtype?
interviewBank.answer: `np.iinfo(dtype)` gives its minimum and maximum; `np.finfo` does the same for floats.

interviewBank.q: Why is `float16` risky for accumulation?
interviewBank.answer: It has roughly three decimal digits, so repeated additions lose precision quickly.

interviewBank.q: A price column is stored as float64 and cast to int to save memory; customers see 99 instead of 99.99. What went wrong?
interviewBank.answer: astype(int) truncates toward zero, it does not round. Either round first (`np.round(price).astype(int)`) or keep cents as integers at the source; casting decimals to integers always loses the fraction.

interviewBank.q: An int32 array of large sensor counters overflows silently negative. How would you have caught it before shipping?
interviewBank.answer: Check np.result_type and the dtype's maximum (np.iinfo(np.int32).max) against the expected range, or promote to int64. NumPy does not raise on overflow for integer arithmetic, so the check has to be explicit.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing coordinates as `float32`.
defenseBank.answer: Screen and sensor coordinates rarely need more than seven digits, and halving the bytes halves bandwidth in rendering and model input. The error is far below one pixel.

defenseBank.q: Explain integer overflow, and why `uint8` arithmetic wraps instead of raising.
defenseBank.answer: Fixed-width integers have a fixed range, so arithmetic is modular: `uint8(200) + uint8(100)` wraps to 44. NumPy keeps the C behaviour rather than paying a check per element.

defenseBank.q: A model expects `float32` but your pipeline produces `float64`. Defend where you convert.
defenseBank.answer: Convert once, at the boundary where the model is called, after all precise arithmetic is finished. Converting early throws away precision the pipeline still needs and gains nothing.

defenseBank.q: Defend float64 until a calculation reaches a money boundary.
defenseBank.answer: Intermediate work needs precision, and rounding should happen once, deliberately, at the boundary. Rounded intermediate values compound error.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `int + float` promoting to float64 surprises people.
defenseBank.answer: The dtype changes silently, so later integer division or exact equality no longer behaves as before. The promotion is correct, but it is not obvious.

defenseBank.q: Defend stating a dtype contract in a data loader.
defenseBank.answer: Every downstream step inherits the dtype, so declaring it once prevents implicit promotions and documents the memory budget.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing `dtype=np.float32` explicitly in a loader.
defenseBank.answer: The default float64 doubles memory and silently changes what downstream code receives.

defenseBank.q: Explain why casting a large float to `int8` can wrap.
defenseBank.answer: The value is forced into a fixed-width integer range, which is modular rather than saturating.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `np.can_cast` instead of trusting `astype`.
defenseBank.answer: `astype` always converts, while `can_cast` states whether information would be lost.

learn.title: Converting with astype
learn.body: astype returns a NEW array with the requested dtype and truncates floats toward zero, so 1.7 becomes 1; the original array is untouched.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.7, 2.9])
print(a.astype(int))
learn.simple: astype se array ka type badal sakte ho — jaise float se int. Ye naya array banata hai, purana waisa hi rehta hai.
learn.pro: astype returns a new array with the requested dtype and leaves the original untouched. The conversion happens element by element, so it costs a full copy and can lose information when the target type is narrower.

learn.title: Overflow is silent
learn.body: Integer dtypes wrap around on overflow instead of raising, so uint8 arithmetic can turn a large result into a small one — use a wider dtype when the range is not guaranteed.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + 10)
learn.simple: Chhote type me bada number daal do to NumPy error nahi deta — number palat kar negative ho jaata hai. Isliye type ka range check karna zaruri hai.
learn.pro: Integer overflow wraps around without warning, so int8 arithmetic above 127 becomes negative. NumPy does not raise here; guarding means checking the target dtype's range with np.iinfo before casting.

learn.title: Smaller dtype, smaller memory
learn.body: float32 uses four bytes per element against eight for float64; choosing it deliberately cuts memory and bandwidth in half, at the cost of precision.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
print(a.dtype, a.nbytes)
learn.simple: Chhota type chuniye to memory bachegi — int32, int64 se aadha leti hai. Par values us range me honi chahiye.
learn.pro: Memory scales with itemsize, so int32 halves an int64 array's footprint. The trade is range and precision: choose the narrowest dtype whose full value range the data actually fits.

learn.title: astype truncates toward zero
learn.body: Casting float to int does not round: it drops the fractional part, so 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int))
learn.simple: astype(int) round nahi karta, decimal ko kaat deta hai — 1.9 bhi 1 ban jaata hai aur −1.9 bhi −1. Pehle round karo to sahi answer milega.
learn.pro: Casting a float to an integer truncates toward zero rather than rounding. When the value must not lose its fraction, call np.round first and then cast; otherwise 1.9 and 1.1 both become 1.

learn.title: Text becomes a number with astype
learn.body: Numeric strings cast cleanly to int or float, which is exactly why one bad token in a loaded column raises instead of silently becoming zero.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(float))
learn.simple: String wale number ko astype(float) se asli number bana sakte ho — par text galat ho to error aayega.
learn.pro: astype parses numeric strings into the requested dtype and raises ValueError on anything unparsable. Parse at the boundary, before arithmetic, so a bad cell fails loudly instead of becoming a string array.

learn.title: Division always yields floats
learn.body: True division produces float64 even when both operands are integers, so `int / int` never silently loses the remainder.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2]) / 2).dtype)
learn.simple: Division (/) hamesha float deta hai, chahe dono number integer hon. Integer division ke liye // use karo.
learn.pro: True division always returns a floating dtype, even for two integers, because the result may be fractional. Use floor division (//) when an integer quotient is the intent, and expect the dtype change.

learn.title: Numbers become booleans by truthiness
learn.body: Casting to bool keeps only whether a value is non-zero, so 0 becomes False and every other number becomes True.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([0, 1, 2]).astype(bool))
learn.simple: 0 False ban jaata hai aur baaki sab (negative bhi) True. Isliye boolean conversion se sirf 'zero tha ya nahi' pata chalta hai.
learn.pro: Casting to bool follows truthiness: zero is False and every non-zero value, including negatives, is True. It answers 'was this cell zero', not 'was this cell positive'.

learn.title: Count with a boolean array
learn.body: Booleans add as 1 and 0, so sum() on a mask counts the matches without any branching code.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.sum())
learn.simple: Boolean array ka sum True ki ginti deta hai, kyunki True ko 1 gina jaata hai. Isliye mask.sum() se count milta hai.
learn.pro: A boolean array sums as ones and zeros, so sum() counts the True cells, mean() gives the fraction that pass, and any()/all() answer existence questions without a loop.

learn.title: dtype reports the element type
learn.body: The dtype belongs to the whole array, not to each element. Mixing an int and a float array promotes to float.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0]).dtype)
learn.simple: Integer list se int array banta hai, decimal list se float array. dtype batata hai kaunsa type hai.
learn.pro: dtype is inferred from the literals: an integer list yields int64, a list containing a decimal yields float64. Reading dtype first explains every later behaviour, from division to memory.

learn.title: A float array prints a decimal point
learn.body: The printed form already tells you the dtype: `[1. 2.]` is float, `[1 2]` is int. Reading the output is faster than checking.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2], dtype=float))
learn.simple: Float array me 1 bhi 1. dikhta hai — ye batata hai ki values float hain, integer nahi.
learn.pro: The trailing decimal is NumPy showing the dtype, not extra precision: [1. 2.] holds exact whole values in a float array. Use dtype=int when the values are counts and the decimal is misleading.

learn.title: Each dtype has a size in bytes
learn.body: `itemsize` is bytes per element. Ten million `int64` values need 80 MB before any copy, which is why dtype choice is a memory decision.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dtype('int64').itemsize, np.dtype('int32').itemsize)
learn.simple: Har type ka apna size hota hai — int64 ka 8 byte, int32 ka 4 byte. Isse memory ka hisaab lagta hai.
learn.pro: np.dtype(name).itemsize gives bytes per element, so int64 is 8 and int32 is 4. Multiply by the element count for the real footprint and compare before committing to a large array.

learn.title: A comparison produces booleans
learn.body: Masks are a dtype, not a special object. `bool` arrays are one byte per element and are the currency of filtering.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([1, 2, 3]) > 1).dtype)
learn.simple: Comparison ka result True/False ka array hota hai, ek single answer nahi. Usi ko mask bolte hain.
learn.pro: A comparison is elementwise, so it returns a boolean array of the same shape, never one truth value. That mask is what indexing and counting consume; wrapping it in if requires .any() or .all().

learn.title: Casting a float to an integer truncates
learn.body: astype does not round; it drops the fractional part toward zero. Convert after rounding when the value should not lose precision.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.9, -1.9, 2.5])
print(a.astype(np.int64))
print(np.round(a).astype(np.int64))
learn.simple: Round karke int banane se 1.9 ka 2 milta hai, sirf astype karne par 1 milta hai. Difference yahi hai.
learn.pro: np.round applies round-half-to-even before the cast, while astype alone truncates. The order matters for every reported total, so decide explicitly whether the business rule is rounding or truncation.

learn.title: Type promotion with result_type
learn.body: When two dtypes meet in an operation NumPy promotes to one that can hold both. result_type tells you which dtype that will be before you compute anything.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.result_type(np.int32, np.float32))
print((np.array([1], dtype=np.int8) + 0.5).dtype)
learn.simple: Do alag type milte hain to NumPy bada type chunta hai — int aur float milne par float. result_type se pehle hi pata chal jaata hai.
learn.pro: np.result_type reports the dtype an operation will produce, which is how you predict promotion before allocating the result. Mixing an int8 array with 0.5 promotes to float64, not float32, because the Python scalar is treated as a double.

interview.q: Why does adding `0.0` to an integer array change more than the values?
interview.answer: It promotes the dtype to float64, doubling memory and changing later arithmetic. Integer division and overflow are no longer possible after that promotion.

interview.q: How do you choose between `float32` and `float64`?
interview.answer: `float64` for accumulation and anything needing precision; `float32` when memory and bandwidth dominate and about seven significant digits are enough, as in many model inputs.

interview.q: What is the risk of `astype(int)` on float data?
interview.answer: It truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so 1.9 becomes 1, and it silently discards fractional data. For rounding, use `np.round` first and say so.

interview.q: What do you gain and lose with `dtype="int8"`?
interview.answer: Four times less memory than int64, at the cost of a range of only -128 to 127, so overflow becomes possible.

interview.q: What happens to a float array cast to `int32`?
interview.answer: Each value is truncated toward zero, losing the fractional part without warning.

interview.q: Why is `0.1 + 0.2` not exactly `0.3` in float64?
interview.answer: Neither decimal is representable exactly in binary, so the stored approximations add to a value one bit away from the nearest 0.3.

interview.q: What does `np.result_type` decide?
interview.answer: The dtype that a set of operands would promote to in an operation.

interview.q: How do you inspect the range of an integer dtype?
interview.answer: `np.iinfo(dtype)` gives its minimum and maximum; `np.finfo` does the same for floats.

interview.q: Why is `float16` risky for accumulation?
interview.answer: It has roughly three decimal digits, so repeated additions lose precision quickly.

interview.q: A price column is stored as float64 and cast to int to save memory; customers see 99 instead of 99.99. What went wrong?
interview.answer: astype(int) truncates toward zero, it does not round. Either round first (`np.round(price).astype(int)`) or keep cents as integers at the source; casting decimals to integers always loses the fraction.

interview.q: An int32 array of large sensor counters overflows silently negative. How would you have caught it before shipping?
interview.answer: Check np.result_type and the dtype's maximum (np.iinfo(np.int32).max) against the expected range, or promote to int64. NumPy does not raise on overflow for integer arithmetic, so the check has to be explicit.

defense.q: Defend storing coordinates as `float32`.
defense.answer: Screen and sensor coordinates rarely need more than seven digits, and halving the bytes halves bandwidth in rendering and model input. The error is far below one pixel.

defense.q: Explain integer overflow, and why `uint8` arithmetic wraps instead of raising.
defense.answer: Fixed-width integers have a fixed range, so arithmetic is modular: `uint8(200) + uint8(100)` wraps to 44. NumPy keeps the C behaviour rather than paying a check per element.

defense.q: A model expects `float32` but your pipeline produces `float64`. Defend where you convert.
defense.answer: Convert once, at the boundary where the model is called, after all precise arithmetic is finished. Converting early throws away precision the pipeline still needs and gains nothing.

defense.q: Defend float64 until a calculation reaches a money boundary.
defense.answer: Intermediate work needs precision, and rounding should happen once, deliberately, at the boundary. Rounded intermediate values compound error.

defense.q: Explain why `int + float` promoting to float64 surprises people.
defense.answer: The dtype changes silently, so later integer division or exact equality no longer behaves as before. The promotion is correct, but it is not obvious.

defense.q: Defend stating a dtype contract in a data loader.
defense.answer: Every downstream step inherits the dtype, so declaring it once prevents implicit promotions and documents the memory budget.

defense.q: Defend writing `dtype=np.float32` explicitly in a loader.
defense.answer: The default float64 doubles memory and silently changes what downstream code receives.

defense.q: Explain why casting a large float to `int8` can wrap.
defense.answer: The value is forced into a fixed-width integer range, which is modular rather than saturating.

defense.q: Defend checking `np.can_cast` instead of trusting `astype`.
defense.answer: `astype` always converts, while `can_cast` states whether information would be lost.

modules.title: Array Indexing and Selection
modules.goal: Select single values, rows and columns with basic, negative and fancy indexing, and read IndexError correctly.

topics.title: Positive and negative indexing
topics.body: Index 0 is the first element and -1 is the last, so negative indices count from the end without needing the length.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Rows and cells in 2-D
topics.body: The first index selects the row and the second the column; one index alone returns that whole row as a 1-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1, 2], a[0])

topics.title: Fancy indexing with an index array
topics.body: Passing a list of positions returns a new array of those elements in the order you asked for, which is how you reorder or sample rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[[0, 2]])

topics.title: Index with a coordinate pair
topics.body: Two indices in one bracket address a single cell, row first then column, and the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[1, 2])

topics.title: One index drops a dimension
topics.body: Indexing a single row of a (2, 3) array returns shape (3,), because that axis is consumed by the integer index.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[0].shape)

topics.title: Select a whole column
topics.body: A colon keeps the row axis and the integer picks the column, so `a[:, 1]` is the second column of every row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: Fancy indexing picks rows
topics.body: An array of indices selects in exactly the order you give it, so repeats and reordering are allowed and the output grows to match the index list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[[0, 1, 0]])

topics.title: take works along an axis
topics.body: np.take does the same selection as fancy indexing but names the axis, which makes the intent readable in longer pipelines.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(np.take(a, [2, 0], axis=1))

topics.title: Negative indices count from the end
topics.body: `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. The same rule applies to slices and to every axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[-1], a[-2])

topics.title: Slice columns of a matrix
topics.body: The colon means "every row", the number picks one column. The result loses that axis and becomes one-dimensional.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: A boolean mask filters one dimension
topics.body: The mask must match the array's shape. Elements where the mask is `True` are copied into a new, shorter array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[a > 5])

topics.title: Index with paired row and column lists
topics.body: Two index arrays are zipped, not crossed: element `i` of the result comes from row `rows[i]`, column `cols[i]`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[[0, 2], [1, 2]])

topics.title: Rows, columns and single cells
topics.body: In a 2-D array the first index picks the row and the second the column, so a[1] is a row, a[:, 1] is a column and a[1, 2] is one cell.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1])
print(a[:, 1])
print(a[1, 2])

topics.title: Ellipsis and newaxis
topics.body: Ellipsis stands for every axis you did not name, and newaxis inserts a length-one axis so a 1-D array can broadcast against a 2-D one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[..., 0].shape)
print(np.array([1, 2, 3])[np.newaxis, :].shape)

debug.title: Off-by-one on a 1-D array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[3])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[2])
debug.error: IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3

debug.title: Column index outside the row
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 2])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 1])
debug.error: IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 1 with size 2

debug.title: An index that is not an integer
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1.5])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1])
debug.error: IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices

debug.title: A row that is not there
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[5])
debug.error: IndexError: index 5 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[2])

debug.title: One index too many
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[0, 0, 0])
debug.error: IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[0, 0])

debug.title: A mask that is too short
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[np.array([True, False])])
debug.error: IndexError: boolean index did not match indexed array along axis 0; size of axis is 4 but size of corresponding boolean axis is 2
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[np.array([True, False, True, False])])

debug.title: A float index
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1.5])
debug.error: IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1])

debug.title: take past the end
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.take(np.arange(3), 5))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.take(np.arange(3), [0, 2]))
debug.error: IndexError: index 5 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3

debug.title: Indexing with text labels
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[["a"]])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[[0, 2]])
debug.error: IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices

debug.title: Deleting a position that is not there
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.delete(np.arange(3), 5))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.delete(np.arange(3), 0))
debug.error: IndexError: index 5 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3

lab.title: Index practice
lab.brief: Fetch the same value three ways: positive index, negative index and fancy indexing.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between basic and fancy indexing?
interviewBank.answer: Basic indexing (integers, slices) returns a view onto the same buffer; fancy indexing with an integer or boolean array returns a new array, so writing to it does not touch the original.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr[[1, 1]]` work while `arr[1.5]` raises?
interviewBank.answer: An integer array is a list of valid positions and may repeat them. A float is not a position at all, because positions are integral.

interviewBank.q: How do you keep rows where one column exceeds a threshold?
interviewBank.answer: Build the mask from that column, `arr[arr[:, 1] > t]`, which selects whole rows because the mask is one-dimensional over axis 0.

interviewBank.q: What does a negative index select?
interviewBank.answer: A position counted from the end, so `-1` is the last element and `-len` is the first.

interviewBank.q: How do you select a diagonal with two index arrays?
interviewBank.answer: Pass the same positions twice, `arr[np.arange(n), np.arange(n)]`, which pairs them elementwise.

interviewBank.q: Why is `arr[mask]` a copy while `arr[1:3]` is not?
interviewBank.answer: A boolean mask selects arbitrary positions, so the result cannot be described with strides. A basic slice can.

interviewBank.q: What does `arr[..., 0]` select?
interviewBank.answer: The first slice of the last axis, for any number of leading axes.

interviewBank.q: How do you select rows 1 and 3 of a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: `arr[[1, 3]]`, an integer array along axis 0.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr[mask] = 0` modify the original array?
interviewBank.answer: Boolean assignment writes into the array; only reading through a mask produces a copy.

interviewBank.q: A log array has 1000 rows and you need the last 10 rows only. Which expression keeps memory low?
interviewBank.answer: `logs[-10:]` returns a view of the last ten rows without copying the other 990. Copy only if the slice will be mutated after the original is reused.

interviewBank.q: Why does `matrix[:, 1]` give a different result shape than `matrix[:, 1:2]`, and which one should be used before subtracting a column vector?
interviewBank.answer: `matrix[:, 1]` is 1-D (shape (rows,)) while `matrix[:, 1:2]` is 2-D (shape (rows, 1)). The 2-D form broadcasts correctly against a row; the 1-D form may broadcast along the wrong axis.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.ix_` over chained bracket indexing for a rectangular selection.
defenseBank.answer: `np.ix_` builds open meshes so `arr[np.ix_(rows, cols)]` selects the outer product of the two lists. Chaining `arr[rows][:, cols]` works but copies in between and is easy to get wrong.

defenseBank.q: `arr[0][1]` and `arr[0, 1]` give the same value. Defend the second.
defenseBank.answer: The tuple form is one indexing operation on the real array; the chained form materialises an intermediate row view first. Same result, less work and clearer intent.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.take` over bracket indexing in a hot path.
defenseBank.answer: `take` makes the gather explicit and accepts an `axis`, and it can write into an `out` buffer to avoid allocating a result. That matters when the selection runs per batch.

defenseBank.q: Defend `arr[:, None]` when keeping a selected column 2-D.
defenseBank.answer: It preserves the column axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts across columns. Dropping to 1-D silently changes what later arithmetic aligns with.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a row-selection mask must be 1-D.
defenseBank.answer: It selects positions along axis 0, one boolean per row. A 2-D mask would select cells, which is a different operation.

defenseBank.q: Defend fancy indexing for drawing a shuffled batch.
defenseBank.answer: An integer array of row positions gathers exactly those rows in the requested order, with no loop and no assumption about contiguity.

defenseBank.q: Defend a mask over a list of indices for a range condition.
defenseBank.answer: The mask states the condition directly and needs no index arithmetic, so it stays correct when the data grows.

defenseBank.q: Explain why indexing with a float raises.
defenseBank.answer: Positions are integral, so a float does not identify an element.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.ix_` when selecting rows and columns together.
defenseBank.answer: It builds the outer product of the two selections instead of chaining two indexing copies.

tasks.title: Value at row two, column two

learn.title: Positive and negative indexing
learn.body: Index 0 is the first element and -1 is the last, so negative indices count from the end without needing the length.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[0], a[-1])
learn.simple: Index 0 se shuru hota hai, isliye a[0] pehla element hai. −1 se aakhri element milta hai, −2 se usse pehle wala.
learn.pro: Indices are zero-based, and negative indices count from the end, so a[-1] is the last element and a[-len(a)] is the first. An index equal to the length is out of bounds and raises IndexError.

learn.title: Rows and cells in 2-D
learn.body: The first index selects the row and the second the column; one index alone returns that whole row as a 1-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1, 2], a[0])
learn.simple: 2-D array me pehla number row batata hai, doosra column. a[1, 2] ka matlab doosri row ka teesra column.
learn.pro: For a 2-D array the first index selects the row and the second the column, so a[1, 2] is one scalar while a[0] is an entire row. Comma indexing is faster and clearer than chained brackets.

learn.title: Fancy indexing with an index array
learn.body: Passing a list of positions returns a new array of those elements in the order you asked for, which is how you reorder or sample rows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[[0, 2]])
learn.simple: List se index karne par kai elements ek saath milte hain — jaise a[[0, 2]] pehla aur teesra. Ye copy deta hai, view nahi.
learn.pro: Integer-array indexing gathers the requested positions in the order given, and it always returns a copy. That copy is why writing into a fancy-indexed result does not modify the source array.

learn.title: Index with a coordinate pair
learn.body: Two indices in one bracket address a single cell, row first then column, and the result is a scalar rather than an array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[1, 2])
learn.simple: a[1, 2] me dono number alag-alag axis ke liye hain — row aur column — isliye result ek single value hota hai.
learn.pro: A coordinate pair indexes each axis independently and returns a scalar for a 2-D array. This is different from a[[1, 2]] which selects rows 1 and 2 along the first axis.

learn.title: One index drops a dimension
learn.body: Indexing a single row of a (2, 3) array returns shape (3,), because that axis is consumed by the integer index.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[0].shape)
learn.simple: a[0] poore pehli row deta hai, aur us row ka apna shape hota hai — matrix ka shape kam ho jaata hai.
learn.pro: Basic indexing removes the indexed axis, so a (3, 4) array gives a (4,) row for a[0]. Keep the axis with a[0:1] when a downstream operation needs 2-D input.

learn.title: Select a whole column
learn.body: A colon keeps the row axis and the integer picks the column, so `a[:, 1]` is the second column of every row.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])
learn.simple: Column lene ke liye row ki jagah colon lagate hain: a[:, 1] ka matlab 'saari rows, column 1'.
learn.pro: a[:, 1] keeps every row and fixes the column, returning a 1-D array of shape (rows,). Use a[:, 1:2] when the column must stay 2-D for broadcasting against a row.

learn.title: Fancy indexing picks rows
learn.body: An array of indices selects in exactly the order you give it, so repeats and reordering are allowed and the output grows to match the index list.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[[0, 1, 0]])
learn.simple: a[[0, 1, 0]] se rows chun sakte ho, aur wahi row baar-baar bhi le sakte ho — order aur repetition aapke control me hai.
learn.pro: A list of row indices selects rows in exactly that order and may repeat them, producing a new first axis matching the list's length. The result is a copy of the selected rows, not a view.

learn.title: take works along an axis
learn.body: np.take does the same selection as fancy indexing but names the axis, which makes the intent readable in longer pipelines.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(np.take(a, [2, 0], axis=1))
learn.simple: np.take se kisi bhi axis par positions chun sakte ho — axis=1 likho to columns chunenge.
learn.pro: np.take(a, indices, axis=k) gathers along the named axis, which fancy indexing cannot express directly for axes after the first. It is the readable form for column selection by position.

learn.title: Negative indices count from the end
learn.body: `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. The same rule applies to slices and to every axis.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[-1], a[-2])
learn.simple: −1 aakhri, −2 usse pehle — count peeche se. Ye length badalne par bhi kaam karta hai.
learn.pro: Negative indices resolve as length + index, so they stay correct when the array grows or shrinks. Going past -length raises IndexError rather than clamping.

learn.title: Slice columns of a matrix
learn.body: The colon means "every row", the number picks one column. The result loses that axis and becomes one-dimensional.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])
learn.simple: Colon se 'sab' bolte hain, isliye a[:, 1] me saari rows aur sirf column 1 aata hai.
learn.pro: The colon preserves an axis and the number selects one position, so a[:, 1] returns a 1-D column. Mixing a slice with a scalar is the standard way to keep one axis while dropping another.

learn.title: A boolean mask filters one dimension
learn.body: The mask must match the array's shape. Elements where the mask is `True` are copied into a new, shorter array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[a > 5])
learn.simple: a[a > 5] me pehle True/False ka array banta hai, phir sirf True wale values chun liye jaate hain. Result chhota ho sakta hai.
learn.pro: Boolean indexing selects the cells where the mask is True and returns a 1-D copy whose length equals the True count. Because the shape can change, masks are for filtering, not for assignment of a fixed-shape block.

learn.title: Index with paired row and column lists
learn.body: Two index arrays are zipped, not crossed: element `i` of the result comes from row `rows[i]`, column `cols[i]`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[[0, 2], [1, 2]])
learn.simple: a[[0, 2], [1, 2]] me pehla list rows aur doosra columns batata hai — pairs bante hain: (0,1) aur (2,2).
learn.pro: Two index arrays broadcast position by position, so the result is a[(0,1)] and a[(2,2)], not a 2×2 block. That pairing is the most common source of surprising fancy-index results.

learn.title: Rows, columns and single cells
learn.body: In a 2-D array the first index picks the row and the second the column, so a[1] is a row, a[:, 1] is a column and a[1, 2] is one cell.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1])
print(a[:, 1])
print(a[1, 2])
learn.simple: a[1] row deta hai, a[:, 1] column, aur a[1, 2] ek hi cell. Teen tarah ke selection, teen shapes.
learn.pro: The three forms answer different questions: a[1] is a row view, a[:, 1] a column view, and a[1, 2] a scalar. Printing .shape after each is the habit that keeps multi-axis code honest.

learn.title: Ellipsis and newaxis
learn.body: Ellipsis stands for every axis you did not name, and newaxis inserts a length-one axis so a 1-D array can broadcast against a 2-D one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[..., 0].shape)
print(np.array([1, 2, 3])[np.newaxis, :].shape)
learn.simple: Ellipsis (...) bachi hui saari axes ke liye hota hai, aur np.newaxis ek nayi axis add karta hai — broadcasting ke liye kaam aata hai.
learn.pro: Ellipsis expands to every axis not named, which keeps indexing readable for 3-D and 4-D arrays. np.newaxis inserts a length-one axis, turning a (3,) vector into (1, 3) or (3, 1) to control how it broadcasts.

interview.q: What is the difference between basic and fancy indexing?
interview.answer: Basic indexing (integers, slices) returns a view onto the same buffer; fancy indexing with an integer or boolean array returns a new array, so writing to it does not touch the original.

interview.q: Why does `arr[[1, 1]]` work while `arr[1.5]` raises?
interview.answer: An integer array is a list of valid positions and may repeat them. A float is not a position at all, because positions are integral.

interview.q: How do you keep rows where one column exceeds a threshold?
interview.answer: Build the mask from that column, `arr[arr[:, 1] > t]`, which selects whole rows because the mask is one-dimensional over axis 0.

interview.q: What does a negative index select?
interview.answer: A position counted from the end, so `-1` is the last element and `-len` is the first.

interview.q: How do you select a diagonal with two index arrays?
interview.answer: Pass the same positions twice, `arr[np.arange(n), np.arange(n)]`, which pairs them elementwise.

interview.q: Why is `arr[mask]` a copy while `arr[1:3]` is not?
interview.answer: A boolean mask selects arbitrary positions, so the result cannot be described with strides. A basic slice can.

interview.q: What does `arr[..., 0]` select?
interview.answer: The first slice of the last axis, for any number of leading axes.

interview.q: How do you select rows 1 and 3 of a matrix?
interview.answer: `arr[[1, 3]]`, an integer array along axis 0.

interview.q: Why does `arr[mask] = 0` modify the original array?
interview.answer: Boolean assignment writes into the array; only reading through a mask produces a copy.

interview.q: A log array has 1000 rows and you need the last 10 rows only. Which expression keeps memory low?
interview.answer: `logs[-10:]` returns a view of the last ten rows without copying the other 990. Copy only if the slice will be mutated after the original is reused.

interview.q: Why does `matrix[:, 1]` give a different result shape than `matrix[:, 1:2]`, and which one should be used before subtracting a column vector?
interview.answer: `matrix[:, 1]` is 1-D (shape (rows,)) while `matrix[:, 1:2]` is 2-D (shape (rows, 1)). The 2-D form broadcasts correctly against a row; the 1-D form may broadcast along the wrong axis.

defense.q: Defend `np.ix_` over chained bracket indexing for a rectangular selection.
defense.answer: `np.ix_` builds open meshes so `arr[np.ix_(rows, cols)]` selects the outer product of the two lists. Chaining `arr[rows][:, cols]` works but copies in between and is easy to get wrong.

defense.q: `arr[0][1]` and `arr[0, 1]` give the same value. Defend the second.
defense.answer: The tuple form is one indexing operation on the real array; the chained form materialises an intermediate row view first. Same result, less work and clearer intent.

defense.q: Defend `np.take` over bracket indexing in a hot path.
defense.answer: `take` makes the gather explicit and accepts an `axis`, and it can write into an `out` buffer to avoid allocating a result. That matters when the selection runs per batch.

defense.q: Defend `arr[:, None]` when keeping a selected column 2-D.
defense.answer: It preserves the column axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts across columns. Dropping to 1-D silently changes what later arithmetic aligns with.

defense.q: Explain why a row-selection mask must be 1-D.
defense.answer: It selects positions along axis 0, one boolean per row. A 2-D mask would select cells, which is a different operation.

defense.q: Defend fancy indexing for drawing a shuffled batch.
defense.answer: An integer array of row positions gathers exactly those rows in the requested order, with no loop and no assumption about contiguity.

defense.q: Defend a mask over a list of indices for a range condition.
defense.answer: The mask states the condition directly and needs no index arithmetic, so it stays correct when the data grows.

defense.q: Explain why indexing with a float raises.
defense.answer: Positions are integral, so a float does not identify an element.

defense.q: Defend `np.ix_` when selecting rows and columns together.
defense.answer: It builds the outer product of the two selections instead of chaining two indexing copies.

modules.title: Slicing and Array Views
modules.goal: Slice arrays with start/stop/step, slice rows and columns, and know when a slice shares memory.

topics.title: Slice with a step
topics.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns
topics.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

topics.title: A slice is a view
topics.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

topics.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

topics.title: Slice assignment writes through
topics.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Step in both dimensions
topics.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

topics.title: Copy breaks the view link
topics.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

topics.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
topics.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

topics.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
topics.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

topics.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
topics.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

topics.title: A step of two skips elements
topics.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns at once
topics.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

topics.title: Writing through a slice edits the original
topics.body: Slicing returns a view of the same buffer, so writing through the slice changes the original. Use copy when the two must be independent.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a, b)

topics.title: Reverse with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the axis backwards and keeps the shape otherwise unchanged. The same syntax works per axis on a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1])
print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])[::-1, ::-1])
