lab.title: Slice a matrix
lab.brief: From a 4x4 matrix, print the top-left 2x2 block and the last column.

interviewBank.q: When does a slice return a view rather than a copy?
interviewBank.answer: Always for basic slicing: it only changes offset, shape and strides on the existing buffer. Fancy indexing and boolean masks are the operations that copy.

interviewBank.q: Why does assigning to a slice change the original array?
interviewBank.answer: The slice shares the buffer, so the assignment writes through it. Use `.copy()` when the caller must keep the original intact.

interviewBank.q: What does a negative step such as `arr[::-1]` actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It reverses the traversal by negating the stride; no data moves, so the result is a view that reads backwards.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `arr[::2]` and `arr[1::2]`?
interviewBank.answer: The first takes even positions starting at 0; the second starts at 1 and takes every second value after it.

interviewBank.q: How do you reverse only the rows of a 2-D array?
interviewBank.answer: Use `arr[::-1]`, which flips axis 0 and leaves the columns in order.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr[2:2]` return an empty array instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: A slice with equal bounds is a legal empty selection, not an error, which keeps loop code simple.

interviewBank.q: What does a slice with step -1 return?
interviewBank.answer: A reversed view over the same buffer, with no data moved.

interviewBank.q: How do you take every second row of a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: `arr[::2]`, which slices axis 0 and keeps the columns.

interviewBank.q: Why is `arr[:]` not a copy?
interviewBank.answer: It is a full slice of the same buffer, so writes through it reach the original.

interviewBank.q: A rolling window is extracted with `series[i:i+window]` and stored in a list; later someone edits one window and the whole series changes. Why?
interviewBank.answer: Each slice is a view of the same buffer, so editing the window edits the series. Copy the window (`series[i:i+window].copy()`) when it will be stored and modified independently.

interviewBank.q: Reversing a 200 MB price series with `[::-1]` takes almost no time. What did NumPy actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It returned a view with negative strides — no data was moved. Any operation that needs contiguous order (such as some libraries' C-API calls) will copy later, which is where the cost appears.

defenseBank.q: Defend calling `.copy()` when trimming a training set.
defenseBank.answer: A slice keeps the whole original buffer alive, so a small training split can pin a large dataset in memory. The copy lets the original be freed.

defenseBank.q: Explain how `arr[1:3] = 0` can surprise a caller who still holds a slice of `arr`.
defenseBank.answer: Both names point at the same buffer, so the write is visible through the slice too. That aliasing is the source of many "the data changed by itself" reports.

defenseBank.q: A slice with step 2 has non-contiguous strides. Defend that as a feature, not a bug.
defenseBank.answer: Strides describe how to walk the buffer, so a step of 2 is just a doubled stride. Nothing is copied, and any ufunc reads the elements correctly.

defenseBank.q: Defend clamping slice bounds in a parser.
defenseBank.answer: Input lengths vary, and Python slicing already clamps, so explicit `min(n, len(a))` documents the intent without changing behaviour.

defenseBank.q: Explain why writing to `arr[:, 0]` changes every reference to that array.
defenseBank.answer: The column is a view on the shared buffer, so assignment writes real memory rather than a copy. Any other name for that array sees it.

defenseBank.q: Defend a negative-step slice over `np.flip` when trimming.
defenseBank.answer: It expresses the reversal without a function call and returns a view, so it is cheaper when no copy is needed.

defenseBank.q: Defend copying a slice before handing it to another function.
defenseBank.answer: The callee may mutate it, and a view would change the caller's data as a side effect.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a slice can keep a large source array alive.
defenseBank.answer: The view holds a reference to the buffer, so the whole allocation stays in memory.

defenseBank.q: Defend slicing over fancy indexing for contiguous blocks.
defenseBank.answer: A slice needs no gather and returns a view, while fancy indexing always copies.

learn.title: Slice with a step
learn.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns
learn.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

learn.title: A slice is a view
learn.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

learn.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
learn.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

learn.title: Slice assignment writes through
learn.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

learn.title: Step in both dimensions
learn.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

learn.title: Copy breaks the view link
learn.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

learn.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
learn.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

learn.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
learn.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

learn.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
learn.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

learn.title: A step of two skips elements
learn.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns at once
learn.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

learn.title: Writing through a slice edits the original
learn.body: Slicing returns a view of the same buffer, so writing through the slice changes the original. Use copy when the two must be independent.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a, b)

learn.title: Reverse with a negative step
learn.body: A step of -1 walks the axis backwards and keeps the shape otherwise unchanged. The same syntax works per axis on a 2-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1])
print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])[::-1, ::-1])

interview.q: When does a slice return a view rather than a copy?
interview.answer: Always for basic slicing: it only changes offset, shape and strides on the existing buffer. Fancy indexing and boolean masks are the operations that copy.

interview.q: Why does assigning to a slice change the original array?
interview.answer: The slice shares the buffer, so the assignment writes through it. Use `.copy()` when the caller must keep the original intact.

interview.q: What does a negative step such as `arr[::-1]` actually do?
interview.answer: It reverses the traversal by negating the stride; no data moves, so the result is a view that reads backwards.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr[::2]` and `arr[1::2]`?
interview.answer: The first takes even positions starting at 0; the second starts at 1 and takes every second value after it.

interview.q: How do you reverse only the rows of a 2-D array?
interview.answer: Use `arr[::-1]`, which flips axis 0 and leaves the columns in order.

interview.q: Why does `arr[2:2]` return an empty array instead of raising?
interview.answer: A slice with equal bounds is a legal empty selection, not an error, which keeps loop code simple.

interview.q: What does a slice with step -1 return?
interview.answer: A reversed view over the same buffer, with no data moved.

interview.q: How do you take every second row of a matrix?
interview.answer: `arr[::2]`, which slices axis 0 and keeps the columns.

interview.q: Why is `arr[:]` not a copy?
interview.answer: It is a full slice of the same buffer, so writes through it reach the original.

interview.q: A rolling window is extracted with `series[i:i+window]` and stored in a list; later someone edits one window and the whole series changes. Why?
interview.answer: Each slice is a view of the same buffer, so editing the window edits the series. Copy the window (`series[i:i+window].copy()`) when it will be stored and modified independently.

interview.q: Reversing a 200 MB price series with `[::-1]` takes almost no time. What did NumPy actually do?
interview.answer: It returned a view with negative strides — no data was moved. Any operation that needs contiguous order (such as some libraries' C-API calls) will copy later, which is where the cost appears.

defense.q: Defend calling `.copy()` when trimming a training set.
defense.answer: A slice keeps the whole original buffer alive, so a small training split can pin a large dataset in memory. The copy lets the original be freed.

defense.q: Explain how `arr[1:3] = 0` can surprise a caller who still holds a slice of `arr`.
defense.answer: Both names point at the same buffer, so the write is visible through the slice too. That aliasing is the source of many "the data changed by itself" reports.

defense.q: A slice with step 2 has non-contiguous strides. Defend that as a feature, not a bug.
defense.answer: Strides describe how to walk the buffer, so a step of 2 is just a doubled stride. Nothing is copied, and any ufunc reads the elements correctly.

defense.q: Defend clamping slice bounds in a parser.
defense.answer: Input lengths vary, and Python slicing already clamps, so explicit `min(n, len(a))` documents the intent without changing behaviour.

defense.q: Explain why writing to `arr[:, 0]` changes every reference to that array.
defense.answer: The column is a view on the shared buffer, so assignment writes real memory rather than a copy. Any other name for that array sees it.

defense.q: Defend a negative-step slice over `np.flip` when trimming.
defense.answer: It expresses the reversal without a function call and returns a view, so it is cheaper when no copy is needed.

defense.q: Defend copying a slice before handing it to another function.
defense.answer: The callee may mutate it, and a view would change the caller's data as a side effect.

defense.q: Explain why a slice can keep a large source array alive.
defense.answer: The view holds a reference to the buffer, so the whole allocation stays in memory.

defense.q: Defend slicing over fancy indexing for contiguous blocks.
defense.answer: A slice needs no gather and returns a view, while fancy indexing always copies.

modules.title: Array Reshaping and Manipulation
modules.goal: Reshape, flatten, transpose, combine and split arrays so data fits the shape an operation needs.

topics.title: reshape
topics.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

topics.title: ravel and transpose
topics.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

topics.title: concatenate and stack
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

topics.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
topics.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

topics.title: newaxis makes a column
topics.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[:, np.newaxis].shape)

topics.title: stack adds a new axis
topics.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

topics.title: vstack stacks arrays into rows

topics.title: Transpose swaps the axes

topics.title: reshape returns a view when it can

interviewBank.q: What does `reshape(-1, 3)` mean?
interviewBank.answer: Three columns are fixed and the row count is inferred from the total element count. It fails if the size is not divisible by three.

interviewBank.q: How do `ravel`, `flatten` and `reshape(-1)` differ?
interviewBank.answer: `ravel` returns a view when it can, `flatten` always copies, and `reshape(-1)` is a view when the memory layout allows it.

interviewBank.q: When do you use `stack` rather than `concatenate`?
interviewBank.answer: `stack` adds a new axis and requires equal shapes; `concatenate` joins along an existing axis of the same rank.

interviewBank.q: What does `reshape` require about the element count?
interviewBank.answer: The target shape must hold exactly the same number of elements, or NumPy raises instead of padding.

interviewBank.q: How do you add a batch axis to one sample?
interviewBank.answer: `sample[np.newaxis, ...]` or `expand_dims(sample, 0)`, giving shape `(1, ...)` that a batched model accepts.

interviewBank.q: Why does `ravel()` sometimes copy?
interviewBank.answer: When the memory layout cannot be traversed in the requested order with strides, it must materialise a contiguous copy.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.concatenate` require of its inputs?
interviewBank.answer: Matching ranks and matching shapes on every axis except the one being joined.

interviewBank.q: How do you turn a column into a row?
interviewBank.answer: `arr.reshape(1, -1)`, or `.T` when the data is genuinely a matrix.

interviewBank.q: Why does `flatten()` always copy?
interviewBank.answer: It guarantees a new contiguous array, independent of the source layout.

interviewBank.q: A model expects (samples, features) but the loader produced (features, samples). Which fix is safer: reshape, transpose or resize?
interviewBank.answer: Transpose (`.T`) or reshape with explicit dimensions; resize is not a NumPy ndarray method and reshape alone can scramble the value order. Verify with a known 2×3 array before trusting the shape.

interviewBank.q: Two arrays of shape (100, 3) are joined with np.vstack and the result is (200, 3). Was np.concatenate with axis=0 the same thing here?
interviewBank.answer: Yes — vstack is concatenate along axis 0 after promoting 1-D inputs to rows. The distinction matters for 1-D inputs, where vstack adds a row axis and concatenate does not.

defenseBank.q: Defend C order for a freshly built feature matrix.
defenseBank.answer: Rows are samples and each row is contiguous, so slicing a sample or feeding a row-major consumer reads sequential memory. Fortran order is for column-major consumers.

defenseBank.q: How do you know whether a reshape copied?
defenseBank.answer: Check `result.base is not None` or `np.shares_memory(original, result)`. A reshape copies only when the requested order cannot be expressed with strides.

defenseBank.q: A model wants `(N, C, H, W)` and your data is `(N, H, W, C)`. Defend the transformation you choose.
defenseBank.answer: Move the channel axis with `transpose(0, 3, 1, 2)` rather than reshaping, because reshaping would interleave values instead of permuting axes, and follow it with `ascontiguousarray` if the model needs contiguous input.

defenseBank.q: Defend `reshape(-1)` at the end of a feature pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: It states that the flattened length is whatever the data implies, so a changed batch size does not break the call.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `concatenate` needs matching ranks.
defenseBank.answer: It joins along an existing axis, so every operand must have the same number of axes and match on the others. `stack` is the operation that adds an axis.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing images as `(N, H, W, C)`.
defenseBank.answer: Channels last keeps each pixel's channels adjacent, which matches how most image decoders write memory and what many frameworks accept.

defenseBank.q: Defend `reshape` over `flatten` in a hot path.
defenseBank.answer: Reshape returns a view when the layout allows it, so it avoids a full copy.

defenseBank.q: Explain why reshaping after a transpose may not be a view.
defenseBank.answer: The memory order no longer matches the requested traversal, so NumPy must materialise a copy.

defenseBank.q: Defend stacking with a named axis over transposing afterwards.
defenseBank.answer: The axis is stated where the array is created, which is easier to check than a later permutation.

learn.title: reshape
learn.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

learn.title: ravel and transpose
learn.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

learn.title: concatenate and stack
learn.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
learn.code:

a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

learn.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
learn.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.

print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

learn.title: newaxis makes a column
learn.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.

learn.title: stack adds a new axis
learn.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
learn.code:

print(np.stack([np.zeros(2), np.ones(2)]).shape)

interview.q: What does `reshape(-1, 3)` mean?
interview.answer: Three columns are fixed and the row count is inferred from the total element count. It fails if the size is not divisible by three.

interview.q: How do `ravel`, `flatten` and `reshape(-1)` differ?
interview.answer: `ravel` returns a view when it can, `flatten` always copies, and `reshape(-1)` is a view when the memory layout allows it.

interview.q: When do you use `stack` rather than `concatenate`?
interview.answer: `stack` adds a new axis and requires equal shapes; `concatenate` joins along an existing axis of the same rank.

interview.q: What does `reshape` require about the element count?
interview.answer: The target shape must hold exactly the same number of elements, or NumPy raises instead of padding.

interview.q: How do you add a batch axis to one sample?
interview.answer: `sample[np.newaxis, ...]` or `expand_dims(sample, 0)`, giving shape `(1, ...)` that a batched model accepts.

interview.q: Why does `ravel()` sometimes copy?
interview.answer: When the memory layout cannot be traversed in the requested order with strides, it must materialise a contiguous copy.

interview.q: What does `np.concatenate` require of its inputs?
interview.answer: Matching ranks and matching shapes on every axis except the one being joined.

interview.q: How do you turn a column into a row?
interview.answer: `arr.reshape(1, -1)`, or `.T` when the data is genuinely a matrix.

interview.q: Why does `flatten()` always copy?
interview.answer: It guarantees a new contiguous array, independent of the source layout.

interview.q: A model expects (samples, features) but the loader produced (features, samples). Which fix is safer: reshape, transpose or resize?
interview.answer: Transpose (`.T`) or reshape with explicit dimensions; resize is not a NumPy ndarray method and reshape alone can scramble the value order. Verify with a known 2×3 array before trusting the shape.

interview.q: Two arrays of shape (100, 3) are joined with np.vstack and the result is (200, 3). Was np.concatenate with axis=0 the same thing here?
interview.answer: Yes — vstack is concatenate along axis 0 after promoting 1-D inputs to rows. The distinction matters for 1-D inputs, where vstack adds a row axis and concatenate does not.

defense.q: Defend C order for a freshly built feature matrix.
defense.answer: Rows are samples and each row is contiguous, so slicing a sample or feeding a row-major consumer reads sequential memory. Fortran order is for column-major consumers.

defense.q: How do you know whether a reshape copied?
defense.answer: Check `result.base is not None` or `np.shares_memory(original, result)`. A reshape copies only when the requested order cannot be expressed with strides.

defense.q: A model wants `(N, C, H, W)` and your data is `(N, H, W, C)`. Defend the transformation you choose.
defense.answer: Move the channel axis with `transpose(0, 3, 1, 2)` rather than reshaping, because reshaping would interleave values instead of permuting axes, and follow it with `ascontiguousarray` if the model needs contiguous input.

defense.q: Defend `reshape(-1)` at the end of a feature pipeline.
defense.answer: It states that the flattened length is whatever the data implies, so a changed batch size does not break the call.

defense.q: Explain why `concatenate` needs matching ranks.
defense.answer: It joins along an existing axis, so every operand must have the same number of axes and match on the others. `stack` is the operation that adds an axis.

defense.q: Defend storing images as `(N, H, W, C)`.
defense.answer: Channels last keeps each pixel's channels adjacent, which matches how most image decoders write memory and what many frameworks accept.

defense.q: Defend `reshape` over `flatten` in a hot path.
defense.answer: Reshape returns a view when the layout allows it, so it avoids a full copy.

defense.q: Explain why reshaping after a transpose may not be a view.
defense.answer: The memory order no longer matches the requested traversal, so NumPy must materialise a copy.

defense.q: Defend stacking with a named axis over transposing afterwards.
defense.answer: The axis is stated where the array is created, which is easier to check than a later permutation.

modules.title: Array Operations and Universal Functions
modules.goal: Use arithmetic, math and comparison ufuncs elementwise, and read a ufunc type error correctly.

topics.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
topics.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

topics.title: Math ufuncs
topics.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

topics.title: Comparisons produce masks
topics.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

topics.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
topics.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

topics.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
topics.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: clip limits every element
topics.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

topics.title: round, floor and ceil differ
topics.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

topics.title: sign tells you direction
topics.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

topics.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
topics.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

topics.title: abs works on whole arrays
topics.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

topics.title: cumsum keeps every running total
topics.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: log and exp invert each other
topics.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

topics.title: reduce and accumulate
topics.body: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))

topics.title: Never compare floats with ==
topics.body: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

lab.title: Vectorised calculator
lab.brief: Compute square root, square and absolute value of one array in three lines.

interviewBank.q: What is a ufunc?
interviewBank.answer: A compiled elementwise operation with its own loop selection, broadcasting and dtype resolution, plus methods such as `reduce`, `accumulate` and `outer`.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.sqrt` on an array faster than `math.sqrt` in a loop?
interviewBank.answer: The ufunc dispatches once and loops in C over a typed buffer, while the Python loop pays call, type and attribute overhead per element.

interviewBank.q: What does passing `out=` buy you?
interviewBank.answer: The result is written into an existing array, so no allocation happens and repeated calls reuse memory, which matters in hot loops over large arrays.

interviewBank.q: Is `np.add(a, b)` different from `a + b`?
interviewBank.answer: No: `+` calls the same ufunc. The explicit form matters when you need ufunc methods or an `out` buffer.

interviewBank.q: How do you apply a ufunc per row instead of globally?
interviewBank.answer: Apply it elementwise as usual, then reduce with the ufunc's method, for example `np.add.reduce(arr, axis=1)`.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.divide` return `inf` on a zero denominator instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: A ufunc processes a whole buffer and cannot abort on one element, so it follows IEEE semantics and warns.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.add.reduce` do?
interviewBank.answer: It applies the ufunc pairwise along an axis, producing that reduction.

interviewBank.q: How do you compute a running product?
interviewBank.answer: `np.multiply.accumulate(arr)`.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.exp` overflow instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: The ufunc follows float semantics and returns `inf` with a warning.

interviewBank.q: A revenue calculation is off by 0.01 in the last row. Is the formula wrong?
interviewBank.answer: Almost certainly not — binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality checks and repeated additions drift. Compare with np.isclose and round only for display, not for intermediate maths.

interviewBank.q: A running total is needed per row. Which is cheaper: a Python loop with a counter or np.add.accumulate?
interviewBank.answer: accumulate runs one compiled pass and allocates one output array; the loop pays interpreter overhead per element. For very long arrays the difference is orders of magnitude.

defenseBank.q: Defend clipping model predictions into `[0, 1]`.
defenseBank.answer: A metric or downstream consumer may assume a probability range, and clipping states that contract explicitly instead of letting outliers through.

defenseBank.q: Why does `np.sqrt(-1)` return `nan` instead of raising?
defenseBank.answer: The ufunc runs over a whole buffer and cannot stop on one element; it reports the domain error as `nan` and warns via `np.errstate`. Check with `np.isnan` when it matters.

defenseBank.q: A reviewer asks for a Python loop because it is easier to read. Defend a ufunc for 10 million rows.
defenseBank.answer: Ten million Python iterations cost seconds of interpreter overhead and allocate per element, while the ufunc loops in C. Readability is served by naming the vectorised step.

defenseBank.q: Defend wrapping a risky division in `np.errstate`.
defenseBank.answer: It states that division by zero is expected here, so the warning is suppressed deliberately rather than flooding logs. The handling stays local.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.abs` on a boolean array is meaningless.
defenseBank.answer: A boolean has no magnitude beyond true or false, so the operation either errors or silently converts. Use the values you actually mean.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.clip` over an `if` per element.
defenseBank.answer: One vectorised call replaces a Python loop and handles both bounds consistently, including for non-finite inputs.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.errstate(over="raise")` in a numerical pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: It turns a silent infinity into a failure you can locate.

defenseBank.q: Explain why applying a ufunc to a Python list returns an array.
defenseBank.answer: The ufunc converts the input to an array before it runs.

defenseBank.q: Defend using `out=` for a repeated large computation.
defenseBank.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call and keeps peak memory predictable.

learn.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
learn.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

learn.title: Math ufuncs
learn.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

learn.title: Comparisons produce masks
learn.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

learn.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
learn.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

learn.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
learn.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

learn.title: clip limits every element
learn.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

learn.title: round, floor and ceil differ
learn.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

learn.title: sign tells you direction
learn.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

learn.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
learn.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

learn.title: abs works on whole arrays
learn.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

learn.title: cumsum keeps every running total
learn.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

learn.title: log and exp invert each other
learn.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

learn.title: reduce and accumulate
learn.body: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))

learn.title: Never compare floats with ==
learn.body: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

interview.q: What is a ufunc?
interview.answer: A compiled elementwise operation with its own loop selection, broadcasting and dtype resolution, plus methods such as `reduce`, `accumulate` and `outer`.

interview.q: Why is `np.sqrt` on an array faster than `math.sqrt` in a loop?
interview.answer: The ufunc dispatches once and loops in C over a typed buffer, while the Python loop pays call, type and attribute overhead per element.

interview.q: What does passing `out=` buy you?
interview.answer: The result is written into an existing array, so no allocation happens and repeated calls reuse memory, which matters in hot loops over large arrays.

interview.q: Is `np.add(a, b)` different from `a + b`?
interview.answer: No: `+` calls the same ufunc. The explicit form matters when you need ufunc methods or an `out` buffer.

interview.q: How do you apply a ufunc per row instead of globally?
interview.answer: Apply it elementwise as usual, then reduce with the ufunc's method, for example `np.add.reduce(arr, axis=1)`.

interview.q: Why does `np.divide` return `inf` on a zero denominator instead of raising?
interview.answer: A ufunc processes a whole buffer and cannot abort on one element, so it follows IEEE semantics and warns.

interview.q: What does `np.add.reduce` do?
interview.answer: It applies the ufunc pairwise along an axis, producing that reduction.

interview.q: How do you compute a running product?
interview.answer: `np.multiply.accumulate(arr)`.

interview.q: Why does `np.exp` overflow instead of raising?
interview.answer: The ufunc follows float semantics and returns `inf` with a warning.

interview.q: A revenue calculation is off by 0.01 in the last row. Is the formula wrong?
interview.answer: Almost certainly not — binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality checks and repeated additions drift. Compare with np.isclose and round only for display, not for intermediate maths.

interview.q: A running total is needed per row. Which is cheaper: a Python loop with a counter or np.add.accumulate?
interview.answer: accumulate runs one compiled pass and allocates one output array; the loop pays interpreter overhead per element. For very long arrays the difference is orders of magnitude.

defense.q: Defend clipping model predictions into `[0, 1]`.
defense.answer: A metric or downstream consumer may assume a probability range, and clipping states that contract explicitly instead of letting outliers through.

defense.q: Why does `np.sqrt(-1)` return `nan` instead of raising?
defense.answer: The ufunc runs over a whole buffer and cannot stop on one element; it reports the domain error as `nan` and warns via `np.errstate`. Check with `np.isnan` when it matters.

defense.q: A reviewer asks for a Python loop because it is easier to read. Defend a ufunc for 10 million rows.
defense.answer: Ten million Python iterations cost seconds of interpreter overhead and allocate per element, while the ufunc loops in C. Readability is served by naming the vectorised step.

defense.q: Defend wrapping a risky division in `np.errstate`.
defense.answer: It states that division by zero is expected here, so the warning is suppressed deliberately rather than flooding logs. The handling stays local.

defense.q: Explain why `np.abs` on a boolean array is meaningless.
defense.answer: A boolean has no magnitude beyond true or false, so the operation either errors or silently converts. Use the values you actually mean.

defense.q: Defend `np.clip` over an `if` per element.
defense.answer: One vectorised call replaces a Python loop and handles both bounds consistently, including for non-finite inputs.

defense.q: Defend `np.errstate(over="raise")` in a numerical pipeline.
defense.answer: It turns a silent infinity into a failure you can locate.

defense.q: Explain why applying a ufunc to a Python list returns an array.
defense.answer: The ufunc converts the input to an array before it runs.

defense.q: Defend using `out=` for a repeated large computation.
defense.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call and keeps peak memory predictable.

print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))
checkpoint.answer: True

checkpoint.q: Short answer: state what this log and exp invert each other code computes, and why the printed result looks the way it does.
checkpoint.answer: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
rubric: Names the operation, not just the output: log and exp invert each other.
Mentions the concrete values or shape involved (True).

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about reduce and accumulate.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))

checkpoint.q: Short answer: state what this reduce and accumulate code computes, and why the printed result looks the way it does.
checkpoint.answer: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
rubric: Names the operation, not just the output: reduce and accumulate.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about never compare floats with ==.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
checkpoint.answer:
False
True

checkpoint.q: Short answer: state what this never compare floats with == code computes, and why the printed result looks the way it does.
checkpoint.answer: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.

modules.title: Broadcasting
modules.goal: Apply the broadcasting rules to scalars, rows and columns, and fix incompatible-shape errors.

topics.title: Scalar broadcasting
topics.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Row and column broadcasting
topics.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

topics.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
topics.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

topics.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: A column broadcasts down
topics.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

topics.title: Outer product uses two new axes
topics.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

topics.title: Comparison broadcasts too
topics.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

topics.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
topics.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

topics.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

topics.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
topics.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Broadcast a column against a row
topics.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

topics.title: A size of one stretches automatically
topics.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

topics.title: A column broadcasts against a row
topics.body: Shape (3, 1) against (1, 4) stretches both to (3, 4): each row value meets each column value. That single rule is how standardising every column is written without a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
col = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])
row = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4]])
print(col + row)

topics.title: expand_dims adds the axis explicitly
topics.body: expand_dims is the function form of newaxis: it inserts a length-one axis at the position you name, which makes the intended broadcast shape obvious in code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.shape, np.expand_dims(a, 0).shape, np.expand_dims(a, 1).shape)

debug.fix:

print(np.broadcast_shapes((2, 1), (1, 3)))

arr *= np.ones((2, 3))
print(arr)

arr = np.ones(3)
arr *= np.ones(3)
print(arr)

lab.title: Broadcast a batch
lab.brief: Apply three per-feature weights to a (4, 3) batch and prove the output shape stays (4, 3).

interviewBank.q: State the broadcasting rules in one sentence.
interviewBank.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair of axes must be equal or one of them must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as 1.

interviewBank.q: Why does `(3, 1) + (1, 4)` produce a `(3, 4)` grid?
interviewBank.answer: The first operand varies down rows and the second across columns, so every combination is paired exactly once.

interviewBank.q: How do you subtract a per-column mean from a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: Compute `arr.mean(axis=0)`, which has shape `(n_features,)`, and subtract it; the trailing axis aligns with the columns.

interviewBank.q: What happens when a `(2, 3)` array is added to a `(3,)` array?
interviewBank.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis and is reused for both rows, producing `(2, 3)`.

interviewBank.q: Why can a scalar broadcast against any shape?
interviewBank.answer: It has no axes to conflict with, so it applies to every element.

interviewBank.q: How do you build an outer product with broadcasting?
interviewBank.answer: Make one operand a column and the other a row, `a[:, None] * b[None, :]`, and the result is the full grid.

interviewBank.q: How do you subtract a row vector from every row of a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: Compute the vector with shape `(n_features,)` and subtract it; it aligns with the columns.

interviewBank.q: What shape does `(4, 1, 3) + (2, 1)` produce?
interviewBank.answer: `(4, 2, 3)`, after the trailing axes align.

interviewBank.q: Why is broadcasting not a copy?
interviewBank.answer: The smaller array is read with zero strides rather than materialised across the larger shape.

interviewBank.q: A store table has shape (500, 1) of discounts and a product table (1, 12) of prices. What happens on addition, and how much memory does the result take?
interviewBank.answer: Both broadcast to (500, 12): every product price meets every store discount. The result is materialised, so it costs 500×12 values even though the inputs are tiny — a real memory risk at scale.

interviewBank.q: An operation fails with 'operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3, 1)'. What is the actual mismatch?
interviewBank.answer: The trailing dimensions must match or be 1: (4,) is treated as (1, 4), which cannot pair with (3, 1) on the last axis (4 vs 1 is fine, but 1 vs 3 on the first axis gives 4 vs 3 ... ). Fix by reshaping to (4, 1) or (1, 3) so the intended axis pairs.

defenseBank.q: Defend standardising columns with broadcasting instead of a loop over columns.
defenseBank.answer: One subtraction and one division do the whole matrix with no Python loop, and the shape of the statistic documents that it is per column.

defenseBank.q: Describe a bug caused by mixing `(3,)` and `(3, 1)`.
defenseBank.answer: The `(3,)` vector aligns with the last axis, so adding it to a `(3, 3)` matrix adds along columns, not rows. The code runs and returns a plausible but wrong answer.

defenseBank.q: Broadcasting a `(1000, 1) + (1, 1000)` allocates a million values. Defend when that is acceptable.
defenseBank.answer: It is fine when the result is genuinely needed at that size and fits in memory. If only a reduction is wanted, use `einsum` or `sum` with an axis to avoid materialising it.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing shapes in comments beside broadcast arithmetic.
defenseBank.answer: The same expression means different things for `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`, and a comment makes the intended axis explicit for the next reader.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a column times a row is not a dot product.
defenseBank.answer: Broadcasting multiplies every pair and keeps both axes, while a dot product contracts the shared axis into one number.

defenseBank.q: Defend reshaping explicitly before an operation that relies on broadcasting.
defenseBank.answer: An explicit shape states which axis is being aligned, so a later data change fails loudly instead of broadcasting in the wrong direction.

defenseBank.q: Defend explicit `reshape` over relying on broadcast alignment.
defenseBank.answer: The intended axis is stated, so a shape change fails loudly instead of broadcasting the wrong way.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `(3,) + (3, 1)` gives `(3, 3)`.
defenseBank.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis, so every pair is combined into a grid.

defenseBank.q: Defend computing a reduction instead of materialising a broadcast grid.
defenseBank.answer: The reduction is far smaller and avoids allocating the full grid.

interview.q: State the broadcasting rules in one sentence.
interview.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair of axes must be equal or one of them must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as 1.

interview.q: Why does `(3, 1) + (1, 4)` produce a `(3, 4)` grid?
interview.answer: The first operand varies down rows and the second across columns, so every combination is paired exactly once.

interview.q: How do you subtract a per-column mean from a matrix?
interview.answer: Compute `arr.mean(axis=0)`, which has shape `(n_features,)`, and subtract it; the trailing axis aligns with the columns.

interview.q: What happens when a `(2, 3)` array is added to a `(3,)` array?
interview.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis and is reused for both rows, producing `(2, 3)`.

interview.q: Why can a scalar broadcast against any shape?
interview.answer: It has no axes to conflict with, so it applies to every element.

interview.q: How do you build an outer product with broadcasting?
interview.answer: Make one operand a column and the other a row, `a[:, None] * b[None, :]`, and the result is the full grid.

interview.q: How do you subtract a row vector from every row of a matrix?
interview.answer: Compute the vector with shape `(n_features,)` and subtract it; it aligns with the columns.

interview.q: What shape does `(4, 1, 3) + (2, 1)` produce?
interview.answer: `(4, 2, 3)`, after the trailing axes align.

interview.q: Why is broadcasting not a copy?
interview.answer: The smaller array is read with zero strides rather than materialised across the larger shape.

interview.q: A store table has shape (500, 1) of discounts and a product table (1, 12) of prices. What happens on addition, and how much memory does the result take?
interview.answer: Both broadcast to (500, 12): every product price meets every store discount. The result is materialised, so it costs 500×12 values even though the inputs are tiny — a real memory risk at scale.

interview.q: An operation fails with 'operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3, 1)'. What is the actual mismatch?
interview.answer: The trailing dimensions must match or be 1: (4,) is treated as (1, 4), which cannot pair with (3, 1) on the last axis (4 vs 1 is fine, but 1 vs 3 on the first axis gives 4 vs 3 ... ). Fix by reshaping to (4, 1) or (1, 3) so the intended axis pairs.

defense.q: Defend standardising columns with broadcasting instead of a loop over columns.
defense.answer: One subtraction and one division do the whole matrix with no Python loop, and the shape of the statistic documents that it is per column.

defense.q: Describe a bug caused by mixing `(3,)` and `(3, 1)`.
defense.answer: The `(3,)` vector aligns with the last axis, so adding it to a `(3, 3)` matrix adds along columns, not rows. The code runs and returns a plausible but wrong answer.

defense.q: Broadcasting a `(1000, 1) + (1, 1000)` allocates a million values. Defend when that is acceptable.
defense.answer: It is fine when the result is genuinely needed at that size and fits in memory. If only a reduction is wanted, use `einsum` or `sum` with an axis to avoid materialising it.

defense.q: Defend writing shapes in comments beside broadcast arithmetic.
defense.answer: The same expression means different things for `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`, and a comment makes the intended axis explicit for the next reader.

defense.q: Explain why a column times a row is not a dot product.
defense.answer: Broadcasting multiplies every pair and keeps both axes, while a dot product contracts the shared axis into one number.

defense.q: Defend reshaping explicitly before an operation that relies on broadcasting.
defense.answer: An explicit shape states which axis is being aligned, so a later data change fails loudly instead of broadcasting in the wrong direction.

defense.q: Defend explicit `reshape` over relying on broadcast alignment.
defense.answer: The intended axis is stated, so a shape change fails loudly instead of broadcasting the wrong way.

defense.q: Explain why `(3,) + (3, 1)` gives `(3, 3)`.
defense.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis, so every pair is combined into a grid.

defense.q: Defend computing a reduction instead of materialising a broadcast grid.
defense.answer: The reduction is far smaller and avoids allocating the full grid.

modules.title: Aggregation and Statistics
modules.goal: Summarise arrays with sum, mean, std, argmin and cumulative functions along a chosen axis.

topics.title: Mean along an axis
topics.body: Without an axis every element is reduced to one number; with axis=1 each ROW is reduced, so a (2, 2) array gives two means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(), a.mean(axis=1))

topics.title: Standard deviation and variance
topics.body: var is the mean squared deviation and std is its square root; both use ddof=0 by default, which is the population form.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a.std(), a.var())

topics.title: Position and running totals
topics.body: argmin returns WHERE the smallest value is (not the value) and cumsum returns the running total at every position.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(a.argmin(), a.cumsum())

topics.title: median is not the mean
topics.body: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median, so reporting both is how you notice a skewed column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.median([1, 2, 100]), np.mean([1, 2, 100]))

topics.title: keepdims keeps a column
topics.body: keepdims=True leaves the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array without a reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: average can weight values
topics.body: np.average accepts weights, so a weighted mean is one call instead of a manual sum of products divided by a sum of weights.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 2], weights=[1, 3]))

topics.title: any and all answer yes/no
topics.body: On a boolean array, any asks whether at least one element is True and all asks whether every element is, each returning a single bool.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False])
print(m.any(), m.all())

topics.title: prod multiplies the elements
topics.body: prod folds with multiplication instead of addition, which is how compound growth and factorial-style products are computed in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.prod(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])))

topics.title: mean of a matrix returns one number
topics.body: Without `axis`, a reduction flattens the array first. The result is a scalar, not a one-element array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).mean())

topics.title: axis=1 reduces each row
topics.body: The reduced axis disappears. Row sums are therefore one value per row, in a `(2,)` array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

lab.title: Statistics report
lab.brief: Produce a five-number summary (min, mean, median, std, max) for one array.

interviewBank.q: What does `axis=0` mean in `arr.mean(axis=0)`?
interviewBank.answer: The reduction collapses axis 0, the rows, leaving one value per column.

interviewBank.q: Population versus sample standard deviation: which does NumPy compute by default?
interviewBank.answer: Population, dividing by N. `ddof=1` divides by N-1 for the sample estimate.

interviewBank.q: What does `cumsum` return, and how does it differ from `sum`?
interviewBank.answer: A running total of the same shape as the input; `sum` collapses to one value per axis.

interviewBank.q: What does `keepdims=True` preserve, and why does it help?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array.

interviewBank.q: How do you normalise each row by its own mean in one expression?
interviewBank.answer: `arr - arr.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, which aligns the row means with the rows.

interviewBank.q: Why is `argmin` ambiguous on ties?
interviewBank.answer: It returns the first occurrence by position, so several equal minima report only one index.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.ptp` compute?
interviewBank.answer: The difference between the maximum and the minimum.

interviewBank.q: How do you get the index of the maximum per column?
interviewBank.answer: `arr.argmax(axis=0)`.

interviewBank.q: Why is the mean of an empty array NaN?
interviewBank.answer: There is no value to average, and NumPy reports that rather than inventing zero.

interviewBank.q: A dashboard reports the mean order value as 850, but the median is 120. Which number should be shown to explain 'typical' spending?
interviewBank.answer: The median — a few very large orders pull the mean up. Report both when the distribution is skewed, and say which is which.

interviewBank.q: A (1000, 12) table of monthly sales needs the yearly total per product. Which axis, and what does the result shape look like?
interviewBank.answer: axis=1 collapses the months, giving one value per row (shape (1000,)); axis=0 would give one value per month.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting `argmax` alongside `max` when classifying.
defenseBank.answer: `max` gives the score but not which class produced it, and the class index is what a prediction means. `argmax` returns exactly that.

defenseBank.q: Why is the mean of an empty array `nan`, and when should you guard it?
defenseBank.answer: There is no value to average, so NumPy returns `nan` rather than inventing zero. Guard with a size check when a report must not show a missing number.

defenseBank.q: A report needs per-column medians. Defend your axis choice and mention the cost.
defenseBank.answer: `np.median(arr, axis=0)` collapses rows and keeps one median per column. It sorts along each column, so it is O(n log n) per column, unlike a mean.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting mean together with standard deviation.
defenseBank.answer: A mean alone hides spread, and two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently. The pair is the minimum honest summary.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a percentile is not a mean band.
defenseBank.answer: A percentile is a position in the sorted data and tolerates skew; mean plus standard deviation assumes a roughly symmetric spread.

defenseBank.q: Defend naming the axis that disappears when you choose `axis`.
defenseBank.answer: Axis errors are silent, and saying "rows collapse" out loud makes `axis=0` the obvious choice rather than a guess.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting a median when the data has outliers.
defenseBank.answer: The median is robust to extreme values, while the mean moves with them.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `std` with `ddof=0` and `ddof=1` differ.
defenseBank.answer: The denominator changes from N to N-1, which matters for small samples.

defenseBank.q: Defend a cumulative sum over recomputing partial sums in a loop.
defenseBank.answer: One compiled pass replaces repeated Python work and allocates a single result.

learn.title: Mean along an axis

learn.title: Standard deviation and variance
learn.body: var is the mean squared deviation and std is its square root; both use ddof=0 by default, which is the population form.
learn.code:

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a.std(), a.var())

learn.title: Position and running totals

learn.code:

learn.title: median is not the mean
learn.body: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median, so reporting both is how you notice a skewed column.

learn.title: keepdims keeps a column

interview.q: What does `axis=0` mean in `arr.mean(axis=0)`?
interview.answer: The reduction collapses axis 0, the rows, leaving one value per column.

interview.q: Population versus sample standard deviation: which does NumPy compute by default?
interview.answer: Population, dividing by N. `ddof=1` divides by N-1 for the sample estimate.

interview.q: What does `cumsum` return, and how does it differ from `sum`?
interview.answer: A running total of the same shape as the input; `sum` collapses to one value per axis.

interview.q: What does `keepdims=True` preserve, and why does it help?
interview.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array.

interview.q: How do you normalise each row by its own mean in one expression?
interview.answer: `arr - arr.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, which aligns the row means with the rows.

interview.q: Why is `argmin` ambiguous on ties?
interview.answer: It returns the first occurrence by position, so several equal minima report only one index.

interview.q: What does `np.ptp` compute?
interview.answer: The difference between the maximum and the minimum.

interview.q: How do you get the index of the maximum per column?
interview.answer: `arr.argmax(axis=0)`.

interview.q: Why is the mean of an empty array NaN?
interview.answer: There is no value to average, and NumPy reports that rather than inventing zero.

interview.q: A dashboard reports the mean order value as 850, but the median is 120. Which number should be shown to explain 'typical' spending?
interview.answer: The median — a few very large orders pull the mean up. Report both when the distribution is skewed, and say which is which.

interview.q: A (1000, 12) table of monthly sales needs the yearly total per product. Which axis, and what does the result shape look like?
interview.answer: axis=1 collapses the months, giving one value per row (shape (1000,)); axis=0 would give one value per month.

defense.q: Defend reporting `argmax` alongside `max` when classifying.
defense.answer: `max` gives the score but not which class produced it, and the class index is what a prediction means. `argmax` returns exactly that.

defense.q: Why is the mean of an empty array `nan`, and when should you guard it?
defense.answer: There is no value to average, so NumPy returns `nan` rather than inventing zero. Guard with a size check when a report must not show a missing number.

defense.q: A report needs per-column medians. Defend your axis choice and mention the cost.
defense.answer: `np.median(arr, axis=0)` collapses rows and keeps one median per column. It sorts along each column, so it is O(n log n) per column, unlike a mean.

defense.q: Defend reporting mean together with standard deviation.
defense.answer: A mean alone hides spread, and two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently. The pair is the minimum honest summary.

defense.q: Explain why a percentile is not a mean band.
defense.answer: A percentile is a position in the sorted data and tolerates skew; mean plus standard deviation assumes a roughly symmetric spread.

defense.q: Defend naming the axis that disappears when you choose `axis`.
defense.answer: Axis errors are silent, and saying "rows collapse" out loud makes `axis=0` the obvious choice rather than a guess.

defense.q: Defend reporting a median when the data has outliers.
defense.answer: The median is robust to extreme values, while the mean moves with them.

defense.q: Explain why `std` with `ddof=0` and `ddof=1` differ.
defense.answer: The denominator changes from N to N-1, which matters for small samples.

defense.q: Defend a cumulative sum over recomputing partial sums in a loop.
defense.answer: One compiled pass replaces repeated Python work and allocates a single result.

modules.title: Boolean Indexing and Filtering
modules.goal: Filter arrays with masks, replace values with where and test membership with isin.

topics.title: Filter with a mask
topics.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

topics.title: np.where chooses without a loop
topics.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

topics.title: Membership with isin
topics.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

topics.title: Combine masks with & and |
topics.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

topics.title: Invert a mask with ~
topics.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

topics.title: Assign through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Count how many match
topics.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

topics.title: Filter rows by one column
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

topics.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
topics.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

topics.title: where chooses between two values
topics.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

topics.title: Sum the mask to count matches
topics.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

topics.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
topics.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

topics.title: where chooses between two arrays
topics.body: np.where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is true and y where it is false, which replaces an if/else loop over the elements.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
print(np.where(marks >= 50, 'pass', 'fail'))

topics.title: Updating through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask can be used on the left of an assignment, so only the selected cells change and the rest keep their values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-5, 3, -2, 8])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

debug.title: A mask shorter than the array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False]])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False, True]])

debug.fix:

lab.brief: Flag readings outside 0–100, count them and replace them with the mean of the valid readings.

interviewBank.q: Why do you combine masks with `&` and `|` rather than `and` and `or`?
interviewBank.answer: The bitwise operators act elementwise on boolean arrays; `and` forces one truth value for the whole array and raises on a multi-element mask.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.where(mask, a, b)` return?
interviewBank.answer: An array that takes `a` where the mask is true and `b` elsewhere, with broadcasting applied to the branches.

interviewBank.q: How do you count how many elements satisfy a condition?
interviewBank.answer: `mask.sum()` or `np.count_nonzero(mask)`, both of which count true entries.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `arr > 5` and `arr[arr > 5]`?
interviewBank.answer: The first is the boolean mask; the second applies it and returns only the selected values.

interviewBank.q: How do you invert a boolean mask?
interviewBank.answer: Use `~mask`, the elementwise negation, which keeps the array shape.

interviewBank.q: Why do mask expressions need parentheses?
interviewBank.answer: `&` binds tighter than comparison, so `a > 1 & a < 3` compares against the result of the bitwise operation. Parenthesise each comparison.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.count_nonzero` count on a boolean mask?
interviewBank.answer: The number of true entries.

interviewBank.q: How do you replace negative values with zero?
interviewBank.answer: `np.where(arr < 0, 0, arr)`, or clipping at zero when only that bound matters.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr > 1 and arr < 3` fail?
interviewBank.answer: `and` needs one truth value, and a multi-element array does not have one.

interviewBank.q: Customers with no purchases for 90 days must be flagged. Why is a boolean mask better than a loop that appends indices?
interviewBank.answer: The mask is one vectorised comparison over the whole column, and it can be reused for counting, filtering and assignment. A Python loop grows a list and pays per-row overhead.

interviewBank.q: A codebase updates churn labels with `df[mask] = 1` then checks `df` and finds nothing changed. What kind of object was df likely to be?
interviewBank.answer: A NumPy array's boolean assignment does mutate in place, so if nothing changed the value was probably a copy (advanced indexing on a pandas object, or a slice that was copied earlier). Verify with `base is`/`np.shares_memory`.

defenseBank.q: Defend masking over an `if` loop when filtering a million rows.
defenseBank.answer: The mask is computed once as one vectorised comparison and applied as a single gather, instead of a million interpreter iterations and list appends.

defenseBank.q: Why must a mask match the length of the axis it filters?
defenseBank.answer: It selects positions of that axis, so a shorter or longer mask has no defined mapping and NumPy raises rather than guessing.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.isin` for membership tests instead of a Python `in` loop.
defenseBank.answer: `isin` sorts or hashes internally and answers for the whole array at once. A loop over `in` against a list is quadratic in the worst case.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.where` over assignment through a mask for three-way choices.
defenseBank.answer: `where` returns a complete new array from two branches, so no element is left in an intermediate state and the intent is one expression.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a mask of the wrong length raises.
defenseBank.answer: The mask maps one-to-one onto positions of an axis, so a different length has no defined alignment. Failing is better than guessing.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.isin` for filtering against a whitelist.
defenseBank.answer: It answers the whole array in one operation and stays fast for large lists, unlike a per-element Python membership loop.

defenseBank.q: Defend a mask expression over a Python filter loop.
defenseBank.answer: The comparison runs once over the buffer with no per-element call or list append.

defenseBank.q: Explain why an empty mask selects nothing rather than everything.
defenseBank.answer: It selects the positions it marks, and there are none.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.where` over mutating the input inside a helper.
defenseBank.answer: It returns a new array, so the caller's data is untouched and the function stays predictable.

learn.title: Filter with a mask
learn.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

learn.title: np.where chooses without a loop
learn.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

learn.title: Membership with isin
learn.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

learn.title: Combine masks with & and |
learn.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

learn.title: Invert a mask with ~
learn.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

learn.title: Assign through a mask
learn.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

learn.title: Count how many match
learn.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

learn.title: Filter rows by one column
learn.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

learn.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
learn.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

learn.title: where chooses between two values
learn.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

learn.title: Sum the mask to count matches
learn.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

learn.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
learn.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

learn.title: where chooses between two arrays
learn.body: np.where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is true and y where it is false, which replaces an if/else loop over the elements.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
print(np.where(marks >= 50, 'pass', 'fail'))

learn.title: Updating through a mask
learn.body: A boolean mask can be used on the left of an assignment, so only the selected cells change and the rest keep their values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-5, 3, -2, 8])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)
