interview.q: Why do you combine masks with `&` and `|` rather than `and` and `or`?
interview.answer: The bitwise operators act elementwise on boolean arrays; `and` forces one truth value for the whole array and raises on a multi-element mask.

interview.q: What does `np.where(mask, a, b)` return?
interview.answer: An array that takes `a` where the mask is true and `b` elsewhere, with broadcasting applied to the branches.

interview.q: How do you count how many elements satisfy a condition?
interview.answer: `mask.sum()` or `np.count_nonzero(mask)`, both of which count true entries.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr > 5` and `arr[arr > 5]`?
interview.answer: The first is the boolean mask; the second applies it and returns only the selected values.

interview.q: How do you invert a boolean mask?
interview.answer: Use `~mask`, the elementwise negation, which keeps the array shape.

interview.q: Why do mask expressions need parentheses?
interview.answer: `&` binds tighter than comparison, so `a > 1 & a < 3` compares against the result of the bitwise operation. Parenthesise each comparison.

interview.q: What does `np.count_nonzero` count on a boolean mask?
interview.answer: The number of true entries.

interview.q: How do you replace negative values with zero?
interview.answer: `np.where(arr < 0, 0, arr)`, or clipping at zero when only that bound matters.

interview.q: Why does `arr > 1 and arr < 3` fail?
interview.answer: `and` needs one truth value, and a multi-element array does not have one.

interview.q: Customers with no purchases for 90 days must be flagged. Why is a boolean mask better than a loop that appends indices?
interview.answer: The mask is one vectorised comparison over the whole column, and it can be reused for counting, filtering and assignment. A Python loop grows a list and pays per-row overhead.

interview.q: A codebase updates churn labels with `df[mask] = 1` then checks `df` and finds nothing changed. What kind of object was df likely to be?
interview.answer: A NumPy array's boolean assignment does mutate in place, so if nothing changed the value was probably a copy (advanced indexing on a pandas object, or a slice that was copied earlier). Verify with `base is`/`np.shares_memory`.

defense.q: Defend masking over an `if` loop when filtering a million rows.
defense.answer: The mask is computed once as one vectorised comparison and applied as a single gather, instead of a million interpreter iterations and list appends.

defense.q: Why must a mask match the length of the axis it filters?
defense.answer: It selects positions of that axis, so a shorter or longer mask has no defined mapping and NumPy raises rather than guessing.

defense.q: Defend `np.isin` for membership tests instead of a Python `in` loop.
defense.answer: `isin` sorts or hashes internally and answers for the whole array at once. A loop over `in` against a list is quadratic in the worst case.

defense.q: Defend `np.where` over assignment through a mask for three-way choices.
defense.answer: `where` returns a complete new array from two branches, so no element is left in an intermediate state and the intent is one expression.

defense.q: Explain why a mask of the wrong length raises.
defense.answer: The mask maps one-to-one onto positions of an axis, so a different length has no defined alignment. Failing is better than guessing.

defense.q: Defend `np.isin` for filtering against a whitelist.
defense.answer: It answers the whole array in one operation and stays fast for large lists, unlike a per-element Python membership loop.

defense.q: Defend a mask expression over a Python filter loop.
defense.answer: The comparison runs once over the buffer with no per-element call or list append.

defense.q: Explain why an empty mask selects nothing rather than everything.
defense.answer: It selects the positions it marks, and there are none.

defense.q: Defend `np.where` over mutating the input inside a helper.
defense.answer: It returns a new array, so the caller's data is untouched and the function stays predictable.

modules.title: Sorting, Searching and Set Operations
modules.goal: Sort along an axis, recover order with argsort, locate insertion points and compare sets of values.

topics.title: sort and argsort
topics.body: np.sort returns a sorted copy while argsort returns the INDICES that would sort the array — the second is what you use to reorder parallel arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(np.sort(a), np.argsort(a))

topics.title: searchsorted
topics.body: searchsorted finds the insertion index that keeps a sorted array ordered, which is how you bucket a value without scanning.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 3, 5])
print(np.searchsorted(a, 4))

topics.title: Unique values and set operations
topics.body: unique returns sorted distinct values and intersect1d/union1d/setdiff1d answer the set questions directly on arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 2, 3])
print(np.unique(a), np.intersect1d(a, [2, 4]))

topics.title: sort each row separately
topics.body: axis=1 sorts inside each row and leaves rows in place, while axis=0 would sort down each column instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [9, 7, 8]])
print(np.sort(a, axis=1))

topics.title: Reverse a sorted array for descending order
topics.body: sort only goes ascending, so descending order is a sort followed by a reverse slice — two views, no extra list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1])

topics.title: partition keeps only k small values in front
topics.body: partition is cheaper than a full sort when you only need the k smallest elements to be correct, which is enough for top-k work.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
part = np.partition([5, 1, 4, 2, 3], 2)
print(part[:3].sum(), part[3:].sum())

topics.title: lexsort orders by the last key first
topics.body: lexsort takes several keys and sorts by the last one primarily, which is how you order by two columns without building tuples.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['b', 'a', 'b', 'a'])
scores = np.array([2, 2, 1, 1])
order = np.lexsort((scores, names))
print(names[order], scores[order])

topics.title: argmax finds the best position
topics.body: argmax returns the index of the largest value, so you keep the label or row that produced the maximum instead of the maximum alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.argmax([3, 9, 5]))

topics.title: argsort returns the order, not the values
topics.body: The output holds positions, so it is the right tool for sorting one array by another. Feed it to the data to reorder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.argsort(np.array([3, 1, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: sort can work in place
topics.body: `ndarray.sort()` rearranges the array itself and returns `None`. `np.sort` returns a new array instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
a.sort(axis=1)
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: unique removes repeats and sorts
topics.body: The result is always sorted, even if the input was not. Add `return_counts=True` to see how often each value appeared.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.unique(np.array([3, 1, 3, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: argmin finds the smallest position
topics.body: It returns the first occurrence on ties, which makes it safe for lookups where duplicates are possible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.argmin(np.array([4, 2, 8])))

topics.title: argsort gives positions, sort gives values
topics.body: argsort returns the indices that would sort the array, which is what you need to reorder a second array the same way.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['b', 'a', 'c'])
score = np.array([2, 9, 5])
order = np.argsort(score)
print(order, names[order], score[order])

topics.title: Set operations on arrays
topics.body: intersect1d, union1d and setdiff1d treat the arrays as sets and return sorted unique values, which is how duplicate detection and reconciliation are written.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 3])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.intersect1d(a, b))
print(np.union1d(a, b))
print(np.setdiff1d(a, b))

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `sort` and `argsort`?
interviewBank.answer: `sort` returns the sorted values; `argsort` returns the positions that would produce them, which is how you reorder a parallel array.

interviewBank.q: What does a stable sort guarantee, and when do you need it?
interviewBank.answer: Equal keys keep their original order. That matters when sorting by a secondary key already applied, or when output order must be reproducible.

interviewBank.q: How do you find where a value belongs in a sorted array?
interviewBank.answer: `np.searchsorted(sorted_arr, value)` returns the insertion position, with `side` deciding where duplicates go.

interviewBank.q: How do you sort a 2-D array by its second column?
interviewBank.answer: Take the order from `np.argsort(arr[:, 1])` and apply it, `arr[order]`, which reorders whole rows.

interviewBank.q: What does `argsort` do with equal values by default?
interviewBank.answer: It uses an unstable algorithm, so tied values may come back in any order unless you request `kind="stable"`.

interviewBank.q: Why is searching a sorted array faster?
interviewBank.answer: A sorted array supports binary search, so the position is found in logarithmically many steps instead of a linear scan.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.argsort` return?
interviewBank.answer: The indices that would sort the array, not the sorted values.

interviewBank.q: How do you sort an array in descending order?
interviewBank.answer: Sort ascending and reverse the result with `[::-1]`, or negate the values first.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.unique` sort before returning?
interviewBank.answer: Sorting is how it detects duplicates efficiently, and it makes the output deterministic.

interviewBank.q: The top 5 products by revenue are needed from 200k rows. Why is np.argpartition usually better than np.argsort here?
interviewBank.answer: argpartition only guarantees that the k smallest/largest are separated, in O(n) expected time, while argsort sorts everything in O(n log n). Sort the 5 selected values afterwards for presentation.

interviewBank.q: Two product id arrays are compared to find ids in this month but not last month. Which operation gives that, and does order matter?
interviewBank.answer: np.setdiff1d(this_month, last_month) — it returns sorted unique values in the first array that are absent from the second. The result is sorted, not in input order.

defenseBank.q: Defend `partition` over a full sort when you only need the top ten.
defenseBank.answer: `partition` is linear on average because it only places the k-th element, while a full sort is O(n log n). For a top-k report the extra ordering is wasted work.

defenseBank.q: Why can sorting a view surprise a caller who holds the original array?
defenseBank.answer: `arr.sort()` sorts in place, so every name pointing at that buffer sees the new order. Use `np.sort(arr)`, which returns a sorted copy, when the original must stay.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.unique(..., return_counts=True)` over `collections.Counter`.
defenseBank.answer: It works on a typed array, returns arrays ready for further vectorised work, and sorts once. `Counter` requires converting to Python objects and pays per-element overhead.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.sort` over `list.sort` for a numeric column.
defenseBank.answer: `np.sort` works on the typed buffer with no Python comparisons and returns an array ready for further vectorised work.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.unique` returns sorted values.
defenseBank.answer: Sorting is how it detects duplicates efficiently, and a sorted result is deterministic and searchable afterwards.

defenseBank.q: Defend keeping the index array returned by `argsort`.
defenseBank.answer: Sorting values alone loses which row they came from. The index array is what lets labels and features stay aligned.

defenseBank.q: Defend `argsort` over sorting a copy when labels must follow.
defenseBank.answer: The index array keeps features and labels aligned after the reorder.

defenseBank.q: Explain why sorting in place can surprise a caller.
defenseBank.answer: `arr.sort()` rewrites the shared buffer, so the caller's original order is gone.

defenseBank.q: Defend `partition` when only the k largest values matter.
defenseBank.answer: It places the k-th element without ordering the rest, which is cheaper than a full sort.

learn.title: sort and argsort
learn.body: np.sort returns a sorted copy while argsort returns the INDICES that would sort the array — the second is what you use to reorder parallel arrays.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(np.sort(a), np.argsort(a))

learn.title: searchsorted
learn.body: searchsorted finds the insertion index that keeps a sorted array ordered, which is how you bucket a value without scanning.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.searchsorted(a, 4))

learn.title: Unique values and set operations
learn.body: unique returns sorted distinct values and intersect1d/union1d/setdiff1d answer the set questions directly on arrays.
learn.code:

print(np.unique(a), np.intersect1d(a, [2, 4]))

learn.title: sort each row separately
learn.body: axis=1 sorts inside each row and leaves rows in place, while axis=0 would sort down each column instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

learn.title: Reverse a sorted array for descending order
learn.body: sort only goes ascending, so descending order is a sort followed by a reverse slice — two views, no extra list.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1])

learn.title: partition keeps only k small values in front
learn.body: partition is cheaper than a full sort when you only need the k smallest elements to be correct, which is enough for top-k work.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
part = np.partition([5, 1, 4, 2, 3], 2)
print(part[:3].sum(), part[3:].sum())

learn.title: lexsort orders by the last key first
learn.body: lexsort takes several keys and sorts by the last one primarily, which is how you order by two columns without building tuples.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['b', 'a', 'b', 'a'])
scores = np.array([2, 2, 1, 1])
order = np.lexsort((scores, names))
print(names[order], scores[order])

learn.title: argmax finds the best position
learn.body: argmax returns the index of the largest value, so you keep the label or row that produced the maximum instead of the maximum alone.
learn.code:

learn.title: argsort returns the order, not the values
learn.body: The output holds positions, so it is the right tool for sorting one array by another. Feed it to the data to reorder.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.argsort(np.array([3, 1, 2])).tolist())

learn.title: sort can work in place
learn.body: `ndarray.sort()` rearranges the array itself and returns `None`. `np.sort` returns a new array instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
a.sort(axis=1)
print(a.tolist())

learn.title: unique removes repeats and sorts
learn.body: The result is always sorted, even if the input was not. Add `return_counts=True` to see how often each value appeared.

learn.title: argmin finds the smallest position
learn.body: It returns the first occurrence on ties, which makes it safe for lookups where duplicates are possible.

learn.title: argsort gives positions, sort gives values
learn.body: argsort returns the indices that would sort the array, which is what you need to reorder a second array the same way.

learn.body: intersect1d, union1d and setdiff1d treat the arrays as sets and return sorted unique values, which is how duplicate detection and reconciliation are written.

interview.q: What is the difference between `sort` and `argsort`?
interview.answer: `sort` returns the sorted values; `argsort` returns the positions that would produce them, which is how you reorder a parallel array.

interview.q: What does a stable sort guarantee, and when do you need it?
interview.answer: Equal keys keep their original order. That matters when sorting by a secondary key already applied, or when output order must be reproducible.

interview.q: How do you find where a value belongs in a sorted array?
interview.answer: `np.searchsorted(sorted_arr, value)` returns the insertion position, with `side` deciding where duplicates go.

interview.q: How do you sort a 2-D array by its second column?
interview.answer: Take the order from `np.argsort(arr[:, 1])` and apply it, `arr[order]`, which reorders whole rows.

interview.q: What does `argsort` do with equal values by default?
interview.answer: It uses an unstable algorithm, so tied values may come back in any order unless you request `kind="stable"`.

interview.q: Why is searching a sorted array faster?
interview.answer: A sorted array supports binary search, so the position is found in logarithmically many steps instead of a linear scan.

interview.q: What does `np.argsort` return?
interview.answer: The indices that would sort the array, not the sorted values.

interview.q: How do you sort an array in descending order?
interview.answer: Sort ascending and reverse the result with `[::-1]`, or negate the values first.

interview.q: Why does `np.unique` sort before returning?
interview.answer: Sorting is how it detects duplicates efficiently, and it makes the output deterministic.

interview.q: The top 5 products by revenue are needed from 200k rows. Why is np.argpartition usually better than np.argsort here?
interview.answer: argpartition only guarantees that the k smallest/largest are separated, in O(n) expected time, while argsort sorts everything in O(n log n). Sort the 5 selected values afterwards for presentation.

interview.q: Two product id arrays are compared to find ids in this month but not last month. Which operation gives that, and does order matter?
interview.answer: np.setdiff1d(this_month, last_month) — it returns sorted unique values in the first array that are absent from the second. The result is sorted, not in input order.

defense.q: Defend `partition` over a full sort when you only need the top ten.
defense.answer: `partition` is linear on average because it only places the k-th element, while a full sort is O(n log n). For a top-k report the extra ordering is wasted work.

defense.q: Why can sorting a view surprise a caller who holds the original array?
defense.answer: `arr.sort()` sorts in place, so every name pointing at that buffer sees the new order. Use `np.sort(arr)`, which returns a sorted copy, when the original must stay.

defense.q: Defend `np.unique(..., return_counts=True)` over `collections.Counter`.
defense.answer: It works on a typed array, returns arrays ready for further vectorised work, and sorts once. `Counter` requires converting to Python objects and pays per-element overhead.

defense.q: Defend `np.sort` over `list.sort` for a numeric column.
defense.answer: `np.sort` works on the typed buffer with no Python comparisons and returns an array ready for further vectorised work.

defense.q: Explain why `np.unique` returns sorted values.
defense.answer: Sorting is how it detects duplicates efficiently, and a sorted result is deterministic and searchable afterwards.

defense.q: Defend keeping the index array returned by `argsort`.
defense.answer: Sorting values alone loses which row they came from. The index array is what lets labels and features stay aligned.

defense.q: Defend `argsort` over sorting a copy when labels must follow.
defense.answer: The index array keeps features and labels aligned after the reorder.

defense.q: Explain why sorting in place can surprise a caller.
defense.answer: `arr.sort()` rewrites the shared buffer, so the caller's original order is gone.

defense.q: Defend `partition` when only the k largest values matter.
defense.answer: It places the k-th element without ordering the rest, which is cheaper than a full sort.

modules.title: Copies, Views, Strides and Memory
modules.goal: Tell a view from a copy, prove sharing with shares_memory, and read strides and contiguity.

topics.title: view shares, copy does not
topics.body: a.view() shares the same buffer so a write through the view changes the original; a.copy() allocates new memory and leaves the original alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
v = a.view()
c = a.copy()
v[0] = 9
print(a, c)

topics.title: Prove sharing with shares_memory
topics.body: Slicing usually returns a view, but an explicit copy never shares; shares_memory answers the question with a real check instead of a guess.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.shares_memory(a, a[1:3]), np.shares_memory(a, a.copy()))

topics.title: Strides describe memory steps
topics.body: strides are the bytes to move per axis; a (2, 3) int64 array steps 24 bytes per row and 8 bytes per column, which is why layout affects speed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)

topics.title: reshape usually returns a view
topics.body: When the memory is contiguous, reshape hands back a new shape over the same buffer, so shares_memory is True and writes travel both ways.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(np.shares_memory(a, b))

topics.title: base points at the source array
topics.body: A view keeps a reference to the array it came from in .base, which is the quickest way to prove two names share one buffer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1:].base is a)

topics.title: Transpose is a view with new strides
topics.body: Transposing changes only the strides, not the data, so a (2, 3) float64 array transposes to strides (8, 24) with the same bytes.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.strides)

topics.title: A reversed slice has negative strides
topics.body: A step of -1 stores a negative stride, which is why reversing is free: the array simply walks its memory backwards.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(4)[::-1].strides)

topics.title: copy owns its memory
topics.body: The OWNDATA flag tells you whether an array owns its buffer or borrows it, which is the truth behind the view/copy question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a.copy().flags['OWNDATA'])

topics.title: A slice is a view into the source
topics.body: Assigning into the slice writes into the original buffer. Nothing was copied when the slice was taken.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: A copy stops the sharing

interviewBank.q: How do you prove two arrays share memory?
interviewBank.answer: `np.shares_memory(a, b)` gives a definite answer, while `np.may_share_memory(a, b)` is the cheap conservative check.

interviewBank.q: What are strides?
interviewBank.answer: The number of bytes to step to move one position along each axis. Shape plus strides fully describe how to read the buffer.

interviewBank.q: Why can a transpose be free?
interviewBank.answer: It reverses the order of the shape and the strides, so no data moves; reads simply walk the buffer differently.

interviewBank.q: What does `arr.base` tell you?
interviewBank.answer: It points at the array whose buffer this one borrows, and is `None` when this array owns its data.

interviewBank.q: Why do C and Fortran order have different strides?
interviewBank.answer: C order walks the last axis fastest, Fortran the first, so the byte step per axis differs even for the same shape.

interviewBank.q: How can a copy hide a memory bug?
interviewBank.answer: A copy breaks the link between two names, so a write that should be visible through an alias silently is not.

interviewBank.q: What does `arr.strides` measure?
interviewBank.answer: The number of bytes to step to move one position along each axis.

interviewBank.q: How do you tell whether an array owns its data?
interviewBank.answer: `arr.base is None` means it owns the buffer; otherwise it is a view over another array.

interviewBank.q: Why can a view be cheaper than a copy?
interviewBank.answer: It stores only metadata over existing memory instead of duplicating values.

interviewBank.q: A function slices an array, modifies the slice and returns it; the caller's original data changes too. Is that a bug?
interviewBank.answer: It is a view, so yes for callers who did not expect mutation. Either copy before modifying or document that the function mutates its input; np.shares_memory is the check that proves which one happened.

interviewBank.q: A 1 GB array is transposed and the memory use doubles. Why, when transposing should be free?
interviewBank.answer: `.T` returns a view with swapped strides, but any later operation that requires C-contiguous layout (a library call, ascontiguousarray, some reductions) materialises a copy, which doubles memory.

defenseBank.q: Defend copying at an API boundary even though views avoid allocations.
defenseBank.answer: A caller that keeps a slice can pin memory or observe later writes. A copy makes ownership explicit and removes whole classes of aliasing bugs.

defenseBank.q: Why can `arr.T.reshape(-1)` copy when `arr.reshape(-1)` does not?
defenseBank.answer: The transpose makes the traversal non-contiguous in the requested order, so the flat order cannot be expressed with strides and NumPy copies.

defenseBank.q: A 2 GB array must be transposed for a model. Defend adding `ascontiguousarray`.
defenseBank.answer: The model likely reads contiguous memory; a non-contiguous input forces per-element address arithmetic or an internal copy. Paying for one explicit copy is predictable.

defenseBank.q: Defend copying a function argument before mutating it.
defenseBank.answer: Callers pass views and expect their data intact; mutating in place makes the function's effect depend on aliasing they cannot see.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a transpose followed by a reshape may copy.
defenseBank.answer: After the transpose, the logical order no longer matches memory order, so flattening needs a real copy to produce the requested sequence.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `nbytes` before loading a file.
defenseBank.answer: The size on disk predicts the memory the array needs, and discovering a 20 GB allocation at load time is worse than refusing early.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.shares_memory` over a manual `base` check.
defenseBank.answer: It answers the question for two arrays directly, including overlapping slices.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a copy can be the safe default at an API edge.
defenseBank.answer: The callee cannot then mutate the caller's data through an alias.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `flags.writeable` before assigning.
defenseBank.answer: Broadcast and read-only views raise on write, and the check states the assumption up front.

interview.q: How do you prove two arrays share memory?
interview.answer: `np.shares_memory(a, b)` gives a definite answer, while `np.may_share_memory(a, b)` is the cheap conservative check.

interview.q: What are strides?
interview.answer: The number of bytes to step to move one position along each axis. Shape plus strides fully describe how to read the buffer.

interview.q: Why can a transpose be free?
interview.answer: It reverses the order of the shape and the strides, so no data moves; reads simply walk the buffer differently.

interview.q: What does `arr.base` tell you?
interview.answer: It points at the array whose buffer this one borrows, and is `None` when this array owns its data.

interview.q: Why do C and Fortran order have different strides?
interview.answer: C order walks the last axis fastest, Fortran the first, so the byte step per axis differs even for the same shape.

interview.q: How can a copy hide a memory bug?
interview.answer: A copy breaks the link between two names, so a write that should be visible through an alias silently is not.

interview.q: What does `arr.strides` measure?
interview.answer: The number of bytes to step to move one position along each axis.

interview.q: How do you tell whether an array owns its data?
interview.answer: `arr.base is None` means it owns the buffer; otherwise it is a view over another array.

interview.q: Why can a view be cheaper than a copy?
interview.answer: It stores only metadata over existing memory instead of duplicating values.

interview.q: A function slices an array, modifies the slice and returns it; the caller's original data changes too. Is that a bug?
interview.answer: It is a view, so yes for callers who did not expect mutation. Either copy before modifying or document that the function mutates its input; np.shares_memory is the check that proves which one happened.

interview.q: A 1 GB array is transposed and the memory use doubles. Why, when transposing should be free?
interview.answer: `.T` returns a view with swapped strides, but any later operation that requires C-contiguous layout (a library call, ascontiguousarray, some reductions) materialises a copy, which doubles memory.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: view shares, copy does not
practice.task: a.view() shares the same buffer so a write through the view changes the original; a.copy() allocates new memory and leaves the original alone.

a = np.arange(4)
v = a.view()
c = a.copy()
v[0] = 9
print(a, c)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Prove sharing with shares_memory
practice.task: Slicing usually returns a view, but an explicit copy never shares; shares_memory answers the question with a real check instead of a guess.

print(np.shares_memory(a, a[1:3]), np.shares_memory(a, a.copy()))

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Strides describe memory steps
practice.task: strides are the bytes to move per axis; a (2, 3) int64 array steps 24 bytes per row and 8 bytes per column, which is why layout affects speed.
practice.solution:

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: reshape usually returns a view
practice.task: When the memory is contiguous, reshape hands back a new shape over the same buffer, so shares_memory is True and writes travel both ways.
practice.solution:

a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(np.shares_memory(a, b))

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: base points at the source array
practice.task: A view keeps a reference to the array it came from in .base, which is the quickest way to prove two names share one buffer.

print(a[1:].base is a)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Transpose is a view with new strides
practice.task: Transposing changes only the strides, not the data, so a (2, 3) float64 array transposes to strides (8, 24) with the same bytes.
practice.solution:

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A reversed slice has negative strides
practice.task: A step of -1 stores a negative stride, which is why reversing is free: the array simply walks its memory backwards.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: copy owns its memory

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A slice is a view into the source
practice.task: Assigning into the slice writes into the original buffer. Nothing was copied when the slice was taken.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A copy stops the sharing
practice.task: `.copy()` allocates a new buffer, so writes to it never reach the source. This is the fix for accidental mutation.

b = a[:2].copy()

defense.q: Defend copying at an API boundary even though views avoid allocations.
defense.answer: A caller that keeps a slice can pin memory or observe later writes. A copy makes ownership explicit and removes whole classes of aliasing bugs.

defense.q: Why can `arr.T.reshape(-1)` copy when `arr.reshape(-1)` does not?
defense.answer: The transpose makes the traversal non-contiguous in the requested order, so the flat order cannot be expressed with strides and NumPy copies.

defense.q: A 2 GB array must be transposed for a model. Defend adding `ascontiguousarray`.
defense.answer: The model likely reads contiguous memory; a non-contiguous input forces per-element address arithmetic or an internal copy. Paying for one explicit copy is predictable.

defense.q: Defend copying a function argument before mutating it.
defense.answer: Callers pass views and expect their data intact; mutating in place makes the function's effect depend on aliasing they cannot see.

defense.q: Explain why a transpose followed by a reshape may copy.
defense.answer: After the transpose, the logical order no longer matches memory order, so flattening needs a real copy to produce the requested sequence.

defense.q: Defend checking `nbytes` before loading a file.
defense.answer: The size on disk predicts the memory the array needs, and discovering a 20 GB allocation at load time is worse than refusing early.

defense.q: Defend `np.shares_memory` over a manual `base` check.
defense.answer: It answers the question for two arrays directly, including overlapping slices.

defense.q: Explain why a copy can be the safe default at an API edge.
defense.answer: The callee cannot then mutate the caller's data through an alias.

defense.q: Defend checking `flags.writeable` before assigning.
defense.answer: Broadcast and read-only views raise on write, and the check states the assumption up front.

modules.title: Random Number Generation
modules.goal: Use default_rng, reproduce runs with a seed, and sample from the common distributions.

topics.title: default_rng and reproducibility
topics.body: default_rng(seed) returns a Generator; the same seed reproduces the same stream on every run, which is what makes a simulation debuggable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 3)
print(len(a), a.min() >= 0, a.max() < 10)

topics.title: Normal draws
topics.body: rng.normal(loc, scale, size) samples a Gaussian; rounding the printed values keeps a demo readable without changing the data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.normal(0, 1, 2).shape)

topics.title: choice and shuffle
topics.body: choice samples with replacement by default (replace=False for a draw without repeats) and shuffle reorders an array in place.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(len(np.unique(rng.choice([1, 2, 3], 2, replace=False))))

topics.title: integers draw inside a half-open range
topics.body: integers(low, high) returns values from low up to but excluding high, and the seeded generator makes the draw reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, 5))

topics.title: random floats sit between 0 and 1
topics.body: random returns floats in [0, 1), which you scale and shift into any interval you need.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(rng.random(3).round(3))

topics.title: the same seed gives the same numbers
topics.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce identical streams, which is the whole reason experiments are reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
b = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
print(np.allclose(a, b))

topics.title: size controls the shape of a draw
topics.body: Passing a tuple to size returns a multi-dimensional draw, so a batch of samples is one call instead of a loop of calls.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.normal(size=(2, 3)).shape)

topics.title: permutation shuffles a copy
topics.body: permutation returns a shuffled copy and leaves the input alone, so sorting the result recovers the original values exactly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
print(np.sort(rng.permutation(5)))

topics.title: integers excludes the high value
topics.body: `rng.integers(low, high)` is half-open, like `range`. Asking for `(0, 2)` can only yield 0 or 1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.integers(0, 2, size=5).max() <= 1)

topics.title: The seed decides the whole stream
topics.body: Two generators made with the same seed produce identical draws. That is how a random example becomes reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

first = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
second = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
print(first == second)

topics.title: choice samples without replacement
topics.body: `replace=False` behaves like drawing cards: no value repeats. With `replace=True` a value can appear several times.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
draw = rng.choice(5, 3, replace=False)
print(len(set(draw.tolist())) == 3)

topics.title: normal draws cluster around the mean
topics.body: The mean of many standard normal draws approaches zero. Increasing the sample size tightens the estimate, not the spread.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
sample = rng.normal(0, 1, 10000)
print(abs(sample.mean()) < 0.05)

topics.title: A seed makes randomness repeatable
topics.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce the same stream, which is how an experiment becomes reproducible. A different seed gives a different stream.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
r1 = np.random.default_rng(42)
r2 = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(r1.random(3))
print(r2.random(3))

topics.title: Choice with and without replacement
topics.body: rng.choice samples from a list; replace=False samples without repeating an item, which is what a shuffled train/test split needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(rng.choice([10, 20, 30, 40], size=2, replace=False))
print(rng.permutation(5))

debug.title: A range with no room
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.integers(10, 0, 3))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np

print(rng.integers(0, 10, 3))

print(rng.integers(1, 5, size=3))

debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.random._generator.Generator' object has no attribute 'rand'. Did you mean: 'random'?

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.random(2))

import numpy as np

debug.fix:

debug.error: TypeError: SeedSequence expects int or sequence of ints for entropy not seed

debug.fix:

debug.error: ValueError: scale < 0

interviewBank.q: Why does NumPy recommend `default_rng` over `np.random.seed`?
interviewBank.answer: A generator carries its own state, so two parts of a program cannot silently reset each other, and its algorithms are the modern ones.

interviewBank.q: How do you make a sampling run reproducible?
interviewBank.answer: Construct a generator with an explicit seed and pass it around, rather than reseeding a global state.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between sampling with and without replacement?
interviewBank.answer: Without replacement each value can appear once, which is what a train/test split needs; with replacement values may repeat.

interviewBank.q: What is a generator's state, and why pass one around?
interviewBank.answer: It is the internal position in the random stream. Passing the object keeps draws reproducible and independent of any global state.

interviewBank.q: How do you draw reproducible batches in a training loop?
interviewBank.answer: Create one seeded generator and keep calling it; each batch advances the same stream in a fixed order.

interviewBank.q: Why are `random` floats in `[0, 1)` and not `[0, 1]`?
interviewBank.answer: The upper bound is exclusive so the result is uniform over a half-open interval and never equals 1.0, which scaling relies on.

interviewBank.q: What range does `Generator.integers` use by default?
interviewBank.answer: The half-open range `[low, high)`, unless `endpoint=True`.

interviewBank.q: How do you get the same train/test split twice?
interviewBank.answer: Reuse one generator with a fixed seed and make the same calls in the same order.

interviewBank.q: Why is `choice` with probabilities slower than uniform choice?
interviewBank.answer: It builds a cumulative distribution and searches it for each draw.

interviewBank.q: An A/B test assigns users with `np.random.rand(n) < 0.5`. Why is that worse than `default_rng(seed).random(n) < 0.5`?
interviewBank.answer: The legacy global RNG shares state across the process and cannot be reproduced independently per experiment. A seeded Generator gives a reproducible stream and avoids interference from other code drawing random numbers.

interviewBank.q: A train/test split keeps 80% for training but the same user appears in both sets. What sampling detail was missed?
interviewBank.answer: Sampling rows with replacement (or sampling rows when the unit is a user) splits a user's records across sets. Sample unique user ids without replacement and then select their rows.

defenseBank.q: Defend seeding per experiment rather than once at import.
defenseBank.answer: A global seed couples unrelated code: one extra draw shifts every later result. A per-experiment generator keeps runs independent and reproducible.

defenseBank.q: Why do two generators with the same seed produce identical draws?
defenseBank.answer: The seed initialises the same internal state and the same algorithm consumes it, so the sequence is deterministic.

defenseBank.q: Defend sampling the test split without replacement.
defenseBank.answer: A row appearing in both train and test leaks the answer and inflates the score. Sampling without replacement makes the split disjoint by construction.

defenseBank.q: Defend fixed seeds in tests but varying seeds in training.
defenseBank.answer: Tests need identical inputs to be meaningful, while training benefits from different sampling each run. Both follow from owning the generator explicitly.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `shuffle` changes the caller's array.
defenseBank.answer: It permutes in place, so every reference to that buffer sees the new order. Use `permutation` when a new array is wanted.

defenseBank.q: Defend `choice` with probabilities for weighted sampling.
defenseBank.answer: It states the weights directly and samples accordingly, instead of building a duplicated pool whose size can explode.

defenseBank.q: Defend passing a generator as an argument instead of seeding globally.
defenseBank.answer: The caller controls reproducibility without global side effects on other code.

defenseBank.q: Explain why re-seeding inside a loop destroys randomness.
defenseBank.answer: Every iteration restarts the same stream, so the draws repeat.

defenseBank.q: Defend generating a permutation over shuffling in place.
defenseBank.answer: The original order stays available for comparison and the input is left untouched.

learn.title: default_rng and reproducibility
learn.body: default_rng(seed) returns a Generator; the same seed reproduces the same stream on every run, which is what makes a simulation debuggable.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 3)
print(len(a), a.min() >= 0, a.max() < 10)

learn.title: Normal draws
learn.body: rng.normal(loc, scale, size) samples a Gaussian; rounding the printed values keeps a demo readable without changing the data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.normal(0, 1, 2).shape)

learn.title: choice and shuffle
learn.body: choice samples with replacement by default (replace=False for a draw without repeats) and shuffle reorders an array in place.
learn.code:

print(len(np.unique(rng.choice([1, 2, 3], 2, replace=False))))

learn.title: integers draw inside a half-open range
learn.body: integers(low, high) returns values from low up to but excluding high, and the seeded generator makes the draw reproducible.
learn.code:

print(rng.integers(1, 7, 5))

learn.title: random floats sit between 0 and 1
learn.body: random returns floats in [0, 1), which you scale and shift into any interval you need.

print(rng.random(3).round(3))

learn.title: the same seed gives the same numbers
learn.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce identical streams, which is the whole reason experiments are reproducible.

b = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
print(np.allclose(a, b))

learn.body: permutation returns a shuffled copy and leaves the input alone, so sorting the result recovers the original values exactly.

interview.q: Why does NumPy recommend `default_rng` over `np.random.seed`?
interview.answer: A generator carries its own state, so two parts of a program cannot silently reset each other, and its algorithms are the modern ones.

interview.q: How do you make a sampling run reproducible?
interview.answer: Construct a generator with an explicit seed and pass it around, rather than reseeding a global state.

interview.q: What is the difference between sampling with and without replacement?
interview.answer: Without replacement each value can appear once, which is what a train/test split needs; with replacement values may repeat.

interview.q: What is a generator's state, and why pass one around?
interview.answer: It is the internal position in the random stream. Passing the object keeps draws reproducible and independent of any global state.

interview.q: How do you draw reproducible batches in a training loop?
interview.answer: Create one seeded generator and keep calling it; each batch advances the same stream in a fixed order.

interview.q: Why are `random` floats in `[0, 1)` and not `[0, 1]`?
interview.answer: The upper bound is exclusive so the result is uniform over a half-open interval and never equals 1.0, which scaling relies on.

interview.q: What range does `Generator.integers` use by default?
interview.answer: The half-open range `[low, high)`, unless `endpoint=True`.

interview.q: How do you get the same train/test split twice?
interview.answer: Reuse one generator with a fixed seed and make the same calls in the same order.

interview.q: Why is `choice` with probabilities slower than uniform choice?
interview.answer: It builds a cumulative distribution and searches it for each draw.

interview.q: An A/B test assigns users with `np.random.rand(n) < 0.5`. Why is that worse than `default_rng(seed).random(n) < 0.5`?
interview.answer: The legacy global RNG shares state across the process and cannot be reproduced independently per experiment. A seeded Generator gives a reproducible stream and avoids interference from other code drawing random numbers.

interview.q: A train/test split keeps 80% for training but the same user appears in both sets. What sampling detail was missed?
interview.answer: Sampling rows with replacement (or sampling rows when the unit is a user) splits a user's records across sets. Sample unique user ids without replacement and then select their rows.

defense.q: Defend seeding per experiment rather than once at import.
defense.answer: A global seed couples unrelated code: one extra draw shifts every later result. A per-experiment generator keeps runs independent and reproducible.

defense.q: Why do two generators with the same seed produce identical draws?
defense.answer: The seed initialises the same internal state and the same algorithm consumes it, so the sequence is deterministic.

defense.q: Defend sampling the test split without replacement.
defense.answer: A row appearing in both train and test leaks the answer and inflates the score. Sampling without replacement makes the split disjoint by construction.

defense.q: Defend fixed seeds in tests but varying seeds in training.
defense.answer: Tests need identical inputs to be meaningful, while training benefits from different sampling each run. Both follow from owning the generator explicitly.

defense.q: Explain why `shuffle` changes the caller's array.
defense.answer: It permutes in place, so every reference to that buffer sees the new order. Use `permutation` when a new array is wanted.

defense.q: Defend `choice` with probabilities for weighted sampling.
defense.answer: It states the weights directly and samples accordingly, instead of building a duplicated pool whose size can explode.

defense.q: Defend passing a generator as an argument instead of seeding globally.
defense.answer: The caller controls reproducibility without global side effects on other code.

defense.q: Explain why re-seeding inside a loop destroys randomness.
defense.answer: Every iteration restarts the same stream, so the draws repeat.

defense.q: Defend generating a permutation over shuffling in place.
defense.answer: The original order stays available for comparison and the input is left untouched.

modules.title: Linear Algebra
modules.goal: Multiply matrices, solve systems with solve instead of inv, and read determinant and eigenvalue output.

topics.title: Matrix multiplication
topics.body: The @ operator (and np.matmul) performs matrix multiplication, not elementwise multiplication; multiplying by an identity returns the same matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.eye(2)
print(A @ B)

topics.title: Solve instead of invert
topics.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is numerically safer and faster than computing inv(A) @ b.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([5., 10.])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))

topics.title: Determinant and eigenvalues
topics.body: det tells you whether a matrix is singular and eigvals returns the eigenvalues; for a diagonal matrix those eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 0.], [0., 3.]])
print(np.linalg.det(A), np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)

topics.title: dot product of two vectors is a scalar
topics.body: The @ operator on two 1-D arrays sums the pairwise products, so the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a @ b)

topics.title: matrix times vector keeps the rows
topics.body: A (2, 2) matrix times a (2,) vector returns one value per row, so the output length is the number of rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(A @ v)

topics.title: solve then verify
topics.body: solve returns the x in Ax = b directly; checking A @ x against b is how you prove the answer instead of trusting it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([3., 5.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x, np.allclose(A @ x, b))

topics.title: norm measures length
topics.body: np.linalg.norm gives the Euclidean length by default, so a (3, 4) vector reports 5.0 and needs no manual square root.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linalg.norm([3, 4]))

topics.title: lstsq also fits inconsistent systems
topics.body: When the system has no exact solution, lstsq returns the least-squares answer so a tall, over-determined fit still works.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])
b = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
x = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
print(np.allclose(A @ x, b))

topics.title: identity is the matrix version of one
topics.body: Multiplying by `np.identity(n)` leaves a matrix unchanged. It is the natural sanity check for a matmul pipeline.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]])
print(np.allclose(A @ np.identity(2), A))

topics.title: Transpose flips a matrix product
topics.body: `(A @ B).T` equals `B.T @ A.T`. The order swaps, which is the property behind many derivations.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
B = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
print(np.allclose((A @ B).T, B.T @ A.T))

topics.title: A zero determinant means no unique solution
topics.body: A singular matrix has linearly dependent rows, so `solve` cannot return one answer. Check the determinant before trusting a fit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.linalg.det(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]]))), 6))

topics.title: trace sums the diagonal
topics.body: The trace needs no square-matrix maths beyond the diagonal. It equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.trace(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])))

topics.title: Matrix multiplication with @
topics.body: The @ operator contracts the last axis of the left operand with the second-to-last of the right. Elementwise * is a different operation with a different result.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(a @ b)
print(a * b)

topics.title: Solve, do not invert
topics.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is more stable and faster than computing inv(A) @ b. Inversion also loses accuracy on ill-conditioned matrices.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
b = np.array([9.0, 8.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(a, b))
print(np.linalg.det(a))

lab.title: Matrix toolkit
lab.brief: For one matrix print determinant, inverse, rank and the product with its inverse.
milestones: Print A @ inv(A) rounded to 6 decimals

interviewBank.q: Why solve a linear system instead of multiplying by the inverse?
interviewBank.answer: `solve` factorises the matrix directly and is faster and more stable; forming an inverse adds rounding and does more work.

interviewBank.q: What does a zero determinant tell you?
interviewBank.answer: The matrix is singular: its rows are linearly dependent, so a system may have no solution or infinitely many.

interviewBank.q: When is a matrix ill-conditioned, and why does it matter?
interviewBank.answer: When its condition number is large, small input changes produce large output changes, so a solve can be numerically unreliable.

interviewBank.q: What shapes does `np.dot` require for matrices?
interviewBank.answer: The inner dimensions must match: `(m, k)` with `(k, n)` gives `(m, n)`.

interviewBank.q: Why is `@` preferred to `np.dot` for matrix products?
interviewBank.answer: It is the dedicated matrix operator, it reads like the maths, and it does not change meaning for higher-rank inputs the way `dot` does.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.linalg.norm` measure with no arguments?
interviewBank.answer: The Euclidean (Frobenius for matrices) norm, the square root of the sum of squares.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.linalg.solve` return?
interviewBank.answer: The vector or matrix x that satisfies `A x = b`.

interviewBank.q: How do you compute a matrix inverse safely?
interviewBank.answer: Usually you do not: solve the system instead, because the inverse adds error and work.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.trace` compute?
interviewBank.answer: The sum of the main diagonal.

interviewBank.q: A recommender scores 1000 users × 500 items by `user_vec @ item_matrix.T`. What are the shapes, and roughly how many multiplications?
interviewBank.answer: user_vec is (1000, k), item_matrix is (500, k), so the product is (1000, 500): 500,000 scores and 500,000×k multiplications. That is why k is kept small and why chunking matters at scale.

interviewBank.q: Someone solves a regression with `inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y` and gets a warning about a singular matrix. What should replace it?
interviewBank.answer: np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) (or solve on the normal equations only when well-conditioned). Inverting a near-singular matrix amplifies numerical error; lstsq is the stable, intended tool.

defenseBank.q: Defend least squares over the normal equations.
defenseBank.answer: Squaring the matrix doubles the condition number and loses precision. `lstsq` uses a factorisation that avoids forming `A.T @ A`.

defenseBank.q: Explain why computing an inverse then multiplying is worse in practice.
defenseBank.answer: It costs an extra factorisation, adds rounding from the inverse, and hides singularity detection that `solve` reports.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `cond` before trusting a solve in production.
defenseBank.answer: A large condition number predicts that the answer is sensitive to noise in the data, which is a property of the problem, not a bug you can fix afterwards.

defenseBank.q: Defend verifying a solve with `allclose` rather than equality.
defenseBank.answer: Floating-point factorisation introduces rounding, so exact equality fails even for a correct answer. A tolerance states the accuracy expected.

defenseBank.q: Explain why an identity matrix is used to test a multiplication.
defenseBank.answer: Multiplying by the identity must return the operand, so any deviation isolates a bug in the multiplication or the shape handling.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing a factorisation instead of an inverse.
defenseBank.answer: The factorisation is stable, can be reused for many right-hand sides, and never forms the numerically worse inverse.

defenseBank.q: Defend `lstsq` for an overdetermined system.
defenseBank.answer: It returns the least-squares solution instead of failing on inconsistent equations.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `matrix_power` with a negative exponent needs an invertible matrix.
defenseBank.answer: A negative power computes an inverse, which does not exist when the matrix is singular.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `matrix_rank` before solving a square system.
defenseBank.answer: A rank-deficient matrix has no unique solution, so a solve would be meaningless or unstable.

tasks.title: Inverse undoes a matrix
tasks.statement: Store `True` in `result` if `np.linalg.inv(np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]]))` multiplied by that matrix is the identity.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]])
result = np.allclose(np.linalg.inv(A) @ A, np.identity(2))
print(result)

learn.title: Matrix multiplication
learn.body: The @ operator (and np.matmul) performs matrix multiplication, not elementwise multiplication; multiplying by an identity returns the same matrix.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.eye(2)
print(A @ B)

learn.title: Solve instead of invert
learn.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is numerically safer and faster than computing inv(A) @ b.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([5., 10.])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))

learn.title: Determinant and eigenvalues
learn.body: det tells you whether a matrix is singular and eigvals returns the eigenvalues; for a diagonal matrix those eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 0.], [0., 3.]])
print(np.linalg.det(A), np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)

learn.title: dot product of two vectors is a scalar
learn.body: The @ operator on two 1-D arrays sums the pairwise products, so the result is a scalar rather than an array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a @ b)

learn.title: matrix times vector keeps the rows
learn.body: A (2, 2) matrix times a (2,) vector returns one value per row, so the output length is the number of rows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(A @ v)

learn.title: solve then verify
learn.body: solve returns the x in Ax = b directly; checking A @ x against b is how you prove the answer instead of trusting it.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([3., 5.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x, np.allclose(A @ x, b))

learn.title: norm measures length
learn.body: np.linalg.norm gives the Euclidean length by default, so a (3, 4) vector reports 5.0 and needs no manual square root.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linalg.norm([3, 4]))

learn.title: lstsq also fits inconsistent systems
learn.body: When the system has no exact solution, lstsq returns the least-squares answer so a tall, over-determined fit still works.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])
b = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
x = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
print(np.allclose(A @ x, b))

learn.title: identity is the matrix version of one
learn.body: Multiplying by `np.identity(n)` leaves a matrix unchanged. It is the natural sanity check for a matmul pipeline.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]])
print(np.allclose(A @ np.identity(2), A))

learn.title: Transpose flips a matrix product
learn.body: `(A @ B).T` equals `B.T @ A.T`. The order swaps, which is the property behind many derivations.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
B = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
print(np.allclose((A @ B).T, B.T @ A.T))

learn.title: A zero determinant means no unique solution
learn.body: A singular matrix has linearly dependent rows, so `solve` cannot return one answer. Check the determinant before trusting a fit.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.linalg.det(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]]))), 6))

learn.title: trace sums the diagonal
learn.body: The trace needs no square-matrix maths beyond the diagonal. It equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.trace(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])))

learn.title: Matrix multiplication with @
learn.body: The @ operator contracts the last axis of the left operand with the second-to-last of the right. Elementwise * is a different operation with a different result.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(a @ b)
print(a * b)

learn.title: Solve, do not invert
learn.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is more stable and faster than computing inv(A) @ b. Inversion also loses accuracy on ill-conditioned matrices.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
b = np.array([9.0, 8.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(a, b))
print(np.linalg.det(a))

interview.q: Why solve a linear system instead of multiplying by the inverse?
interview.answer: `solve` factorises the matrix directly and is faster and more stable; forming an inverse adds rounding and does more work.

interview.q: What does a zero determinant tell you?
interview.answer: The matrix is singular: its rows are linearly dependent, so a system may have no solution or infinitely many.

interview.q: When is a matrix ill-conditioned, and why does it matter?
interview.answer: When its condition number is large, small input changes produce large output changes, so a solve can be numerically unreliable.

interview.q: What shapes does `np.dot` require for matrices?
interview.answer: The inner dimensions must match: `(m, k)` with `(k, n)` gives `(m, n)`.

interview.q: Why is `@` preferred to `np.dot` for matrix products?
interview.answer: It is the dedicated matrix operator, it reads like the maths, and it does not change meaning for higher-rank inputs the way `dot` does.

interview.q: What does `np.linalg.norm` measure with no arguments?
interview.answer: The Euclidean (Frobenius for matrices) norm, the square root of the sum of squares.

interview.q: What does `np.linalg.solve` return?
interview.answer: The vector or matrix x that satisfies `A x = b`.

interview.q: How do you compute a matrix inverse safely?
interview.answer: Usually you do not: solve the system instead, because the inverse adds error and work.

interview.q: What does `np.trace` compute?
interview.answer: The sum of the main diagonal.

interview.q: A recommender scores 1000 users × 500 items by `user_vec @ item_matrix.T`. What are the shapes, and roughly how many multiplications?
interview.answer: user_vec is (1000, k), item_matrix is (500, k), so the product is (1000, 500): 500,000 scores and 500,000×k multiplications. That is why k is kept small and why chunking matters at scale.

interview.q: Someone solves a regression with `inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y` and gets a warning about a singular matrix. What should replace it?
interview.answer: np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) (or solve on the normal equations only when well-conditioned). Inverting a near-singular matrix amplifies numerical error; lstsq is the stable, intended tool.

defense.q: Defend least squares over the normal equations.
defense.answer: Squaring the matrix doubles the condition number and loses precision. `lstsq` uses a factorisation that avoids forming `A.T @ A`.

defense.q: Explain why computing an inverse then multiplying is worse in practice.
defense.answer: It costs an extra factorisation, adds rounding from the inverse, and hides singularity detection that `solve` reports.

defense.q: Defend checking `cond` before trusting a solve in production.
defense.answer: A large condition number predicts that the answer is sensitive to noise in the data, which is a property of the problem, not a bug you can fix afterwards.

defense.q: Defend verifying a solve with `allclose` rather than equality.
defense.answer: Floating-point factorisation introduces rounding, so exact equality fails even for a correct answer. A tolerance states the accuracy expected.

defense.q: Explain why an identity matrix is used to test a multiplication.
defense.answer: Multiplying by the identity must return the operand, so any deviation isolates a bug in the multiplication or the shape handling.

defense.q: Defend storing a factorisation instead of an inverse.
defense.answer: The factorisation is stable, can be reused for many right-hand sides, and never forms the numerically worse inverse.

defense.q: Defend `lstsq` for an overdetermined system.
defense.answer: It returns the least-squares solution instead of failing on inconsistent equations.

defense.q: Explain why `matrix_power` with a negative exponent needs an invertible matrix.
defense.answer: A negative power computes an inverse, which does not exist when the matrix is singular.

defense.q: Defend checking `matrix_rank` before solving a square system.
defense.answer: A rank-deficient matrix has no unique solution, so a solve would be meaningless or unstable.

modules.title: NumPy File Input and Output
modules.goal: Persist arrays with save/load, read text and CSV data, and pack several arrays into one NPZ file.

topics.title: save and load
topics.body: np.save writes the array's bytes and dtype to a .npy file and np.load reads them back exactly; the file is binary, so text editors show noise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.save('/tmp/a.npy', np.arange(3))
print(np.load('/tmp/a.npy'))

topics.title: Text and CSV round-trip
topics.body: savetxt writes human-readable numbers and loadtxt parses them back as floats, which is the portable option when another tool must read the file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savetxt('/tmp/a.txt', np.array([1, 2]))
print(np.loadtxt('/tmp/a.txt'))

topics.title: Several arrays in one NPZ
topics.body: savez stores named arrays in a single compressed-free archive and load returns a mapping whose keys are the names you gave.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savez('/tmp/a.npz', x=np.arange(2))
print(list(np.load('/tmp/a.npz').keys()))

topics.title: skiprows ignores a header line
topics.body: loadtxt has no header concept, so skiprows=1 is how a CSV header is dropped before the numbers are parsed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_head.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('x,y\n1,2\n3,4\n')
print(np.loadtxt(p, delimiter=',', skiprows=1))

topics.title: genfromtxt fills missing values
topics.body: genfromtxt tolerates gaps and puts nan where a value is absent, which is exactly what loadtxt would refuse to parse.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_gap.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('1,2\n3,\n')
print(np.genfromtxt(p, delimiter=','))

topics.title: npz stores several arrays
topics.body: savez writes named arrays into one archive and load exposes them by name through .files, so a whole dataset travels as a single file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_bundle.npz')
np.savez(p, a=np.arange(2), b=np.ones(3))
d = np.load(p)
print(sorted(d.files), d['a'])

topics.title: memmap reads without loading everything
topics.body: memmap maps a binary file onto an array shape, so a very large matrix can be indexed while only the touched pages come from disk.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_raw.bin')
np.arange(10, dtype='float64').tofile(p)
m = np.memmap(p, dtype='float64', mode='r', shape=(2, 5))
print(m.shape, m[1, 0])

topics.title: savetxt writes formatted text
topics.body: savetxt needs an explicit fmt or it falls back to float formatting, so an integer table is written with fmt='%d' and a delimiter you choose.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_out.csv')
np.savetxt(p, np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), delimiter=',', fmt='%d')
print(open(p).read().strip())

topics.title: Save one array and load it back
topics.body: `np.save` writes a binary `.npy` file and `np.load` restores the values and dtype exactly, with no parsing.
topics.code:
import os
import tempfile
import numpy as np

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_roundtrip.npy')
np.save(path, np.array([1, 2, 3]))
print(np.load(path))

topics.title: genfromtxt reads named columns
topics.body: `names=True` treats the first row as field names, turning a CSV into a structured array you index by name.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from io import StringIO

text = 'a,b\n1,2\n3,4'
data = np.genfromtxt(StringIO(text), delimiter=',', names=True)
print(data['a'].tolist())

topics.title: loadtxt skips comment lines
topics.body: Lines starting with `#` are ignored by default. Passing `dtype=int` keeps the numbers as integers instead of floats.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from io import StringIO

print(np.loadtxt(StringIO('# n\n1\n2\n'), dtype=int))

topics.title: An npz file exposes its arrays by key
topics.body: `np.savez` stores several named arrays in one archive. `np.load` returns a mapping-like object that lists those names.
topics.code:
import os
import tempfile
import numpy as np

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_keys.npz')
np.savez(path, a=np.arange(2), b=np.arange(3))
print(sorted(np.load(path)))

topics.title: save and load one array
topics.body: save writes a .npy file that keeps dtype and shape, and load reads it back exactly. Unlike CSV, no text conversion happens.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, tempfile, os
a = np.arange(4, dtype=np.float32)
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'a.npy')
np.save(p, a)
b = np.load(p)
print(b, b.dtype, b.shape)

topics.title: savez stores several arrays
topics.body: savez groups named arrays into one .npz archive, and load returns a mapping you index by name. Use savez_compressed for large, repetitive data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, tempfile, os
a, b = np.arange(3), np.ones((2, 2))
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'pack.npz')
np.savez(p, first=a, second=b)
z = np.load(p)
print(sorted(z.files), z['second'].shape)

lab.title: Numeric file round-trip
lab.brief: Write the same array as .npy and as .txt, then compare load speeds and dtypes.

interviewBank.q: When do you use `savez` instead of several `savetxt` calls?
interviewBank.answer: When the data is numeric and must round-trip exactly with its dtype and shape, and several arrays belong together in one file.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `.npy` over CSV for intermediate arrays?
interviewBank.answer: It stores dtype, shape and exact binary values, so loading is fast and lossless. CSV loses precision and needs parsing.

interviewBank.q: How do you read a CSV whose first row is a header?
interviewBank.answer: Use `loadtxt(..., skiprows=1)` for plain numbers, or `genfromtxt(..., names=True)` to keep the column names.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.save` add to the file name you give it?
interviewBank.answer: It appends `.npy` when the name does not already end in it, which is why a later `open` of the bare name fails.

interviewBank.q: How do you store several arrays in one file under names?
interviewBank.answer: Use `np.savez` or `np.savez_compressed` with keyword arguments, then read them back by key from the loaded archive.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.load` require `allow_pickle=False` on untrusted files?
interviewBank.answer: Pickled payloads can execute constructors, so loading becomes code execution. Array-only files need no pickle at all.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.savez` create?
interviewBank.answer: A `.npz` archive holding several named arrays.

interviewBank.q: How do you read one array out of an `.npz` file?
interviewBank.answer: `np.load(path)` returns a mapping; index it by key.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.loadtxt` slower than `np.load`?
interviewBank.answer: Text must be parsed and converted element by element, while binary values are read directly.

interviewBank.q: A pipeline writes intermediate arrays as CSV and reads them back; float precision changes. Why is .npy the better intermediate format?
interviewBank.answer: CSV stores decimal text, so floats round-trip through formatting and parsing. .npy stores dtype, shape and raw bytes, so the array comes back exactly.

interviewBank.q: A 5 GB feature matrix must be read without loading it all. What does np.memmap buy you, and what does it require?
interviewBank.answer: Memory mapping lets the OS page in the parts of the file you touch, so RAM use stays bounded. It requires the file to exist in the right format/dtype and the access pattern to be reasonably local.

defenseBank.q: Defend a binary format for intermediate pipeline stages.
defenseBank.answer: Intermediate data is read repeatedly and never inspected by hand, so exactness and speed matter more than legibility, and dtype survives the round trip.

defenseBank.q: Explain how text round-trips lose precision.
defenseBank.answer: A float is formatted with a limited number of digits, so values that are not exactly representable come back slightly different. Binary keeps the bits.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.load(..., allow_pickle=False)` for files you did not write.
defenseBank.answer: Unpickling executes arbitrary constructors, so a hostile `.npy` becomes code execution. Array-only files need no pickle.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing a checksum beside a saved array.
defenseBank.answer: Binary corruption is silent until the numbers are wrong, so a checksum turns a bad file into a clear failure at load time.

defenseBank.q: Explain why CSV is a poor intermediate format.
defenseBank.answer: It loses dtype and exact precision, costs parsing time, and cannot represent several arrays in one file without conventions.

defenseBank.q: Defend `usecols` when reading a wide CSV.
defenseBank.answer: Reading only the needed columns saves both parse time and memory, and it documents which fields the pipeline actually depends on.

defenseBank.q: Defend a binary format for large arrays moving between stages.
defenseBank.answer: It is exact and fast and preserves dtype and shape, unlike text.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a relative path can break a saved script.
defenseBank.answer: The working directory differs from the one where the file was written.

defenseBank.q: Defend `usecols` for a wide table you only partly need.
defenseBank.answer: It avoids parsing and holding columns that would be discarded.

learn.title: save and load
learn.body: np.save writes the array's bytes and dtype to a .npy file and np.load reads them back exactly; the file is binary, so text editors show noise.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
np.save('/tmp/a.npy', np.arange(3))
print(np.load('/tmp/a.npy'))

learn.title: Text and CSV round-trip
learn.body: savetxt writes human-readable numbers and loadtxt parses them back as floats, which is the portable option when another tool must read the file.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
np.savetxt('/tmp/a.txt', np.array([1, 2]))
print(np.loadtxt('/tmp/a.txt'))

learn.title: Several arrays in one NPZ
learn.body: savez stores named arrays in a single compressed-free archive and load returns a mapping whose keys are the names you gave.
learn.code:

np.savez('/tmp/a.npz', x=np.arange(2))
print(list(np.load('/tmp/a.npz').keys()))

learn.title: skiprows ignores a header line
learn.body: loadtxt has no header concept, so skiprows=1 is how a CSV header is dropped before the numbers are parsed.
learn.code:

open(p, 'w').write('x,y\n1,2\n3,4\n')
print(np.loadtxt(p, delimiter=',', skiprows=1))

learn.title: genfromtxt fills missing values
learn.body: genfromtxt tolerates gaps and puts nan where a value is absent, which is exactly what loadtxt would refuse to parse.
learn.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_gap.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('1,2\n3,\n')
print(np.genfromtxt(p, delimiter=','))

learn.title: npz stores several arrays
learn.body: savez writes named arrays into one archive and load exposes them by name through .files, so a whole dataset travels as a single file.
learn.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_bundle.npz')
np.savez(p, a=np.arange(2), b=np.ones(3))
d = np.load(p)
print(sorted(d.files), d['a'])

learn.title: memmap reads without loading everything
learn.body: memmap maps a binary file onto an array shape, so a very large matrix can be indexed while only the touched pages come from disk.
learn.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_raw.bin')
np.arange(10, dtype='float64').tofile(p)
m = np.memmap(p, dtype='float64', mode='r', shape=(2, 5))
print(m.shape, m[1, 0])

learn.title: savetxt writes formatted text

interview.q: When do you use `savez` instead of several `savetxt` calls?
interview.answer: When the data is numeric and must round-trip exactly with its dtype and shape, and several arrays belong together in one file.

interview.q: Why prefer `.npy` over CSV for intermediate arrays?
interview.answer: It stores dtype, shape and exact binary values, so loading is fast and lossless. CSV loses precision and needs parsing.

interview.q: How do you read a CSV whose first row is a header?
interview.answer: Use `loadtxt(..., skiprows=1)` for plain numbers, or `genfromtxt(..., names=True)` to keep the column names.

interview.q: What does `np.save` add to the file name you give it?
interview.answer: It appends `.npy` when the name does not already end in it, which is why a later `open` of the bare name fails.

interview.q: How do you store several arrays in one file under names?
interview.answer: Use `np.savez` or `np.savez_compressed` with keyword arguments, then read them back by key from the loaded archive.

interview.q: Why does `np.load` require `allow_pickle=False` on untrusted files?
interview.answer: Pickled payloads can execute constructors, so loading becomes code execution. Array-only files need no pickle at all.

interview.q: What does `np.savez` create?
interview.answer: A `.npz` archive holding several named arrays.

interview.q: How do you read one array out of an `.npz` file?
interview.answer: `np.load(path)` returns a mapping; index it by key.

interview.q: Why is `np.loadtxt` slower than `np.load`?
interview.answer: Text must be parsed and converted element by element, while binary values are read directly.

interview.q: A pipeline writes intermediate arrays as CSV and reads them back; float precision changes. Why is .npy the better intermediate format?
interview.answer: CSV stores decimal text, so floats round-trip through formatting and parsing. .npy stores dtype, shape and raw bytes, so the array comes back exactly.

interview.q: A 5 GB feature matrix must be read without loading it all. What does np.memmap buy you, and what does it require?
interview.answer: Memory mapping lets the OS page in the parts of the file you touch, so RAM use stays bounded. It requires the file to exist in the right format/dtype and the access pattern to be reasonably local.
